# openDemocracy
> openDemocracy is an independent international media platform covering news, ideas and culture which seeks to challenge power and encourage democratic debate.
Public Ghost content for AI and LLM tooling. Use `/llms-full.txt` for consolidated page and post context.
Append `.md` to any post or page URL to get the content in Markdown (for example, `/example-post.md`).

## Pages

## Posts
- [Minister invited Euan Blair to BlackRock meeting as his firm sought investment](https://www.opendemocracy.net/blackrock-meeting-euan-blair-government-tony-hakluyt-secret-peter-kyle-jonathan-reynolds.md) - Secretive event was organised after another minister met BlackRock boss at undeclared party that may have breached rules
- [Two kinds of petrostate sank COP31. Only one is getting the blame](https://www.opendemocracy.net/cop31-petrostate-sank-cop31-united-kingdom-european-union-africa-saudi-arabia-russia.md) - As Russia and Saudi Arabia came under fire, the likes of the EU and UK quietly took a ‘do as I say, not as I do’ position
- [Fortress Europe: Inside the Shadow War on Asylum Seekers](https://www.opendemocracy.net/podcasts/fortress-europe-inside-the-shadow-war-on-asylum-seekers.md) - Writer and researcher Nathan Akehurst joins In Solidarity to trace how aid budgets, Big Tech, and Libyan militias have been fused into a lucrative border industry.
- [Proposed immigration rules risk safety of survivors of rape as weapon of war](https://www.opendemocracy.net/proposed-immigration-rules-risk-safety-of-survivors-of-rape-as-weapon-of-war.md) - Survivors of sexual violence can take years to disclose their trauma. Why is the Home Office ignoring that?
- [Domestic abuse victims ending up behind bars, report finds](https://www.opendemocracy.net/domestic-abuse-victims-ending-up-behind-bars-report-finds.md) - Two-thirds of women in prison in England say domestic abuse played a role in their offending, new data shows
- [Surviving Orbán’s Playbook: Dr. Maja Nenadović on Hungary, Identity, and How to Actually Talk Across Divides](https://www.opendemocracy.net/podcasts/surviving-orbans-playbook-dr-maja-nenadovic-on-hungary-identity-and-how-to-actually-talk-across-divides.md) - After 20 years of training champion debaters across more than 40 countries, civic educator Dr. Maja Nenadović realised her favourite skill was actively making polarisation worse.
- [The trap of radical rhetoric: lessons for Burnham from Spain](https://www.opendemocracy.net/lessons-andy-burnham-spain-election-sanchez-housing-crisis.md) - Spain’s election and housing crisis offer stark warning: technocratic half-measures will open the door to the far right
- [From Secular Activism to Bishop of Croydon: Why Rosemarie Mallett Changed Her Mind on the Church](https://www.opendemocracy.net/podcasts/from-secular-activism-to-bishop-of-croydon-why-rosemarie-mallett-changed-her-mind-on-the-church.md) - In this special live edition of Change My Mind, recorded at the historic Union Chapel in London and hosted in partnership with Place for Hope, Ali Goldsworthy and Laura Osborne sit down with two extraordinary guests: Bishop Rosemarie Mallett and Aman Sethi.
- [Microsoft is a macro problem, Milburn Review + why Lula won](https://www.opendemocracy.net/weekly-email-211126.md) - openDemocracy Weekly Newsletter 21 November 2026
- [How a security scare at RAF Fairford upended US air strategy](https://www.opendemocracy.net/raf-fairford-security-scare-iran-upended-us-air-strategy.md) - As two men face trial next year over alleged Iranian plot, US has quietly pulled its bombers and tankers from Britain
- [I study mass protests: Here’s why GenZ has taken to the streets](https://www.opendemocracy.net/i-study-mass-protests-heres-why-genz-has-taken-to-the-streets.md) - The broligarchs want us to focus on immigration, but young people around the world know where the blame truly lies.
- [Microsoft outage raises questions over UK’s critical digital infrastructure](https://www.opendemocracy.net/microsoft-outage-raises-questions-over-uks-critical-digital-infrastructure.md) - A global failure crippled NHS trusts, courts, and police – exposing the risks of Britain’s US tech dependence
- [Young women aren’t ‘inactive’ – they’re locked out of secure work](https://www.opendemocracy.net/milburn-review-young-women-locked-out-of-work-childcare-mental-health.md) - The Milburn Review overlooks how gender shapes barriers to work. Ministers can’t afford to make the same mistake
- [Scrapping PIP for young adults risks pushing unpaid carers into poverty](https://www.opendemocracy.net/milburn-review-scrapping-pip-young-adults-risks-pushing-unpaid-carers-into-poverty.md) - The Milburn Review aims to get young people working – but charities say its cuts could have far-reaching knock-on effects
- [As winter closes in on Gaza, the UK must offer Palestinians a route to safety](https://www.opendemocracy.net/flooding-gaza-uk-government-burnham-offer-palestinians-asylum-route.md) - With more than 225,000 people affected by severe flooding, Burnham’s government must act on its promise to help
- [How Lula Beat the Far Right: Pedro Rossi on Brazil's Economic Strategy and the Fight for a New Economy](https://www.opendemocracy.net/podcasts/how-lula-beat-the-far-right-pedro-rossi-on-brazils-economic-strategy-and-the-fight-for-a-new-economy.md) - Ahead of Brazil's last election, it seemed the resurgent far-right was unstoppable. But Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva pulled off an unprecedented comeback.
- [‘Will it be settled before I die?’: Miners seek urgent fix to pension promise](https://www.opendemocracy.net/will-it-be-settled-before-i-die-miners-seek-urgent-fix-to-pension-promise.md) - Labour MPs in Coalfield constituencies threaten Burnham’s first Commons rebellion over delay to miners’ pension payout
- [What Morgan McSweeney Did Next](https://www.opendemocracy.net/weekly-email-141126.md) - openDemocracy Weekly Newsletter 14 November 2026
- [‘Coining it in the City’: What Starmer’s Aides Did Next](https://www.opendemocracy.net/coining-it-in-the-city-what-starmers-aides-did-next.md) - After failing to ‘clean up politics’ as promised, top Starmer advisers have set up advisory firms that experts warn can exploit Lobbying Act loopholes
- [The Right Words in the Right Order](https://www.opendemocracy.net/the-right-words-in-the-right-order.md) - Cultural elites and educators of the Global North are now in an advanced state of panic surrounding reading, literacy, and the humanities generally.
- ["More like Putin in his soul": Trump, Ukraine's Drone War, and Russia's Sabotage in the UK](https://www.opendemocracy.net/podcasts/more-like-putin-in-his-soul-trump-ukraines-drone-war-and-russias-sabotage-in-the-uk.md) - Sian Norris on her fifth reporting trip to the frontlines of Kharkiv and the streets of Kyiv.
- [Is it time to break up the UK?](https://www.opendemocracy.net/is-it-time-to-break-up-the-uk.md) - Being Scottish, or for that matter Welsh, often feels a bit like you're sitting in the passenger seat of a car with a driver who's having a nervous breakdown.
- [Flatlining emissions won’t save us from climate crisis – and neither will COP31](https://www.opendemocracy.net/cop31-flatlining-emissions-wont-save-us-from-climate-crisis.md) - While recent election wins and COP31 offer some optimism, they mask a bleak reality. What will it take for real change?
- [Seeking justice for abuse shouldn’t require bravery](https://www.opendemocracy.net/russell-brand-seeking-justice-for-abuse-shouldnt-require-bravery.md) - Police promise compassion after Russell Brand’s sentencing, yet the justice system still re-traumatises survivors
- [The UK must back global bans on AI weapons – before it’s too late](https://www.opendemocracy.net/the-uk-must-back-global-bans-on-ai-weapons-before-its-too-late.md) - New research shows military AI begins poisoning the planet long before it reaches the battlefield
- [It takes a village to ‘Abolish Westminster’](https://www.opendemocracy.net/abolish-westminster-adam-ramsay-book.md) - openDemocracy contributor Adam Ramsay revisits the people and conversations that led to new book on fixing UK democracy
- [The Illusion of Neutral Technology: Dr. Kate Devlin on AI Intimacy, Hidden Harms, and the Scientific Method](https://www.opendemocracy.net/podcasts/the-illusion-of-neutral-technology-dr-kate-devlin-on-ai-intimacy-hidden-harms-and-the-scientific-method.md) - As AI companions skyrocket in popularity and Silicon Valley tightens its grip on the tools shaping our future, are we losing our grip on human connection or just finding new ways to cope?
- [Donald’s done, Rise of the Robots, Google and Gaza](https://www.opendemocracy.net/weekly-email-071126.md) - openDemocracy Weekly Newsletter 07 November 2026
- [Abolish Westminster | With Adam Ramsay](https://www.opendemocracy.net/podcasts/abolish-westminster-with-adam-ramsay.md) - From Andy Burnham’s northern devolution to the electoral rise of Reform, Britain's political consensus is coming apart at the seams. Longtime openDemocracy contributor Adam Ramsay joins Aman to discuss his book Abolish Westminster
- [Ten days of elections around the world may shape future of climate debate](https://www.opendemocracy.net/ten-days-of-elections-around-the-world-may-shape-future-of-climate-debate.md) - From the US to Brazil, Israel and Serbia, the far right have been delivered a number of mammoth blows
- [How a tech start-up lobbied to put delivery robots on UK pavements, and won](https://www.opendemocracy.net/starship-technologies-delivery-robots-uk-pavements-silicon-valley-lobbying.md) - Revealed: Ministers allowed our streets to become ‘test ground’ for robots amid lobbying from Starship Technologies
- [Lula Won. The Markets Want a Third Round](https://www.opendemocracy.net/lula-won-the-markets-want-a-third-round.md) - Brazil’s voters rejected austerity, and its candidate fled to Florida. The markets that backed him stayed, and Lula’s finance minister has begun to give them what the ballot box refused. In Britain, the script is familiar.
- [‘Nice face of the devil’: Google whistleblower on AI, Gaza, and breaking NDA](https://www.opendemocracy.net/nice-face-of-the-devil-google-whistleblower-on-ai-gaza-and-breaking-nda.md) - Sofia Liguori tells openDemocracy about Project Nimbus and resignation that led to Google U-turn on silencing ex-staff
- [MPs willing to rebel if Treasury doesn’t keep new miners’ pension promise](https://www.opendemocracy.net/mps-willing-to-rebel-if-treasury-doesnt-keep-new-miners-pension-promise.md) - A blunder led John Healey to drop vow to release £1.2bn to former miners from last week's Budget, openDemocracy understands
- [A trilogy of John Berger pieces on the centenary of his birth](https://www.opendemocracy.net/a-trilogy-of-john-berger-pieces-on-the-centenary-of-his-birth.md) - openDemocracy co-founder Anthony Barnett remembers friend and contributor, John Berger
- [Did Burnham’s Budget meet the moment?](https://www.opendemocracy.net/weekly-email-311026.md) - openDemocracy Weekly Newsletter 31 October 2026
- [‘Blindsided’ Burnham ‘furious’ as Treasury U-turns on miners’ pension boost](https://www.opendemocracy.net/burnham-furious-u-turn-miners-pensions-healey-budget-treasury.md) - PM ‘clashed’ with Healey over 11th-hour decision that may mean thousands of ex-miners never see promised cash
- [Advertising industry must stop funding online hate, whistleblowing execs warn](https://www.opendemocracy.net/youtube-google-advertising-must-stop-funding-online-hate-whistleblowers-warn.md) - ‘We’re partially responsible,’ ad insiders tell openDemocracy, as report finds YouTube makes millions on hate speech
- [Big talk, small promises: Experts’ verdict on ‘underwhelming’ Budget](https://www.opendemocracy.net/budget-burnham-john-healey-experts-verdict-big-talk-small-promises.md) - Academics, politicians, and campaigners tell openDemocracy of disappointment in the Burnham government’s first Budget
- [Burnham promised a much-needed rupture. Healey delivered gentle tinkering](https://www.opendemocracy.net/budget-burnham-promised-rupture-neoliberalism-healey-delivered-gentle-tinkering.md) - Mild bank levies and one-off handouts won’t undo decades of damage to places like Makerfield
- [Abuse victims arrested by UK police](https://www.opendemocracy.net/weekly-email-241026.md) - openDemocracy Weekly Newsletter 24 October 2026
- [Inside the Israeli military mindset driving endless war](https://www.opendemocracy.net/israel-election-netanyahu-eisenkot-military-driving-endless-war-gaza-palestine-lebanon.md) - For Israel’s generals, peace is merely a bargaining chip – an outlook that will outlast whoever wins next week’s election
- [La IA de Amazon contra los sindicatos](https://www.opendemocracy.net/la-ia-de-amazon-contra-los-sindicatos.md) - Newsletter semanal correspondiente al 23 de octubre de 2026
- [Something is changing in Spain – and tenants are leading the way](https://www.opendemocracy.net/something-is-changing-in-spain-and-tenants-are-leading-the-way.md) - One woman’s tragic fight to save her home sparked a nationwide challenge to the idea that we should settle for survival
- [‘Nosotros, los pueblos’: la ONU necesita una líder para la gente, no para las superpotencias](https://www.opendemocracy.net/es/onu-secretaria-general-mujer-latinoamericana-independencia-sociedad-civil.md) - Una latinoamericana podría encabezar la ONU por primera vez en 80 años, pero para no heredar un cascarón vacío debe blindar su independencia con un mandato único y poder real a la sociedad civil
- [Amazon usa la IA para impedir que sus trabajadores se sindicalicen](https://www.opendemocracy.net/es/amazon-trabajadores-ia-sindicalizacion-vigilancia-control-derechos.md) - Documentos internos indican que Amazon recopila ‘cientos de puntos de datos’ para alimentar una IA ‘antisindicatos’ en Estados Unidos, Canadá y el Reino Unido
- [They were victims of domestic abuse. They ended up under arrest](https://www.opendemocracy.net/domestic-abuse-victims-arrested-policing-prisons-injustice.md) - Exclusive: hundreds of domestic abuse victims arrested for crimes committed under coercion or duress, but figures are tip of the iceberg
- [Brazil election: Trump’s ‘Donroe Doctrine’ faces its most decisive test yet](https://www.opendemocracy.net/brazil-us-bolsonaro-trump-monroe-doctrine-coercion-tariffs-terrorism.md) - White House seeks Bolsonaro win to ensure access to oil and microchips – and isolate American continent from China
- [Periodismo en México: Anatomía de un silencio](https://www.opendemocracy.net/es/mexico-periodismo-asesinatos-persecucion-crimen-organizado-gobierno-censura-silencio.md) - Periodistas de México hablan de cómo lidian con la presión del crimen organizado y de funcionarios públicos, y explican cómo algunas zonas se han convertido en desiertos informativos
- [Latin America is the first target in Trump's global plan. It won't be the last](https://www.opendemocracy.net/project-2025-trump-heritage-foundation-latin-america-argentina-chile-far-right.md) - From Chile to Peru, far-right leaders are adopting Project 2025 policies to dismantle democracy and social rights
- [Amazon’s AI ‘union-busting’](https://www.opendemocracy.net/weekly-email-171026.md) - openDemocracy Weekly Newsletter 17 October 2026
- [Amazon uses AI surveillance to monitor union risk in UK warehouses](https://www.opendemocracy.net/amazon-ai-surveillance-monitor-union-activity-uk-warehouses-birmingham-coventry-atlas-sutton-coldfield.md) - Internal documents suggest tech giant collects ‘hundreds of data points’ for ‘union-busting’ AI model
- [Donald Trump just gave Putin the advantage in Ukraine](https://www.opendemocracy.net/donald-trump-just-gave-putin-the-advantage-in-ukraine.md) - By lifting sanctions on Russian diesel, the US president dooms Ukrainians to a brutal winter in a violent, endless war
- [Brasil: Flávio, el ‘moderado’ del clan Bolsonaro, capitaliza el desgaste de Lula](https://www.opendemocracy.net/es/brasil-lula-dinastia-bolsonaro-democracia-ultraderecha.md) - La sucesión dinástica del expresidente Jair Bolsonaro parece lista para impedir una cuarta presidencia de Lula en Brasil
- [The UK government is hiding crucial climate data – so I’m taking it to court](https://www.opendemocracy.net/the-uk-government-is-hiding-crucial-climate-data-so-im-taking-it-to-court.md) - I’m seeking a judicial review over ministers’ failure to release information on the climate crisis and river pollution
- [Gaza, Green Party, AI Super-intelligence, Abuse in the Military](https://www.opendemocracy.net/weekly-email-101026.md) - openDemocracy Weekly Newsletter 10 October 2026
- [Legal loophole denies justice to child abuse victims in British Army school](https://www.opendemocracy.net/british-army-justice-failed-child-abuse-mod.md) - Exclusive: Questions over whether alleged abuse fell under military police’s jurisdiction is "travesty of justice"
- [La ‘Doctrina Donroe’ en Brasil, Gaza y Maricarmen](https://www.opendemocracy.net/trump-doctrina-donroe-brasil-gaza-maricarmen.md) - Newsletter semanal correspondiente al 9 de octubre de 2026
- [La devastadora simplicidad del genocidio en Gaza](https://www.opendemocracy.net/es/gaza-israel-palestina-genocidio-hamas-7-octubre-netanyahu-terrorismo.md) - Quienes defienden a Israel insisten en que la opresión y la matanza masiva de palestinos son una respuesta legítima al complejo pasado de la región. No lo son
- [Brasil, última batalla de Trump por imponer su doctrina imperial en América Latina](https://www.opendemocracy.net/es/brasil-eeuu-bolsonaro-trump-doctrina-monroe-coaccion-aranceles-terrorismo.md) - La ‘Doctrina Donroe’ de Trump se basa en el petróleo, los chips y un continente americano aislado de China. ¿Funcionará en Brasil?
- [The devastating simplicity of the genocide in Gaza](https://www.opendemocracy.net/the-devastating-simplicity-of-the-genocide-in-gaza.md) - Israel’s supporters insist that the country’s oppression and mass killings of Palestinians is a legitimate response to the region’s complicated past. It isn’t.
- [How the Greens are forcing Labour’s hand on Gaza](https://www.opendemocracy.net/how-the-greens-are-forcing-labours-hand-on-gaza.md) - The Green Party’s ‘Zionism is Racism’ motion proves that uncompromising left-wing pressure is successfully shifting Labour’s stance on Gaza.
- [Con 94 años, Margaret Owen está orgullosa de haber ido presa por Gaza](https://www.opendemocracy.net/es/margaret-owen-veterana-arrestada-protesta-gaza-palestina-reino-unido.md) - La abogada, detenida en Reino Unido por apoyar a Palestine Action, ve un ‘pequeño rayo de luz’ en el Partido Laborista y exige que se escuche a las viudas de Gaza
- [At 94, Margaret Owen was proud to be arrested for Gaza](https://www.opendemocracy.net/at-94-margaret-owen-was-proud-to-be-arrested-for-gaza.md) - Fresh from her arrest at 94, veteran human rights lawyer Margaret Owen reflects on the criminalisation of protest and why Gaza’s widows must shape its future.
- [Polanski’s Greens created prime minister Burnham. Holborn could yet undo him](https://www.opendemocracy.net/polanskis-greens-created-prime-minister-burnham-holborn-could-yet-undo-him.md) - Labour is celebrating the by-election result, but it must not misread a tight win for a total victory
- [Did Iranian drones drive US bombers out of RAF Fairford?](https://www.opendemocracy.net/did-iranian-drones-drive-us-bombers-out-of-raf-fairford.md) - Trump seemed set to expand war on Iran. So why the hasty retreat from the UK? And what does it mean for the conflict?
- [UK wants to lead the world on frontier AI safety. It can't decide where to start](https://www.opendemocracy.net/uk-wants-to-lead-the-world-on-frontier-ai-safety-it-cant-decide-where-to-start.md) - The UK government is positioning itself as a global leader on AI regulation while struggling to agree on how far rules should go — and what risks they should address.
- [Trump, los sobornos rusos y el partido británico Reform](https://www.opendemocracy.net/es/trump-activo-ruso-reform-farage-luke-harding.md) - El primer periodista occidental expulsado de Moscú tras la caída de la Unión Soviética, Luke Harding, analiza a Trump, la guerra en Ucrania y un caso de sobornos rusos en el Reino Unido
- [Trump, Russian bribes, and Reform: What really happened?](https://www.opendemocracy.net/trump-russia-asset-reform-farage-luke-harding-ukraine-war-putin-nathan-gill-bribes.md) - Foreign correspondent Luke Harding tells openDemocracy what he’s learnt from two decades of reporting on Russia
- [Trump, Putin and the  Betrayal of Ukraine](https://www.opendemocracy.net/podcasts/trump-putin-and-the-betrayal-of-ukraine.md) - Luke Harding on Putin’s war, Biden’s hesitancy, Trump acting as a Russian asset, and Kremlin links to Brexit and Britain’s hard right.
- [The next Venezuela? How a US pressure campaign threatens Brazil’s democracy](https://www.opendemocracy.net/brazil-us-lula-bolsonaro-trump-delcy-venezuela-democracy-interference.md) - As Brazilians prepare to elect a new president, the country’s sovereignty hangs in the balance
- [‘The tide is turning’: Palestine solidarity’s impact on British politics](https://www.opendemocracy.net/the-tide-is-turning-palestine-solidaritys-impact-on-british-politics.md) - British Palestinian Committee director on what divestment and electoral pressure have achieved – and where work remains
- [Un desalojo empuja a España a elecciones anticipadas](https://www.opendemocracy.net/es/espana-vivienda-digna-especulacion-desalojo-maricarmen-pedro-sanchez-elecciones-derecho-fondos-buitre.md) - Hace 12 días, Maricarmen Abascal fue desalojada por la fuerza de su casa en Madrid. Las consecuencias pueden cambiar la política de ese país
- [How one eviction pushed Spain to a snap election](https://www.opendemocracy.net/spain-one-eviction-snap-election-maricarmen-abascal-pedro-sanchez.md) - Ten days ago, an 87-year-old woman was forcibly removed from her home. The fallout may shape national politics
- [Who really owns Burnham's Labour?](https://www.opendemocracy.net/weekly-email-031026.md) - openDemocracy Weekly Newsletter 03 October 2026
- [Trump y Brasil: ‘Interferencia crítica’](https://www.opendemocracy.net/trump-y-brasil-interferencia-critica.md) - Newsletter semanal correspondiente al 2 de octubre de 2026

# openDemocracy
> openDemocracy is an independent international media platform covering news, ideas and culture which seeks to challenge power and encourage democratic debate.
Public Ghost content for AI and LLM tooling. This file includes a bounded export of public pages first, then recent public posts.
Append `.md` to any post or page URL to get the content in Markdown (for example, `/example-post.md`).
## Pages
### About Us
URL: https://www.opendemocracy.net/about/
Last updated: 2026-11-10T14:25:18.000Z
openDemocracy is an independent, international media organisation headquartered in London. We produce investigative and movement-focused journalism in English and Spanish at the nexus of gender, geopolitics, migration, technology and rights. 

openDemocracy has operated at this intersection for more than 25 years and we reach a highly engaged global audience of activists, policymakers, academics and civic leaders through our digital platforms and newsletters, offering a rich diversity of stories and perspectives from across the world. Contributors to openDemocracy include senior political leaders, policy advisers, academics, technologists and cultural figures, reflecting our role as a trusted platform for democratic debate.

Our work is regularly amplified through syndication and co-publishing partnerships with major global outlets and regional newsrooms. These include: AFP, Al Jazeera, BBC News, BBC World Service, Channel 4 News, Daily Express, Daily Mail, Daily Mirror, El País, Financial Times, Forbes, Globo, LBC, Metro, People, Perfil, PM (BBC Radio 4), Politics Live (BBC Two), Sky News, The Guardian, The Herald, the i, The Independent, The New Statesman, The New York Times, The Observer, The Sun, The Sunday Times, The Telegraph, The Times, The Washington Post, The Week, Univision, UOL and Yahoo! News/Noticias.

openDemocracy’s journalism consistently drives real-world change and our investigations have helped change laws, trigger official investigations and strengthen accountability worldwide.

openDemocracy.net is published by openDemocracy Limited, a UK-registered company (#3855274) wholly owned by the non-profit openDemocracy Foundation for the Advancement of Global Education (company limited by guarantee #04807614).

## **Writing for openDemocracy**

openDemocracy is an independent global media organisation.

Through reporting and analysis of social and political issues, we seek to educate citizens to challenge power and encourage democratic debate across the world.

We publish written and multimedia content primarily covering the UK, Africa and Latin America, in English, Spanish and Portuguese. Experienced journalists write most of it, but if you have something important to say, and can say it well, we want to hear from you.

We especially want to hear from members of groups that are ignored or under-represented in the media as a whole.

## **How to do it**

Send us a pitch (a short proposal for the piece you want to write). Keep it short and to the point – a few lines is plenty.

Please familiarise yourself with our content. It is useful to check previous coverage of the topic you are addressing, so your proposal complements rather than duplicates it.

If we want to accept your pitch, one of our editors will email you to explain what happens next. If you send a pitch relating to an area outside of the UK, Africa or Latin America it is unlikely we will be able to accept.

We regret that we cannot respond individually to all the pitches we get. If we are interested in taking your idea further, we aim to respond within three UK working days.

If you don’t hear from us, though, don’t lose heart! It doesn’t mean your pitch was bad – it may just be that we didn’t have the capacity to take it on.

Please tell us if you have published a similar article elsewhere, either on the web or in print, providing links if possible.

Do not submit anything written entirely with an AI tool. If you do use generative AI or related tools to create any portion of your submission, that must be cited like any other source.

If you are responding to an article published on our site, please consider posting your response as a comment on the article itself.

## **Copyright & syndication**

When openDemocracy has paid for an article to be written, we own the copyright. When no money has changed hands, copyright remains with the author.

To assure our writers gain as much exposure as possible around the world, openDemocracy has adopted a [**Creative Commons licence**](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/4.0/?ref=opendemocracy.net) for much of its content.

openDemocracy assumes the right to syndicate your writing. Any revenue generated is shared equally between openDemocracy and the author.

We further assume the right to include your work in other republication agreements, such those with academic institutions and in printed journal publications.

## **Requests to authors**

If openDemocracy has published your work and another publication or website approaches you wishing to republish it, please ask them to send an email to syndication@opendemocracy.net so that we can negotiate fees and handle administration.

## **What our authors say**

“Thank you for what you are doing, as a feminist journalist who often finds journalistic spaces really intimidating and exclusionary, because of how they are dominated by patriarchal ideas and masculinity. It’s such a breath of fresh air to even hear about the idea of feminist investigative journalism.” **2018 journalism fellow**

“It really means a lot especially given this is the first time I've written something like this and published it… I really appreciate being given the opportunity to hold space for my voice :)” **First time (activist) writer**

"Writing for openDemocracy gives me a remarkable opportunity to provide contemporary analysis on security issues for many thousands of informed people across the world.

"I find it hugely satisfying because it goes far beyond the readerships that most academics can reach. It is a demanding process and means that you really have to be on top of your subject, but the reward of being able to engage with opinion formers, journalists, teachers, students and many others more than compensates for that." **Paul Rogers, Professor of Peace Studies at Bradford University**

“I found openDemocracy by chance, and corny as it sounds they’ve transformed my writing life. Their willingness to put in the extra work editing helps me shape my precious but convoluted articles into something readable.” **Deborah Padfield (Citizens Advice Bureau adviser, Cambridge)**

“The effects \[of publishing my article on openDemocracy\] were quite significant: I was invited to meet government ministers, including a cabinet minister, as well as the Trades Union Congress.” **Carlota Perez, honorary professor at the Institute for Innovation and Public Purpose at University College London**

"I write for openDemocracy for the same reasons I read it: its internationalism, its rigour of thought and the astonishing wealth of wisdom and debate in its pages. Writing for such a challenging audience and in the company of such excellent writers has a way of pulling your best work from you.

"As a hack, writing for openDemocracy has two juicy advantages. The first is that it is very difficult to persuade the news editor of a British tabloid to take 1,000 words on the injustices of global trade rules. Secondly (and this is not for the faint-hearted), the readers do not suffer fools gladly, if at all." **Tom Burgis, journalist, now at the Financial Times**

## **Data protection**

openDemocracy never gives out email addresses or other contact details of any of the authors we publish.

Our policy when approached for author contact is to forward the request to the author.

We ask that you provide us with contact details that reflect the often very short lead-in times of online media. If you do not check your emails regularly, please provide us with a telephone number.

## Final step

Email your pitch to editors@opendemocracy.net

## *At openDemocracy, we are…*

**Accountable**  
We always seek to act ethically and with integrity. We’re publicly transparent about our aims, funding and affiliations. If we make mistakes, we take responsibility and learn from them.

**Independent**  
We are not beholden to any faction or vested interest. We encourage rebellious, creative, independent thinking.

**Excellent**  
We always strive to do journalism that is accurate, evidence-based and compelling. We set ourselves high standards, and we continually ask if we are being ambitious enough.

**Agile**  
We seek to be nimble and innovative in a fast-changing world.

**Collaborative**  
We’re part of a global independent media ecosystem that we want to support and grow. Wherever possible, we prioritise collaboration over competition. We value working with and learning from others who share our goals.

**Pluralist**  
We value diversity of perspective, culture and lived experience. We resist groupthink and we encourage debate. We are plural but not neutral: we call out injustice and oppression – but we listen to competing ideas about how to address them.

**Intersectional**  
We are feminist, anti-racist, we challenge all forms of unjust power or discrimination. And we invest in leadership, training, mentoring and learning from underrepresented groups – because if we change the media, we change the debate.

## **Privacy notice**

openDemocracy is committed to protecting your privacy in accordance with the Data Protection Act 2018, the General Data Protection Regulation (‘GDPR’) and other relevant legislation. This is the legal framework that sets guidelines for the collection and processing of personal information of individuals within the UK and the European Union.

We will be clear about what data we collect from you and how we use it. We will protect all personal data you share with us and guarantee not to share it with anyone except those described in this policy

This notice describes the kinds of information that openDemocracy processes and how we maintain records of your personal data.

If you have any queries regarding this privacy notice please contact us on [info@opendemocracy.net](mailto:info@opendemocracy.net).

[See your cookie settings here](https://www.opendemocracy.net/en/cookies/).

## **Who are we?**

openDemocracy is an independent global media platform covering world affairs, ideas and culture. We seek to challenge power, inspire change and encourage democratic debate across the world.

openDemocracy.net is published by openDemocracy Limited, a UK-registered company (#3855274) limited by guarantee and wholly owned by the non-profit openDemocracy Foundation for the Advancement of Global Education (company limited by guarantee #04807614).

You can support openDemocracy with charitable grants and gifts to the openDemocracy programme of openTrust, a UK registered charity (#10864094).

openDemocracy also works with[ Neo Philanthropy](https://neophilanthropy.org/?ref=opendemocracy.net) (NEO) (a registered 501(c)3 organisation) as a US-based fiscal sponsor. NEO acts as an umbrella organisation for a project and accepts and administers funds on its behalf.

## **What kinds of information do we collect?**

openDemocracy requests information from you when you subscribe to one of our mailing lists or donate money to us. When you sign up for these reasons, we will ask you for personal information so that we can contact you.

Website usage information is collected using cookies. We use cookies to help us provide you with a good experience when you browse our website. Cookies also allow us to improve our website.

By continuing to browse our website, you are agreeing to our use of cookies.

[See your cookie settings here](https://www.opendemocracy.net/en/cookies/).

### **What is a cookie?**

A cookie is a small text file that is sent from our website and stored in your web browser or on the device you're using.

Our use of cookies complies with all UK data protection and data privacy regulations.

### **Stopping cookies**

Most web browsers accept cookies automatically but you can change your browser’s settings to stop cookies.

You can also[ delete your cookies](http://www.aboutcookies.org/how-to-delete-cookies/?ref=opendemocracy.net) any time you want.

If you choose not to accept cookies you might find some parts of our website does not work as you would expect.

### **Cookie categories**

We have assessed our cookies based on the[ ICC Cookie Guide](https://www.cookielaw.org/media/1096/icc%5Fuk%5Fcookiesguide%5Frevnov.pdf?ref=opendemocracy.net), summarised below. Most of the cookies on our web pages fall into categories one and two.

#### **1\. Strictly necessary**

These cookies are essential in order to enable you to move around the website and use its features, such as accessing secure areas of the website. Without these cookies, we cannot provide services you may ask for, like making a donation.

#### **2\. Analytics cookies**

Analytics cookies allow us to collect information about how readers access our site – for example, counting the number of readers on site, how long they stay on the site for, and what parts of the site they visit. This is also sometimes known as ‘web audience measurement’.

#### **3\. Third-party cookies (targeting or advertising)**

These cookies are used by services not controlled by openDemocracy (e.g. video-hosting platforms) to deliver content and adverts more relevant to you and your interests. They are also used to limit the number of times you see an advertisement as well as help measure the effectiveness of the advertising campaigns. They are usually placed by advertising networks with the website operator’s permission. They remember that you have visited the website and this information is shared with other organisations such as advertisers. Quite often targeting or advertising cookies will be linked to site functionality provided by the other organisation.

### Specific cookies of interest

#### **Google Analytics**

Google Analytics is a web-based service provided by Google, Inc. It sets a cookie to evaluate your use of the website and compile reports for us on activity on the site.

Google stores the information collected by the cookie on servers in the US. Google may also transfer this information to third parties where required to do so by law, or where such third parties process the information on Google's behalf. Google will not associate your IP address with any other data held by Google. By using the openDemocracy website, you consent to the processing of data about you by Google as described above.

You can[ reject or delete cookies from Google Analytics](https://tools.google.com/dlpage/gaoptout?ref=opendemocracy.net).

#### **Tags and pixel tags**

openDemocracy may use tags and pixel tags to track, measure and report on activities that happen on our website after you see or click on an advert or link off-site, for instance on Facebook. These allow us to measure the effectiveness of our adverts. Data collected and shared is anonymous and does not personally identify you.

**Your control over tags**

Pixel tags are not stored on your computer or mobile device. If you disable cookies, the pixel tag will detect only an anonymous website visit.

**Facebook pixel code**

Facebook pixel code is tracking pixel which matches users anonymously with their Facebook ID, enabling remarketing, analysis and reporting of openDemocracy advertising campaigns. For details on these cookies, please read the[ Facebook Cookie Policy.](https://www.facebook.com/policies/cookies/)

#### **Other cookies**

Some of our pages contain embedded content such as YouTube, Vimeo, Twitter and Facebook.

We also provide Facebook, Twitter and email sharing functionality. These sites may set a cookie when you are also logged in to their service. They may use these cookies to serve ads based on your past visits to our website. You can opt out of a third-party vendor's use of cookies by visiting the[ Network Advertising Initiative’s opt-out page](http://optout.networkadvertising.org/?c=1&ref=opendemocracy.net#!%2F).

## **How do we get your consent?**

When collecting information from you, we always

- process data lawfully, fairly and in a transparent manner;
- collect data only for purposes that are legitimate and necessary in relation to the services we provide;
- collect accurate information, keep it up to date and make sure it can be easily deleted or corrected without delay;
- keep data in a form that permits identification no longer than necessary for the purpose for which the personal data is processed;
- keep personal data in a secure place that protects the information against unauthorised or unlawful processing, accidental loss, destruction or damage, making sure we have the appropriate technology to do so.

When you provide us with your personal information, we will tell you why we want to collect and use it. We will ask you to explicitly give us consent to our collecting and using it for that specific reason only. We will ask you to positively opt in to our services, through a two-step process.

### **Making a donation**

When you make a donation via our website, openDemocracy uses third-party organisations to manage the transfer of your money. Our main online payment provider is PayPal, which complies with GDPR, but we also use other organisations such as JustGiving.

### **Direct email marketing**

If you actively give us consent to contact you, we will send you direct email marketing. This will only include the newsletters or campaign information you have requested. You can opt out of these services at any time by unsubscribing to the relevant communication. openDemocracy uses Mailchimp and CiviCRM software to produce our newsletter content.

Emails we send may include tracking tags that tell us information about whether you have opened an email, clicked on a link in an email, and information about the email software and device you use to read the email. They may also allow us to determine some activities you may subsequently undertake on our website.

We try to send a plain text version of our emails with no tracking pixel along with a richer HTML version. If you wish to receive our emails without tracking tags most email software can be set to display the plain text version of the email.

*We will not share any personal information you give us through donations or email subscriptions with anyone else for marketing or sales reasons.*

## **How is your information used?**

The personal information we collect might include your name, address, email address, IP address, and information regarding what pages are accessed and when. The type of personal information we will collect about you will depend on why we are collecting the information. We may use your information to:

- enable us to deliver more relevant content to you through targeted communications;

## **What will we do with things you submit yourself?**

### ***Submissions***

openDemocracy invites you to submit articles, or pitches for articles, that you would like us to publish on our site. We will assess pitches and articles and let you know if we are interested in publishing them; we aim to do this within three weeks. We require you to give us an email address so that we can communicate with you about your article or pitch.

From time to time openDemocracy will conduct voluntary surveys to better understand our readers' views or to support editorial initiatives. This information may be aggregated and then compiled and shared with third parties.

openDemocracy uses a separate company called RecruiterBox to manage our recruitment process. ## **What is our lawful basis for processing your data?**

The lawful basis for processing your information is set out in article 6 of the GDPR. This requires us to be accountable and transparent about any information we ask from you. In line with the GDPR we will provide clear consent from individuals and only ask for information that is necessary. openDemocracy will ensure that we comply with the law. For more information, please see the[ ICO website](https://ico.org.uk/?ref=opendemocracy.net) in regards to processing data.

**Consent:** When you have given clear consent for us to process your personal data for a specific purpose.

**Contract:** When we must process your data in order to fulfill a contract we have with you, or because you have asked us to take specific steps before entering into a contract.

**Legal obligation:** When we must process personal data about you to comply with the law (not including contractual obligations).

**Legitimate interests:** When we need to process your personal data in order to manage and grow our organisation.

openDemocracy will ensure that we have all the necessary processes in place to store your data safely. Under the GDPR, you have the right to access, rectify and erase your data, as well as the right to restrict processing and data portability. ### Independence and Transparency
URL: https://www.opendemocracy.net/independence-and-transparency/
Last updated: 2026-01-20T09:30:15.000Z
Editorial independence and transparency must be at the core of everything we do. Our value and reputation as journalists and as a publisher depends on our editorial independence; and transparency about who we work with, [who funds us](https://www.opendemocracy.net/who-funds-us/), and who we serve is vital for our mission in the world.

This means that no one outside openDemocracy may control what we publish. Further, it is important that openDemocracy does not appear to act as a megaphone for political campaigns or organisations or other vested interests. And it means that when we are working in partnership or collaboration with others, we let our readers know about it.

openDemocracy has many kinds of relationships with other people and organisations. The most important one is with our readers: we exist to serve them, we respond to their comments and questions, and conversely they provide us with vital support by sharing our work in their own networks and donating money to us. However, we will not accept any donation that comes with conditions about what we publish.

We also receive significant levels of funding in grants from trusts and foundations. We work only with those whose values and objectives are compatible with our own; they, of course, support us for the same reason. However, their financial support does not give them any decisive control over what we publish, as explained below.

Lastly, we have editorial partnerships that are distinct from grant funding. In these, an external organisation – often an academic institution – actively participates in identifying and refining themes for a particular strand of content. They may also suggest authors. And they often cover openDemocracy’s costs related to the project, as well as contributing to our core overheads. We identify these partnerships to readers by publishing a partner’s logo or a distinctive banner on any piece of content or landing page that is created as part of the partnership. But, like grant-making trusts and foundations, they have no ultimate control over what we publish.

## Funders and partners

We will never give anyone who funds our work the right to approve copy or any aspect of a video or imagery before publication. Nor will a funder or partner specify how we promote content.

Funders and partners may suggest themes or topics for our editorial content. A partner in a paid-for partnership may supply us with copy or other materials. However, we must always remain free to edit or reject suggestions or content as we see fit.

We may show a partner edited articles before we publish them under the partnership banner – without giving the partner copy approval or anything resembling it. Partners and funders cannot simply overrule the openDemocracy editor working with them.

We must also retain the right to publish content that a funder or partner may not like. In a paid partnership, however, the partner may have the right to veto the public presentation of a piece of content as part of the partnership. In such cases, we remain free to publish the content outside the context of the partnership.

## Transparency

If any content we publish mentions a funder or partner of openDemocracy, we should acknowledge this in the article, video or audio.

## Political independence

Our aim is to challenge power and encourage democratic debate across the world. Beyond that, openDemocracy does not endorse or promote any political party. Nor do we, as an organisation, assume that any particular policy position, point of view, political theory or ideology is correct.

That said, we are “[plural but not neutral](https://cdn-prod.opendemocracy.net/media/documents/openDemocracy%5FStrategic%5FPlan%5F2020-22%5Ffor%5Fwebsite.pdf?ref=opendemocracy.net)”, as our strategic plan for 2020-22 puts it. We call out inequality and injustice, but we value and encourage multiple perspectives on how to tackle them.

There are stricter, legal requirements for content that is funded by a charity. If the charitable purpose is the advancement of education, such content must present “[information in a neutral and balanced way that encourages awareness of different points of view](https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/government/uploads/system/uploads/attachment%5Fdata/file/358536/the-advancement-of-education-for-the-public-benefit.pdf?ref=opendemocracy.net)”.

That does not mean that charity-funded articles have to treat hateful ideologies as valid, or devote equal space to differing points of view. However, there should be balance and fair treatment of different points of view across the output of a charitably funded project.

## Other people's agendas

Editorial independence means that we must not simply lend our platform and audience to organisations, events, campaigns or products that we as individuals happen to approve of.

We should never publish an unedited press release or manifesto.

If editors think that our readers would be interested to hear about an organisation, event, campaign or product, they should write or commission content about it – an article, video or podcast that considers the subject’s weaknesses as well as its strengths.

This is not to say that openDemocracy will never cooperate with other organisations on campaigns, or indeed run campaigns ourselves, as we do from time to time. But the editor-in-chief must approve any such arrangement before we publish anything.

If editors want to publish an **open letter**, they should consider whether it might be more engaging rewritten as an opinion piece – which should not strongly promote the authors or their organisation or campaign or product. If they feel that the open letter format is best, the editor-in-chief or head of news should approve it first. 

The headline must begin 'Open letter:' so that readers understand it is not the collective voice of openDemocracy itself. And editors should simultaneously publish a news article describing the key points of the letter, the context in which it was written and the response it has had or is likely to have ([example here](https://www.opendemocracy.net/en/oureconomy/exclusive-leading-economists-call-short-deep-circuit-breaker-lockdowns/)). 

## Avoiding advertorials

The rules for advertising in the UK also require editorial independence. If anyone outside openDemocracy was able to specify what we publish, or require changes to content, the content would be ‘[advertorial](https://www.asa.org.uk/asset/BAA9CEA7-696F-459D-971B8515B6A96BEB.40C68C48-4825-4561-A9F989E346011616/?ref=opendemocracy.net)’ and so would have to be clearly [labelled as advertising](https://www.asa.org.uk/uploads/assets/uploaded/3af39c72-76e1-4a59-b2b47e81a034cd1d.pdf?ref=opendemocracy.net) and visually presented in a way that distinguished it from editorial content. We do not publish advertorial.

### Minister invited Euan Blair to BlackRock meeting as his firm sought investment
URL: https://www.opendemocracy.net/blackrock-meeting-euan-blair-government-tony-hakluyt-secret-peter-kyle-jonathan-reynolds/
Last updated: 2026-11-27T16:53:13.000Z
[Tony Blair](https://www.opendemocracy.net/tag/tony-blair/)’s son was one of three people invited by the government to a private meeting hosted by [BlackRock](https://www.opendemocracy.net/tag/blackrock/) earlier this year, openDemocracy can reveal. 

The meeting, held in the asset management giant’s London offices in April, was attended by then-business secretary Peter Kyle and the Department for Business and Trade’s permanent secretary, Amanda Brooks, as well as representatives of a major private equity investor, high-growth companies, and industry lobbying groups.

After openDemocracy learned that the event took place through emails obtained under Freedom of Information laws, the government said it holds no records of what was discussed. It also declined to comment on why it invited the former prime minister’s son, Euan Blair, who was at the time seeking investment for his AI company. 

The government emails also reveal that BlackRock’s UK chair originally tried to arrange the meeting with Kyle’s predecessor, Jonathan Reynolds, in July last year, weeks after the pair met at the summer party of [Hakluyt](https://www.opendemocracy.net/tag/hakluyt/), a secretive consulting firm with links to No 10.

Reynolds – whom [Andy Burnham](https://www.opendemocracy.net/tag/andy-burnham/) reinstated as business secretary in August – failed to declare his attendance at the party, in what may be a breach of ministerial rules. 

A former minister told openDemocracy that “questions must be asked about” the failure, while Green Party leader [Zack Polanski](https://www.opendemocracy.net/tag/zack-polanski/) called for an investigation into our findings.

“The public deserves to know who ministers are meeting, what is being discussed and whose interests are being served,” Polanski said. 

“Increasingly, people are seeing the difference between what this government says and what it does and concluding that it isn’t their interests this government is serving. There must be full transparency and accountability. Any breaches of the ministerial code must be properly investigated as a bare minimum.”

## **‘City lobbyists saw an opening’**

The BlackRock event was billed as dinner and a discussion on ‘Financing Growth in the UK’.

While the Department for Business and Trade said no minutes, notes or readouts from this discussion exist, it did release a briefing note prepared for Kyle by civil servants ahead of time.

The note set out several discussion questions “geared towards attendees” that had been proposed by BlackRock. These included “what would give long-term institutional investors greater confidence to commit more capital to UK growth companies?” and “what would make the UK the most attractive place for companies to grow from start-up into global leaders?”

It also told Kyle to stress the growing role of the British Business Bank – the government-owned economic development bank that has an increasing role providing capital to UK firms – in “crowding-in long-term scale-up finance” and the importance of “regulatory clarity and competitiveness” in attracting investors.

Sara Hall, co-executive director at Positive Money, a non-profit pushing for reform to the financial sector, told openDemocracy the briefing note exposes how [Keir Starmer’s](https://www.opendemocracy.net/tag/keir-starmer/) government sought to appease the City.

“As these documents show, the Starmer-led government was overly keen to demonstrate its value to the financial sector, whether that meant cutting regulation or sweetening private investment in our critical infrastructure with public subsidies,” Hall said. 

“The financial sector will always push to be able to take more risks with our money, or sniff around for subsidies,” she added. “Clearly, City lobbyists saw an opening to advance their demands under the Starmer government.”

**'We do appreciate the short notice'**

Five days before the dinner, Kyle's office reached out to extend an invite to executives at three companies: PsiQuantum, which works in quantum computing, Tokamak Energy, a fusion energy firm, and Multiverse, an edtech and AI skills company co-founded and led by Euan Blair.

In the case of both PsiQuantum and Tokamak Energy, Kyle’s office had to be passed the relevant contact details by other specialist teams in the Department of Business and Trade. Its subsequent emails to both firms explained how their attendance would benefit the government. 

The secretary of state was keen to “meet some of our fastest growing companies”, his team told Tokamak chief executive Warrick Matthews, while ministers wanted to better understand PsiQuantum co-founder Mark Thompson’s experience of “founding in the UK but scaling abroad”.

Kyle’s team did not need to be sent an email address for Multiverse’s vice president of corporate affairs – a former Tory special adviser and No 10 staffer – and there was no specific reason given why ministers felt the company’s attendance would benefit them. 

Instead, as the email thread shows, the government appeared to be thinking of the younger Blair’s interests when it reached out to invite him.

“I know you have been in contact with the office about organising a conversation between our Secretary of State and your CEO Euan Blair. Without getting in the way of efforts to get that meeting in the diary, I wanted to flag a dinner next week which we thought Euan might be interested in attending in addition,” the email read.

“Given Euan's interest in the Government's backing for growth companies, the Secretary of State would be delighted if he would be able to join the group and offer his perspectives if by any chance he is available (we do appreciate the short notice)?”

Multiverse is [England's largest apprenticeship provider by revenue](https://feweek.co.uk/masters-of-the-multiverse-net-45-apprenticeship-income-gain/?ref=opendemocracy.net), with much of its income coming from the government’s apprenticeship levy. Its most recent accounts showed a loss of £63.3m for the year to March 2025.

On 15 May, three weeks after the dinner, Multiverse announced it had secured $70m of investment at a funding round valuing it at $2.1bn, its first raise since 2022\. Euan Blair is the company's largest individual shareholder.

openDemocracy asked the government why it had invited Blair, whether the family’s ties to Labour or Kyle – who was a Cabinet Office adviser during Tony Blair’s second term – played a part in the decision to do so, and whether Kyle had personally asked for Blair to attend. It did not respond to any of our questions, although a spokesperson said: “Ministers routinely meet with the CEOs of fast-growing UK firms to support them to scale in the UK.”

“Personal connections inevitably play a role in who gets invited to government events,” Tom Brake, a former whip in the coalition government and the director of Unlock Democracy, a non-partisan organisation campaigning for electoral, constitutional, and political reform. 

“It's up to departments to ensure access is fair and ‘who you know’ does not translate into favouritism,” he added.

## **After the meeting** 

BlackRock's UK chair Sandra Boss, who hosted the dinner, wrote to the Department for Business and Trade after the meeting to say that while the group had discussed “an array of ‘real economy’ ideas”, three in particular “merited further conversation”.

The first, she said, was “planning reform and accelerating the consent process, given our role on the British Infrastructure Taskforce”. BlackRock sits on the taskforce, a government-backed body set up to channel private investment into infrastructure.

The government redacted Boss’s second idea in emails released to openDemocracy, saying its disclosure could harm policy development. The third was public procurement, where Boss said: “The UK could be more professional and deliberate.”

Boss asked for a further one-to-one meeting with Kyle, noting that BlackRock would “be happy to share any further detail on any of the financing-specific topics that arose in our discussion”.

Positive Money’s Hall told openDemocracy: “It’s fallacious to believe that regulation is the key blocker to either investment or growth in the UK economy. Regulation is what’s holding back risk – and growth built on excessive risk-taking isn’t worth having, especially if it heralds another financial crash forcing huge public bailouts.” 

## **Summer party**

Boss originally reached out to Reynolds to arrange the meeting in late June 2025, writing: “It was good to see you at the Hakluyt Summer Party last week.”

Hakluyt, a Mayfair-based consultancy, is among the best-connected firms in British politics. Its former managing partner, Varun Chandra, has been the government's top business and investment adviser since being hired by Starmer in July 2024\. He remains in place under Burnham, despite concerns over his continued stake in Hakluyt and the lack of transparency around its clientele.

The company is well known for its lavish parties, where senior figures from the worlds of business and politics mix. While senior government officials from the Foreign Office, the Ministry of Defence, and the Department for Business and Trade – including the latter’s then permanent secretary, Gareth Davies – declared their attendance at last year’s summer party, Reynolds did not. 

This omission may constitute a breach of the Ministerial Code, which requires ministers’ hospitality, including drinks receptions, to be published monthly. In the same month as the Hakluyt event, Reynolds declared two £75 dinners from lobbying firm Flint Global and accountancy giant KPMG.

MPs have declared the same event. Shadow chancellor Mel Stride registered two tickets to this year's Hakluyt summer party, for himself and his wife, worth £550.

The government declined to answer whether Peter Kyle, who was business secretary at the time of this year’s Hakluyt summer party, on 11 June, had attended and not declared doing so. 

Brake told openDemocracy: “There ought to be no inconsistencies between what ministers and their civil servants declare when attending the same events. If senior officials considered this event worth declaring, questions must be asked about why the then minister did not.”
### Two kinds of petrostate sank COP31. Only one is getting the blame
URL: https://www.opendemocracy.net/cop31-petrostate-sank-cop31-united-kingdom-european-union-africa-saudi-arabia-russia/
Last updated: 2026-11-27T16:53:31.000Z
In the aftermath of COP31, attention has focused on Saudi Arabia and Russia, who, the story goes, killed the climate talks in Antalya. Both governments resisted language in the final agreement that would have reaffirmed the commitment to move away from fossil fuels, leading to the annual summit ending without an agreement for the first time since 2009\. 

It’s true that both countries played their part. Saudi Arabia reprised its long role as the summit’s blocker-in-chief even as it used COP31 to announce a wind and solar deal with the host, Türkiye: clean power for itself, delay for everyone else. Russia told delegates that the scientists’ own pathways leave room for oil and gas. On the final day, Russia and the Arab Group objected to a decision simply because it pointed back to a promise made at COP28 in Dubai three years ago to transition away from fossil fuels.

But blaming them alone lets a second club of petrostates off the hook. A month before COP31 began, Britain approved the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea. In September, Canada’s prime minister cheered a C$33bn expansion that will double the country’s biggest gas export terminal, while Australia, which chaired this year’s negotiations, signed off on the North West Shelf gas project running until 2070\. The EU – which rejected COP31’s final text on 22 November, denouncing it as greenwashing for the fossil fuel industry – has this year promised to buy up to US$750bn of American oil, gas and nuclear fuel by 2028\. 

‘Do as I say, not as I do’ is not a negotiating position. It is the reason the talks failed. That every country cuts emissions is crucial to meeting the aims of the Paris Agreement, a legally binding international treaty agreed in 2015 to limit global average temperature rise to well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels, while aiming for a rise of just 1.5°C. 

Those who caused most of the damage and grew rich doing it must make changes first, then help pay for everyone else to make the shift and protect themselves from what can no longer be avoided. Yet in Antalya, rich countries pressed for stronger action while resisting the finance and support that would make that action possible. 

Three weeks before the summit, the EU’s climate chief, Wopke Hoekstra, had declared that talks on new finance commitments were “dead in the water”. Most European leaders then skipped the Antalya leaders’ summit for a security meeting in Dublin. In the negotiating rooms, Europe resisted putting a number on last year’s promise to triple adaptation finance and opposed giving the new just transition mechanism any substance.

The gap between promise and delivery was stark. The Adaptation Fund, which pays for flood defences and drought-resistant farming in the poorest countries, received US$50m against a target of around US$300m. This summer, the world’s five biggest oil companies made $44m every two hours. 

Russia accused Europe of profiting from the crisis through loans and trade, calling it an “old colonial distribution of labour under a new green banner”. The charge is self-serving, especially as it comes from a government defending its own oil and gas.

Worse still, the draft agreement admitted that warming will now likely overshoot 1.5°C and that developing countries need US$305bn a year to adapt. However, it didn’t provide a credible response to that need. The pledge to triple renewable energy was removed while carbon capture was given a target of its own. The result was an agreement that recognised the scale of the problem but weakened some of the measures needed to address it.

For African countries, what all this means is less protection before the next flood, and more debt after it. Africa needs around US$70bn a year to adapt. In 2021-22 it received about US$14bn, more than half of which came as loans. African governments already borrow at two to three times the rates rich countries pay and spend twice as much servicing debt as investing in clean energy. When adaptation isn’t funded, the disasters still come anyway and African governments borrow again to fix destroyed infrastructure. This is money that never reaches a clinic or a classroom. 

Ethiopia, which will host next year’s COP32, inherits this mess, while some 85 million of its own people still live without electricity. Africa is being asked to borrow to survive a crisis it did not cause so lenders can profit from it.

So then, is the COP dead? No, and we should be concerned about those who say it is. Europe’s climate chief now champions coalitions outside COP and beyond the reach of its unanimity rule. While such coalitions can help countries that are ready to act move faster, COP remains one of the few forums where small and climate-vulnerable states can formally negotiate with the world’s largest economies. It is one room where Tuvalu and Ethiopia sit as equals with the United States and China.

The problem then is not that multilateral negotiations have become pointless. It is that governments continue to treat their commitments as optional. The COP process cannot force countries to act in good faith, but abandoning it would weaken the position of countries that have the least power in the global economy.

So where is the hope? In the gap between governments and their people. Britain has just had its hottest summer on record. Across Europe, people are demanding protection from heat and floods. Communities are turning schools into flood shelters and installing a record 17 gigawatts of solar across Africa this year, roughly 100,000 panels a day. One can only imagine what they could do with finance that builds resilience instead of debt.

Ethiopia has said it wants the summit in Addis Ababa to be a “COP of hope”. That ambition will mean little without decisions that change the terms of the debate. There is an urgent need for adaptation finance that is predictable and provided mainly as grants, a just transition mechanism that addresses debt and the high cost of capital and a funded plan to move away from fossil fuels that recognises the different responsibilities of countries.

Antalya should not be remembered only as a summit blocked by Saudi Arabia and Russia. It also showed how wealthy countries can condemn obstruction while continuing to protect their own fossil fuel interests and refusing to provide the finance they have promised. If Addis is to be different, then those countries will have to be judged not by the language they support in the negotiating room but by what they are prepared to fund and change at home.
