### Proposed immigration rules risk safety of survivors of rape as weapon of war
URL: https://www.opendemocracy.net/proposed-immigration-rules-risk-safety-of-survivors-of-rape-as-weapon-of-war/
Last updated: 2026-11-27T08:56:44.000Z
When Dinah\* arrived in the UK, she was so traumatised that she could not speak. 

Her husband, a political activist in their home country, which openDemocracy is not naming for their safety, had fled ahead of her. Dinah was then abducted by men determined to find out where he was, who gang-raped her repeatedly for a month. 

By the time she sought asylum in the UK, Dinah was “completely disassociated,” said Laura, a psychologist working with the NGO Freedom From Torture, whose surname we cannot publish for security reasons. “She was hospitalised following a suicide attempt and was not able to respond or talk. It’s the rape, it’s the humiliation, that can have hugely damaging effects psychologically, physically, on self-worth and in relationships.”

Now, changes proposed in the government’s Immigration and Asylum Bill risk limiting survivors like Dinah’s chances of securing protection in the UK by stating that those appealing a rejected asylum claim must have raised all relevant matters at the start of the process. 

The new system will not only “[disincentivise late disclosure](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/immigration-and-asylum-bill-2026-factsheets/immigration-and-asylum-bill-independent-immigration-appeals-authority?ref=opendemocracy.net)” of new information, but penalise it. “If an appellant provides late evidence during the course of an appeal, this should be taken into account as damaging to the appellant’s credibility,” the proposed [legislation](https://bills.parliament.uk/publications/68834/documents/9087?ref=opendemocracy.net) states. Decision-makers will be able to consider whether there are “[good reasons](https://bills.parliament.uk/publications/68833/documents/9085?ref=opendemocracy.net#sec%5F15)” to explain the late disclosure.

This proposal is at odds with recent warnings by experts and politicians over the need to avoid perpetuating harmful “rape myths” about how survivors should behave. The trial of rapist Russell Brand has led to criticism – [including in the House of Lords](https://hansard.parliament.uk/lords/2026-11-16/debates/3090B137-D8AC-44BD-B767-3DD9735C43FA/CourtsAndTribunalsBill?ref=opendemocracy.net#:~:text=What%20are%20these,reporting%20is%20common.) last week – of arguments made in court that rape victims would not delay reporting their abusers. 

In reality, there are many reasons why an individual may not come forward in the aftermath of an attack, including that sexual violence trauma can impact the ability to share painful experiences. This has led experts across the migrant rights sector to warn the government that the proposed legislation risks harming the most vulnerable asylum claimants.

“We know even in other circumstances, not only in conflict, that even if the person who experienced violence is now in a safe place, they are not ready to talk, sometimes for years,” said Kateryna Shukh, a Ukrainian psychologist from Mariupol who lives in Norway. These are people “who still don’t have the feeling of safety”. 

The proposed law change comes as the government’s latest immigration statistics show that in the year ending September 2026, [only 38% of asylum-seeking people](https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/immigration-system-statistics-year-ending-september-2026/how-many-people-are-granted-asylum-in-the-uk?ref=opendemocracy.net) were granted protection on their first try, with thousands more having to appeal an initial rejection. Experts told openDemocracy that the plans would penalise women for not feeling ready to talk about their abuse.

Under the plans, people going through a “late claims process” – who raise reasons for their asylum claim after detention or a removal notice – will see their appeals fast-tracked, making it harder to have new evidence heard. 

“An asylum and appeal system that fails to recognise the realities of trauma risks denying survivors meaningful access to sanctuary and justice, compounding the harm they have already endured and potentially sending them back into the hands of their torturers,” said Nadine Tunasi, the head of survivor activism at Freedom from Torture. 

“Access to protection must not depend on a survivor’s ability to disclose traumatic experiences within an arbitrary time frame. Survivors must be given the time, support and fair opportunity to tell their stories and to access justice without fear that the effects of their trauma will be used against them.”

“Particularly with sexual trauma there is an increased likelihood of delayed disclosure as there are often high levels of shame,” said Laura. “That is very hard to verbalise at any point.”

### **Trauma in the system**

The nature of asylum interviews can compound trauma, making it even more difficult for survivors to disclose in a timely manner. 

“Often, it may be the state officials in their country of origin who have that have actually tortured them,” Laura said. “They feel very unsafe at the point that they're being interviewed by members of authority in the UK. They're often very long interviews in rooms that may be reminiscent of a cell. 

“They're being interviewed or interrogated by members of authority that they don't know, so there's often high levels of mistrust, which is very common with people surviving post-traumatic stress disorder.”

Laura finds that this means sexual violence is often not disclosed until much later in the asylum process, including during a medico-legal report, a clinical document produced by an independent clinical psychologist that assesses evidence of torture, serious harm, or health conditions relevant to an asylum or human rights claim. 

The asylum system, says Laura, needs “to have some acknowledgement that in this environment you may not get all the information at that point, because asylum seekers are often terrified, and that's not conducive to being able to open up about experiences of someone's trauma,” not least because of the “high levels of shame that they don't want to disclose.”

Accommodation can also impact trauma, with women who have experienced rape housed alongside men, or in hotels and barracks with male security guards. Men who have been raped and sexually abused can end up sharing rooms with strangers. 

“There are lots of safeguarding concerns with asylum accommodation and Freedom from Torture advocates that vulnerable people shouldn’t be placed in large hotels often with other vulnerable people or be sharing bathrooms, bedrooms, and women and children shouldn’t be placed in accommodation with men,” said Laura.

### **An epidemic of violence** 

Dinah is one of millions of women worldwide who have experienced sexual violence in conflict zones. The United Nations documented 9,788 cases of conflict-related sexual violence across countries including Ukraine, Sudan, Myanmar, Haiti, Afghanistan and the Central African Republic last year. The figures represent a “[sharp](https://www.un.org/sexualviolenceinconflict/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/report/auto-draft/SG-Report-2025.pdf?%5Fgl=1%2Aceu6cm%2A%5Fgcl%5Fau%2AMjAwMDM0MTE0MC4xNzk0MzAwNjA4%2A%5Fga%2AODM0NjI5MjUyLjE3OTQzMDAzNjg.%2A%5Fga%5FS5EKZKSB78%2AczE3OTU0MzMzMDUkbzQkZzEkdDE3OTU0MzMzODUkajYwJGwwJGgw&ref=opendemocracy.net)” increase from 2024\. 

But the documented incidents are a tiny fraction of the overall abuse, [said](https://news.un.org/en/story/2026/05/1167603?ref=opendemocracy.net) UN special representative Pramila Patten. They “should be understood not as the full picture, but as an indication of a much broader pattern of violations that remain largely unseen and underreported.” 

In the Darfur region of Sudan, the charity Médecins Sans Frontières treated nearly [4,000 survivors](https://msf.org.uk/article/sexual-violence-sudans-war-special-msf-report-uncovers-systematic-attacks?ref=opendemocracy.net) of sexual violence between January 2024 and November 2025, in what they described as “systematic attacks.” Across the border in Ethiopia’s Tigray region, [tens of thousands of women](https://www.theguardian.com/global-development/2025/jun/30/sexual-violence-tigray-women-abuse-gang-rape-ethiopia-eritrea?ref=opendemocracy.net) have reported suffering sexual abuse since the 2020 conflict with the government began.

The UN has recorded 1,000 cases of “[widespread and abhorrent](https://news.un.org/en/story/2026/09/1168374?ref=opendemocracy.net)” sexual violence against prisoners of war in the Russian-occupied territories of Ukraine since the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022, while the NGO Save Ukraine found that [one in ten](https://www.opendemocracy.net/en/ukraine-russia-child-abductions-abuse-kyiv/) children rescued from the occupied territories had experienced sexual abuse. 

Shukh, a co-founder of Bereginia – Mariupol's Women Association, has worked with women experiencing gender-based violence since Russia’s invasion that began in 2014\. Speaking to openDemocracy, she is clear that supporting survivors starts “with creating a safe space”. 

It can take a long time for a survivor to disclose violence, and they may discuss other issues and experiences before feeling safe to do so, she explained. “Sometimes it's not a question of talking directly on this experience, but about creating this safety and to help them to continue normal life with that experience.” 

A Home Office spokesperson said:“The Bill will continue to safeguard survivors of sexual violence, while cracking down on wider exploitation of the system.

 “The credibility considerations are well-balanced and contain appropriate safeguards, including taking circumstances such as trauma into account. This will enhance the robustness of all decision-making and ensure survivors are protected.”

As for Dinah, she slowly started to recover. Laura vividly remembers how, after months of being non-verbal, one day Dinah laughed. 

“It was very gradual, and the first conversations were very much about trying to talk about things that she actually enjoyed or gave her pleasure, and that was really the starting point,” Laura explained. “It was being able to connect on a more positive memory and connect through art that she started speaking, and then we moved onto trauma-focused therapy to help process her experiences of rape.”
### Domestic abuse victims ending up behind bars, report finds
URL: https://www.opendemocracy.net/domestic-abuse-victims-ending-up-behind-bars-report-finds/
Last updated: 2026-11-26T14:24:24.000Z
Almost 95% of women in prison in England say they are survivors of domestic abuse, and two-thirds say domestic abuse played a part in their offending, according to [new research](https://www.womeninprison.org.uk/wp/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/See-My-Story-Not-My-Sentence-Digital.pdf?ref=opendemocracy.net) published by the charity Women in Prison. 

The report follows openDemocracy’s groundbreaking [investigation](https://www.opendemocracy.net/domestic-abuse-victims-arrested-policing-prisons-injustice/), which found a fifth of women arrested for offences such as carrying weapons and drugs and handling stolen goods were flagged by police as potential victims of domestic abuse. Half of women arrested for coercive control were themselves recognised as potential victims. 

openDemocracy also found more than [1,400 women arrested](https://www.opendemocracy.net/en/domestic-abuse-victims-criminalised-tory-law/) for assaulting an emergency worker were flagged as potential domestic abuse victims. 

Some 29% of women in custody were arrested during a domestic abuse call-out, according to a survey of 542 women across seven prisons in England – one in seven of the total female prison population – by Women in Prison. There are no women’s prisons in Wales, meaning Welsh women are often jailed far from their family or other support networks. 

Of the 65% who said abusive and controlling behaviour played a part in their offending, 6% said they had been threatened with physical and sexual violence if they did not carry out the offence. 

“Behind these statistics are women whose lives have been shaped by violence, intimidation and coercive control. Some have been forced into offending by abusive partners,” said Cherie Blair KC. “Others have committed offences while trying to survive abusive relationships. As a lawyer, I believe firmly in accountability and the rule of law. But justice also requires us to understand the circumstances in which offences are committed.”

Jasmine, 27, was sentenced to five years in prison for possession of her abusive partner’s gun. She was only 19 when she met him, and described how she “felt protected under his control.” He involved her in illegal activity, making money “to fund his empire. I was followed. His people watched my every move.” She was sentenced, she said, “for surviving his abuse.”

"Women who have survived domestic abuse deserve to be believed and supported,” said the charity’s CEO Sonya Ruparel. “But for women who have been forced into crime to survive their abuser, their stories are silenced by the very system that claims to protect them.

“We're calling on the government to take action to stop the sentencing of survivors. Prisons are overcrowded; domestic abuse is at epidemic levels. The Government says it's committed to reducing the number of women in prison. Now is the time to act."

[They were victims of domestic abuse. They ended up under arrestExclusive: hundreds of domestic abuse victims arrested for crimes committed under coercion or duress, but figures are tip of the iceberg![](https://storage.ghost.io/c/3f/80/3f804bea-4b2d-4ddf-9ff0-6ec7d0afa5fa/content/images/icon/multi_solo-a38a1048-7249-4ae0-823b-561ab3f17599.png)openDemocracySian Norris![](https://storage.ghost.io/c/3f/80/3f804bea-4b2d-4ddf-9ff0-6ec7d0afa5fa/content/images/thumbnail/Handcuffs-Eye-Ubiquitous-Universal-Images-Group-via-Getty-Image-01bc07c4-79dc-4032-98f7-9a24e3d6bcfc.jpg)](https://www.opendemocracy.net/domestic-abuse-victims-arrested-policing-prisons-injustice/)

The report shows how supporting women living in abusive relationships could help reduce the number of female offenders, bringing down the prison population. Just under half (46%) of women said they would not have committed their crime if they could have accessed specialist help earlier. For too many women, it is only when they are in prison that they are finally able to access domestic abuse support. 

As such, the report recommends the government invest in domestic support services and community-based support, in order to help women reach safety and to prevent women’s offending. 

While prevention and support are urgent, the report shows that the criminal justice system must reform in order to recognise when offenders are victimised. Nearly a third (33%) of women in custody said that from the point of arrest onwards, no one asked if they had experienced domestic abuse. As a result, police, lawyers, magistrates and judges are failing to recognise when women are coerced or abused into offending. 

Women in Prison is now calling on the government to create a statutory duty for criminal justice agencies to consider domestic abuse in their decision-making. 

Such a duty would require police, prosecutors, probation services and courts to identify, record and consider evidence of domestic abuse when making decisions about arrest, charge, bail, prosecution and sentencing, ensuring abuse is identified and considered before these decisions are made, not after.

When you demolish someone’s argument in real life, you might win the point — but what do you actually lose?

In this episode of *Change My Mind*, Ali Goldsworthy, Laura Osborne, and Alex Chesterfield are joined by Dr. Maja Nenadović, a political scientist, civic education specialist, and dialogue facilitator who has worked on conflict transformation across nearly 50 countries. Drawing on her life growing up in the former Yugoslavia and living through Viktor Orbán’s Hungary, Maja explores how political elites weaponise fear, why societies dodge uncomfortable history, and how we can talk to people we fundamentally disagree with.

Plus, she becomes the first guest in five series to share *two* major shifts in perspective: the chilling passage in *Mein Kampf* that forced her to abandon competitive debating in everyday life, and how she stopped letting borders and passports dictate her identity.

**What you’ll learn:**

- **Why Real-Life Debate Backfires:** Academic debate has a judge and rules; real life doesn’t. Maja explains how reading page 57 of *Mein Kampf*  made her realise that dismantling people's arguments in daily life was causing real harm.
- **Why Hungary’s Change Might Be Cosmetic:** While the international community applauds recent election results in Hungary, Maja urges caution. Until free media and an independent judiciary are restored, replacing one two-thirds majority with another is just political theatre.
- **The PLEASE Framework:** Born out of 70 deliberate, real-world conversations with people she disagreed with in Hungary, Maja walks through her six-step method for depolarising dialogue: **P**ause, **L**isten, **E**mpathy, **A**nalyse assumptions, **S**peak (only when invited), and manage **E**xpectations.
- **The Hubris of Getting Older:** Why Maja’s workshops in South Korea and beyond revealed that our capacity for open-minded reasoning often shrinks as our education (and ego) grows.
- **Sitting With Discomfort:** How dialogue circles with young people from Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Serbia use shared discomfort to break generational "conspiracies of silence."
- **Refusing the Box:** Growing up in a country that no longer exists, Maja explains how she moved past the pressure to pick a single nationality and embraced being "not a what, but a who."

### The trap of radical rhetoric: lessons for Burnham from Spain
URL: https://www.opendemocracy.net/lessons-andy-burnham-spain-election-sanchez-housing-crisis/
Last updated: 2026-11-27T15:12:17.000Z
**Listen to this article** [Sign up for a free account to do so](#/portal/signup) 

Listen to this article. (8 min 40 sec)

15s 15s 

Audio generated with a low-energy computer, no data-centre used.

Trust in politics across the [UK](https://www.opendemocracy.net/tag/united-kingdom/), [Europe](https://www.opendemocracy.net/tag/europe/) and the globe has fallen; the people know that the political establishment often says one thing and does another. 

For years, political elites have relied on a tired, reliable trick: pair progressive, high-octane rhetoric with cautious, business-as-usual administration, hoping that emotional relief and verbal posturing will substitute for genuine material transformation. 

Nowhere has this fatal tension been more starkly exposed than in [Spain](https://www.opendemocracy.net/tag/spain/). Prime minister Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist Workers’ Party is caught between radical grassroots movements, a desperate working class, and the hard machinery of capital. Voters will this weekend deliver their verdict on this standoff at a snap general election, [called by Sánchez as housing protests gripped the country last month](https://www.opendemocracy.net/spain-one-eviction-snap-election-maricarmen-abascal-pedro-sanchez/). Polls suggest the right-wing Popular Party is on track to win the most votes, and may be able to be propped up in government by the far-right Vox party. 

This should serve as an urgent warning for the UK’s Labour government and figures on the ‘soft-left’, like [Andy Burnham](https://www.opendemocracy.net/tag/andy-burnham/) – one that can be better understood by looking at Spain’s deep-seated political narrative through the clash of left parties, the boiling housing emergency, and the limits of managerial reform.

For example, when the slaughter in [Gaza](https://www.opendemocracy.net/tag/gaza/) intensified, Sánchez’s government mastered the language of moral outrage. It diagnosed the horror, criticised [Israel](https://www.opendemocracy.net/tag/israel/) openly, and championed Palestinian statehood on the international stage. To the outside observer, it played well as a display of defiance against Western complacency. A display captured in fierce rhetoric that won momentary applause.

Yet, for months, the glaring contradiction remained: fiery words at international summits coexisted with administrative loopholes, ongoing defence supply lines, and commercial continuity. It took mounting domestic outrage, relentless tenant and trade union mobilisation, and fierce parliamentary pressure before Madrid was finally forced into a binding stance.

For voters and grassroots movements, this exposed the danger of *palabras huérfanas* (orphan words) rhetoric that hangs in the air without structural backing. If a government talks like an anti-imperialist rebel on foreign policy while quietly keeping the machinery of complicity plugged in behind the scenes, the rhetoric backfires. It breeds profound cynicism and opens a wide flank on the left for movements that refuse to compromise on human rights.

The Spanish progressive model boasted genuine legislative wins, much like the Labour government has with workers’ and renters’ rights reform. Indeed, Sánchez’s government, which has been in power since 2018, sought to take aim at Spain’s historical plague of precarious, temporary contracts, forcing employers into permanent hiring models and raising the national minimum wage.

Yet, working-class Spaniards still feel deeply crushed. Why? Because incremental workplace reforms have been completely eclipsed by macro-level predatory shocks, specifically, a ruthless housing affordability crisis, runaway rents, and soaring everyday living costs. Fixing the employment contract means little if your paycheck is instantly swallowed by rentier capitalism.

The human cost of this systemic failure became a national trauma with [the eviction and subsequent death of María del Carmen Abascal](http://opendemocracy.net/something-is-changing-in-spain-and-tenants-are-leading-the-way/?ref=opendemocracy.net), or Maricarmen as she became known. An 87-year-old wheelchair user living on a fixed pension, in September this year Maricarmen was forcibly thrown out of the Madrid apartment in Retiro Park where she had lived for over seven decades under a lifetime family lease. The courts had blocked three earlier attempts to evict Maricarmen after a corporate landlord bought the property and sought to force a massive rent hike, but she was eventually removed by police on a stretcher, having been given just 30 minutes to collect her belongings. Stripped of her home, she deteriorated rapidly in hospital and passed away.

Her tragic death transformed her into an instant national symbol, sparking massive tent encampments in Madrid’s Puerta del Sol square and across major cities under the banner of “Housing is a right, not a business”. It laid bare the brutal truth of technocratic governance: a government can boast about labour market statistics on paper, but if it allows predatory property speculation to evict pensioners onto the streets, the social contract is shattered. As protesters chanted outside Parliament, her final recorded words – “fight to defend what is yours” – spread like wildfire on the internet, and chants of “Maricarmen lives, the struggle goes on” rang through the streets.

Housing has been the primary engine of social distress during the Sánchez era, as costs have completely outpaced wage gains. A whole generation has been shut out from homeownership as house prices nationwide skyrocketed by 70-80% from 2015 to 2025 – with spikes exceeding double digits year-on-year in major urban centres and tourism hotspots like Madrid, Barcelona, Málaga, and the Balearic Islands. Housing and related utility costs have also shot up (with annual spikes nearing 13% in certain periods), with rent now regularly swallowing 40% to 60% of a median or low-income earner’s monthly earnings, so that workers’ real-terms purchasing power has also fallen significantly. 

It’s in this context that the explosion of public fury over Maricarmen’s eviction and subsequent death gave new muscle to tenant unions and radical labour groups, who flooded the streets demanding an immediate slash to rents by 50%, the outright expropriation of empty speculative housing, and an absolute ban on tourist apartments. Slogans often seen in the demonstrations include “towards a general strike” and “rents are suffocating us, the working class resists”. Refusing to settle for inaction by the government, these grassroots movements and militant unions issued a direct call for a general strike and working-class mobilisation, challenging the government to choose between protecting property speculators or defending human survival.

The broader Spanish left, spanning the historic dynamics of the Socialist Workers' Party, the Unite electoral alliance, and radical municipalist movements, has long wrestled with the friction between institutional compromise and radical transformation. When the parliamentary left tries to navigate housing and economic collapse through half-measures, it creates a dangerous political vacuum.

On one side, it triggers fury from a mobilised working class demanding real expropriation, strict rent caps, and bans on speculative tourism. On the other hand, it gives an opening to the populist right. 

The lesson from Spain’s fractured left is absolute: when social democracy manages the status quo rather than dismantling the mechanisms of extraction, the left insurgency grows out of necessity in the streets, squares, and tent cities. It is hard not to read this as a warning to the UK. With the socialist government in Spain losing votes to the right and an increasingly restless radical left, the election is tough for Sánchez. 

The illusion that a centre-left administration can take its core vote for granted while practising safe, technocratic politics is shattering. If Burnham and Labour want to immunise themselves against a rising left-wing insurgency, the lapse of voters into abstentionism, or voters flirting with the far right, they must question the safety-first posture of Burnham’s first Budget. 

That means moving beyond rhetoric. It means actively ending the 40 years of neoliberalism, as Burnham has said he’s committed to doing. And it means championing decisive, material interventions: a Marshall Plan-style industrial strategy, an uncompromised foreign policy, massive public housebuilding, strict nationwide rent controls, public ownership of utilities, and an unapologetic war on economic inequality. 

Anything less is just managing the decline, and voters know it.

## This week in history

**The Tonypandy Riots • 21 November 1910**

On the nights of 21 and 22 November 1910, the bitter Cambrian Combine coal dispute in South Wales boiled over into the Tonypandy Riots. After nearly 30,000 miners were locked out by owners over a dispute regarding poverty wages, striking workers moved to shut the local pits down entirely. In response, Home Secretary Winston Churchill deployed the Metropolitan Police and British Army units to crush the strike, resulting in hundreds of injuries and at least one death. Tonypandy shattered the myth that the state was a neutral arbiter in class conflict, severely radicalised the British labour movement, and cemented the necessity of uncompromising trade union power.

The memory of Tonypandy helped forge a unique tradition of radical working-class politics on the Celtic fringes of the UK. Our archival piece explores how the lockout of the Rhondda miners fostered enduring political bonds between the Welsh and Scottish left.

### How a security scare at RAF Fairford upended US air strategy
URL: https://www.opendemocracy.net/raf-fairford-security-scare-iran-upended-us-air-strategy/
Last updated: 2026-11-23T19:57:26.000Z
**Listen to this article** [Sign up for a free account to do so](#/portal/signup) 

Listen to this article. (5 min 0 sec)

15s 15s 

Audio generated with a low-energy computer, no data-centre used.

Two men accused of involvement in a security incident that saw petrol-laden vans driven to RAF Fairford two months ago, allegedly on orders from Iran, will stand trial in November next year after appearing in court at the Old Bailey this morning. Their lawyers indicated that the men will plead not guilty.

When police detained five men near Fairford, the large air base in Gloucestershire, back in September, the reasons for their arrests were far from clear. Intense speculation followed, with theories over the alleged wrongdoing ranging from fuel being stolen from nearby farms through to an Iranian plot to target US heavy bombers stationed at the RAF base.

The latter may have seemed unlikely, but only a week later the US Air Force (USAF) suddenly recalled all 12 of its B-1B Lancers at Fairford back to the United States. As I wrote for [openDemocracy](https://www.opendemocracy.net/did-iranian-drones-drive-us-bombers-out-of-raf-fairford/) at the time, if it was true that Iran had the capability to strike the UK, the implications would be huge, forcing the USAF to rethink its standard operating procedures for basing aircraft in friendly countries. 

Since then, several developments have focused attention on this theory. First, after prime minister [Andy Burnham](https://www.opendemocracy.net/tag/andy-burnham/) said there were [“strong indications” that Iran had played a role in the Fairford incident](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cjwyz59k5y75o?ref=opendemocracy.net), the two men were charged under the UK’s National Security Act 2023, which makes it an offence to assist a foreign intelligence service. “In this case,” said the UK’s head of counter terrorism policing, announcing the charges at the end of last month, “we believe that country to be Iran.”

Then, on 10 November, Reuters reported that the USAF had [unexpectedly moved at least ten KC-135R Stratotanker air-to-air refuelling planes](https://www.militarytimes.com/news/your-military/2026/11/10/britain-says-its-bases-are-safe-after-us-refueling-planes-evacuated/?ref=opendemocracy.net) from RAF Mildenhall. One flew to a base in Scotland, two to Spain and one to Germany, with six more moving elsewhere. 

Days later, the US Justice Department indicted three foreign nationals with Iranian links for allegedly conspiring to organise terror attacks and attempted attacks across Europe and the US, including at the RAF base, according to [US defence journal Military Times](https://www.militarytimes.com/news/your-military/2026/11/12/3-iranian-backed-men-indicted-in-attempted-plot-on-raf-fairford/?ref=opendemocracy.net). One of the men was already in prison in New York at the time of the Fairford incident, while the other two were reportedly in Iran.

Details beyond that are sketchy for now. But what seems clear is that the US Air Force has grown concerned about the security of its main bomber base in Europe, and has evacuated its aircraft accordingly. The same appears to be true of its main base for tanker aircraft, RAF Mildenhall in Suffolk.

This is hugely significant. In times of war or even regional crisis in the Middle East, the USAF flies its heavy bombers from their home bases in the continental US to be stationed at Fairford (where it also has personnel permanently based), ready to go whenever they get the signal from the Pentagon. In addition to this and Mildenhall, the USAF also uses Berkshire’s RAF Welford as a huge US munitions dump, storing many different types of bombs and missiles at the site.

All of this is a useful reminder that while [Donald Trump](https://www.opendemocracy.net/tag/donald-trump/)’s [war against Iran](https://www.opendemocracy.net/tag/iran-war/) started without any kind of UN authorisation and breaks international law, Burnham’s government is up to its eyes in the whole operation. But it also raises questions about what will happen if Trump decides to return to a full-scale air war, as he has recently threatened.

If the USAF thinks it is unable to use Fairford, its heavy bombers – which would be essential to such a major operation – will have to fly an additional 8,000 miles from bases in the US and be dependent on multiple air-to-air refuelling operations. It’s yet another sign that Iran’s overall capabilities have exceeded Western expectations. 

Since the war started at the end of February, [Iran has attacked](https://apnews.com/article/iran-war-us-base-damage-trump-26e0f05e01d6f56ff46f7c1a14384f7c?ref=opendemocracy.net) 26 US bases and other military sites across the Middle East, targeting early warning systems, satellite communications platforms, air bases and logistics hubs. One target in particular stands out: the headquarters of the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet in Bahrain, which has been repeatedly attacked by Iranian armed drones and missiles, most recently yesterday.

In earlier attacks, Iran succeeded in inflicting so much damage on the Fifth Fleet’s major logistics hub that it had to be closed down. Several hundred US personnel and their families were evacuated and the Pentagon began to move many of its planes and much of its equipment and supplies away from the region. 

Regardless of how the war ends, the Iranian leadership will continue to exploit the many weaknesses in US warfighting, which will be studied in detail in military ministries across the world, in defence academies, think tanks, arms companies and security and intelligence agencies in the years to come. The US will have much to learn, starting with the need to accept that your opponent is at least as able as you.
### I study mass protests: Here’s why GenZ has taken to the streets
URL: https://www.opendemocracy.net/i-study-mass-protests-heres-why-genz-has-taken-to-the-streets/
Last updated: 2026-11-25T11:41:43.000Z
**Listen to this article** [Sign up for a free account to do so](#/portal/signup) 

Listen to this article. (5 min 46 sec)

15s 15s 

Audio generated with a low-energy computer, no data-centre used.

Over the last few months, we have seen massive protests in country after country. Though current protests have not been limited to young people, many have been driven by them, leading to the label of ‘Gen Z Protests’. 

Protests are often driven by particular national or local grievances, and in some ways that is also true of current protests. But history has also given us distinct international protest waves, spreading through countries, regions, and the world. We are seemingly living through such a protest wave. 

Historically, such protest waves have some shared grievances that say something about the world’s economic, political and social situation at that given time. When we experience an international protest wave, it is therefore important to ask: *why* and *why* *now*? 

I started my academic life studying the 2011 anti-austerity protests in Spain and later turned to the 2019 climate protests in the UK and across the world. Now we need to understand the 2026 Gen Z protests.

[Recent polling ](https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1Oo1EogLdZR-itIZ4oUJyK%5FQEtBPRt9RA?ref=opendemocracy.net)by the Global Fund for a New Economy about the protests in six countries has shown what many of us suspected: These protests are about the cost-of-living increases since the pandemic that have been worsened by Trump’s war on Iran. The same study shows that young people are much more supportive of the protests, giving further credence to the Gen Z label. So, what is the reality that young people are confronted with, which makes them so angry?

The neoliberal policies implemented across the 1980s and 90s started the dismantling of the welfare states that many are now angry about. For sure, neoliberal globalisation was met with significant resistance, from Chiapas to Seattle and Genoa, in what came to be known as the Global Justice Movement. But neoliberal globalisation also created wealthy middle classes across the Global North and South. Whilst there were severe crises in countries from Thailand to Argentina, the model worked for many around the world until the 2008 crash.

Across Europe, the response to that crash was austerity for the many and abundance for the few. This austerity further undermined the welfare states at a time when people needed them more than ever. When the economic crisis and austerity started to be felt through unemployment, precarity and evictions, people across the world responded on the streets through the Indignados, the Arab Spring and Occupy. 

Despite continued austerity and a kind of permanent sense of crisis, the middle classes in many countries carried on. Though wages in many Global North countries stagnated or decreased in relation to inflation, persistently low interest rates kept our consumption afloat. But when interest rates increased sharply after the pandemic, there came a cost-of-living crisis. That crisis has sharpened further with Trump’s war in Iran and sky-rocketing fuel prices. 

This cost-of-living crisis is felt all the much deeper by those trying to enter the labour and housing markets: Gen Z.

What is then the reality confronting Gen Z? Starting with education, the match that set French streets ablaze, educational reforms and budget cuts have vastly increased educational inequality in most countries. That much is clear from looking at the latest Pisa scores. Though the protests are yet to reach the UK, despite its good Pisa scores, students have much reason to be angry here. A highly marketised higher education system has the students being indebted for decades with high fees and loans with high interest. At the same time, their lecturers are being made redundant at a staggering rate and courses are closed in a system crying out for government intervention and investment. 

When these students try to enter the labour market, things are not better. The practically ungoverned AI revolution is removing many entry-level jobs. Many of us are scared of being replaced by AI, but for young people, this is already reality. It is precisely this fast deterioration in labour market expectations that has been central in protests in India.

Housing is another basic necessity that is ever harder to access. Decades of marketising housing has led to every cohort paying a larger share of their income towards housing than the one before. Nowhere is ‘inherit-ocracy’ as evident, with the only hope of buying a home depending on support from your living or dead parents. It is no coincidence that housing is what brought millions of Spanish workers out on a general strike, since that country has one of the most marketised, financialised and unequal housing systems in Europe. 

This inequality and lack of opportunities is experienced at the same time as the ‘broligarchy’ is becoming ever wealthier and powerful globally. Their data centres, popping up all over the world, are stealing our water, our energy, and our jobs. 

They want us to blame it all on immigration. But those taking to the streets around the world know that the blame lies with the broligarchs and with the unwillingness or inability of states to address the true roots of these problems. 

It was particularly interesting, therefore, to see the new survey data from the Global Fund for a New Economy showing huge support for a billionaire’s tax. Even more encouraging was seeing the punishment of the most pro-broligarch candidates in the US midterms. Not to speak of the immediate result of the Spanish general strike being the passing of the housing law intended to protect tenants. Let’s be inspired and continue like that! At the ballot box and on the streets.  
  
[Dr Oscar Berglund](https://www.bristol.ac.uk/people/person/Oscar-Berglund-2742b53a-dfd3-416a-af8d-13655e3f1a6b/?ref=opendemocracy.net) is Senior Lecturer in Policy Studies at University of Bristol and expert in protest and repression of protest
### Microsoft outage raises questions over UK’s critical digital infrastructure
URL: https://www.opendemocracy.net/microsoft-outage-raises-questions-over-uks-critical-digital-infrastructure/
Last updated: 2026-11-25T11:42:25.000Z
**Listen to this article** [Sign up for a free account to do so](#/portal/signup) 

Listen to this article. (11 min 14 sec)

15s 15s 

Audio generated with a low-energy computer, no data-centre used.

The full effects of the global Microsoft outage, which began last Friday and [lasted a few days](https://x.com/MSFT365Status/status/2121485746334777593?ref=opendemocracy.net), are now coming into sharp focus. In the UK, essential and non-essential services were disrupted as millions of users at institutions including [schools, hospitals, police forces](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/13/how-microsoft-outage-has-affected-key-public-services-in-the-uk?ref=opendemocracy.net), and [government agencies](https://www.civilserviceworld.com/news/article/civil-servants-hit-by-global-microsoft-outage?ref=opendemocracy.net) lost access to Microsoft 365, Outlook, Teams, and the generative AI assistant Copilot.

Almost [all NHS Trusts](https://www.bmj.com/content/395/bmj-2026-101456.full?ref=opendemocracy.net) suffered email outages, leaving some medical staff resorting to paper records to deliver healthcare in hospitals and GP surgeries. Some medical appointments and operations, including caesareans, were [cancelled](https://www.bmj.com/content/395/bmj-2026-101456.full?ref=opendemocracy.net). Police forces were unable to receive online crime reports, urging members to report urgent and non-urgent information by phone instead. 

In the justice system, cases set to be heard at magistrates’, Crown, and civil courts were cancelled or delayed, including the [Manchester-based trial](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/13/how-microsoft-outage-has-affected-key-public-services-in-the-uk?ref=opendemocracy.net) of nine men accused of raping a woman drugged by her husband. Even the machinery of government itself ground to a halt, with as many as [99% of civil servants using Microsoft](https://hansard.parliament.uk/commons/2026-11-16/debates/52FEDF8F-7F19-47A6-9FB7-1930054C9061/Microsoft365Outage?ref=opendemocracy.net) for communications, including the Ministry of Defence and the Department for Work and Pensions. 

“Eleanor in the UK could not send urgent cancer referrals. Hugo could not pay his staff, who live paycheque to paycheque. Mohamed, a pharmacist, could not dispense prescriptions,” Victoria Collins, the Liberal Democrats’ spokesperson, told Parliament on 16 November, three days after the outage began. 

Ian Murray, the minister for creative industries, media, and online safety, [reassured parliamentarians](https://hansard.parliament.uk/commons/2026-11-16/debates/52FEDF8F-7F19-47A6-9FB7-1930054C9061/Microsoft365Outage?ref=opendemocracy.net) that “emergency departments remained open” and there were “no major critical service impacts, and public sector resilience plans were in place”. He admitted the “incident could have been more serious if it had lasted longer”.

“No single provider should have such a major impact across the NHS, police and other frontline services,” said Liberal Democrats Cabinet Office spokesperson Lisa Smart in a statement on 13 November. “The government must urgently set out a plan to secure our digital sovereignty and stop relying on a few big US tech firms,” she added. 

## The UK’s digital sovereignty gap

The UK does not currently have a defined digital sovereignty strategy, although the government has invested in domestic technology to reduce dependence on foreign suppliers. 

“We have put £500m in the [sovereign AI fund](https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/6a295455db0592d809052c11/D%5FT%5FSector%5FPlan%5FPDF%5FF%5FA.pdf?ref=opendemocracy.net), £1bn into the [AI hardware plan](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/a-decisive-shift-to-power-british-ai-new-11-billion-plan-to-back-chip-firms-boost-computing-power-and-skills-for-the-ai-revolution?ref=opendemocracy.net) and £2bn into [quantum investment](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/uks-quantum-leap-tohelp-beat-diseasedeliver-high-paid-jobs-and-strengthen-national-security-as-first-country-in-the-world-to-roll-out-quantum?ref=opendemocracy.net), so that the government can be a first customer for some of these technologies, giving them routes to market,” said Murray, in response to [calls from the Liberal Democrats](https://hansard.parliament.uk/commons/2026-11-16/debates/52FEDF8F-7F19-47A6-9FB7-1930054C9061/Microsoft365Outage?ref=opendemocracy.net) to publish a digital sovereign strategy following the outage. 

Murray recognised that reliance on a small number of technology suppliers “can create risks to resilience, competition and value for money”, summing up the government’s approach as “keep(ing) access to the best technology, while building greater choice and stronger UK capability.”

“It is really important that our public sector has access to the best technology, and for now, there isn't necessarily a British version of that to buy that would be good enough,” Roa Powell, senior research fellow at the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR), told Tech Policy Press. 

The think tank defines sovereignty broadly as “the ability for a country to control and shape the technology it relies on”. The recent Microsoft outage specifically highlighted the UK’s lack of what IPPR terms “operational resilience”: the ability to keep “critical systems working if access, terms or suppliers change”.

IPPR broadly agrees with the government that building capability through industrial strategy is a priority, but with [less than £1 in £6](https://files.ippr.org/production/Downloads/Locked%5Fin%5FNov26.pdf?dm=1794219949&ref=opendemocracy.net) spent by the public sector with its biggest technology suppliers going to British companies, far greater investment is needed to tip the scales in favour of British technology.

France, for example, has for years pursued a strategy of building technology in-house – such as La Suite, an open-source digital workplace used by French public servants – and diversifying its supply chains, “so that if you do see a failure like this, not everyone's on Microsoft”, added Powell.

A further weakness highlighted by Powell is that the UK’s sovereign technology strategy has “been largely focused on AI, which does, to an extent, neglect some of the really deeper, long-standing problems, especially in cloud,” she said, “which is one of the most concentrated markets and most fundamental to how the public sector operates.”

The UK government is in agreement with its critics that the country’s lack of digital sovereignty limits control over its digital infrastructure. While efforts to build British infrastructure are underway, the market concentration held by Microsoft and a handful of other US-owned Big Tech providers compounds this dependence.

## Sovereignty requires more than homegrown technology

Building British technology would increase control over the country’s tech stack, but replacing one monopoly with another would still leave services vulnerable to widespread outages. 

“Sovereignty is actually about building resilience, and the best way to do that is through diversification,” Taylor Gese, UK lead at the European think tank Future of Technology Institute, told Tech Policy Press.

“We're not asking the government to quit Microsoft and Amazon tomorrow – it would be totally impossible to do so – but if you diversify your critical national infrastructure across a couple of cloud providers, at least a couple more, then when the Microsoft outage happens again, hopefully your hospitals and schools make it through all right.”

Microsoft [confirmed the outage](https://x.com/Microsoft/status/2121282013600907325?ref=opendemocracy.net) was a “technical issue”, not a cyberattack, attributing the incident to problems involving its network infrastructure, rather than malicious activity.

The fact that UK services could be disrupted by a technical error points to overreliance on a concentrated market as a significant risk to digital sovereignty, not simply the location of technology providers or geopolitical tensions. 

The Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) identified this vulnerability last year in its investigation of the UK cloud infrastructure market. Its findings showed that Microsoft and Amazon Web Services [each hold up to 40%](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/cma-independent-inquiry-group-publishes-provisional-findings-in-cloud-services-market-investigation?ref=opendemocracy.net) of UK cloud customer spend. The regulator concluded that with the market so highly concentrated, “competition is not working well.”

[In a speech delivered at Chatham House](https://www.wired-gov.net/wg/news.nsf/articles/Power+agency+and+good+growth+17112026162500?open&ref=opendemocracy.net) four days after the outage, Sarah Cardell, the CMA’s chief executive, argued that the issue is not that Microsoft is so widely used, but whether “the strength of the ecosystem makes it harder for organisations to switch, or to combine Microsoft products with those of other providers.” 

As Copilot becomes ever more embedded in the everyday technology used by government and public services, the risk is that this dependence “determines the AI technologies it can use in future,” she said.

Powell described this as one of the more “insidious harms” resulting from a lack of digital sovereignty. “Microsoft knows that when they dominate the market, they can charge higher prices. They can bundle together their AI with their software. Like that's the reason why so many people in government use Copilot, right? Because it's not the best AI tool, it's not necessarily the cheapest, but it comes easily available with existing Microsoft services.”

The CMA ultimately concluded its three-year cloud market investigation in March 2026 by accepting [voluntary commitments](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/cma-announces-package-of-actions-on-business-software-and-cloud-services?ref=opendemocracy.net) from Microsoft and Amazon Web Services to lower barriers to switching and multi-cloud adoption, rather than pursuing legally binding obligations. This decision [diverged from recommendations](https://www.techpolicy.press/uk-cloud-regulator-opts-for-voluntary-commitments-launches-microsoft-investigation/?ref=opendemocracy.net) made by the CMA's own investigation board, leaving critics questioning whether the regulator has the teeth to address structural competition problems in a sector that underpins critical infrastructure.

An openDemocracy investigation earlier this year questioned whether the [appointment of ex-Amazon boss Doug Gurr](https://www.opendemocracy.net/en/doug-gurr-amazon-competition-market-authority-tech-regulation-watchdog-natural-history-museum/) to the CMA could shape its “priorities, framing, and appetite for intervention.” 

“Now is the time for the government to signal to the CMA that they should take action,” said Jim Killock, the executive director of digital rights campaigning organisation Open Rights Group.

The CMA, IPPR, and Future of Technology Institute all agree that the UK government can, and should, use its purchasing power to actively shape markets. Public spending accounts for up to [10% of UK demand](https://www.wired-gov.net/wg/news.nsf/articles/Power+agency+and+good+growth+17112026162500?open&ref=opendemocracy.net) for cloud infrastructure services, giving the government considerable purchasing power. The government has already committed to spending [£9bn](https://www.theregister.com/on-prem/2025/08/07/faced-with-40b-budget-hole-uk-commits-9b-to-microsoft/600079?ref=opendemocracy.net) on Microsoft products and services between 2024 and 2029.

At present, government departments are responsible for contracting services separately, but buying technology as one customer, or [pooling budgets with the EU](https://files.ippr.org/production/Downloads/Locked%5Fin%5FNov26.pdf?dm=1794219949&ref=opendemocracy.net) as recommended by IPPR, could force acquiescence to more favourable terms and conditions until the UK can diversify its tech stack with homegrown tech or the best products from different providers. 

“That doesn't just mean cheaper technology; it might mean terms where the UK government has more control over their settings, control over where their data ends up being processed, control over how much notice they have to give to Microsoft before they switch to a new supplier,” said Powell. 

“All of these are things that give the government way more flexibility in how they respond, both in an emergency, but more so in kind of long-term decisions so you don't get locked in in the way that you do with Palantir.”

The controversial US technology firm’s contract to deliver a federated data platform to NHS England has raised widespread [concerns over vendor lock-in](https://www.foxglove.org.uk/2026/11/17/fdp-end-2029-kick-palantir-out-of-the-nhs/?ref=opendemocracy.net), due to clauses that would make it difficult for the NHS to withdraw data from the platform or switch to another supplier. 

Days after the Microsoft outage, health ministers announced that the £330m contract with Palantir would be [extended until 2029](https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026/nov/16/ministers-to-end-palantir-contract-nhs-england-2029?ref=opendemocracy.net), after which a new procurement process would allow UK companies to bid for it. Health minister James Frith said the decision was made to reduce “over-dependence” on one supplier and boost UK sovereignty in health technologies. 

Many campaigners, including Open Rights Group, expressed disappointment that the government didn’t utilise the spring 2027 break clause. While British companies are [lining up](https://www.ft.com/content/f69f1f6b-cdbe-40d6-b76d-fb712ca58b51?accessToken=zwAAAaHwIsv8kdP2nx9rzb5A1tO3bftxLKWLUQ.MEQCIHg0rMI2x9kxIH5apkToznHMwOYbc1bjMHB2zGyeaiR6AiBi-9HwvFu6gzAeSyhWZIpjslE%5Fik1Z3-oLLxjCJTekPw&sharetype=gift&token=856146c4-b2b8-4332-9cea-aa7c8a49220f&syn-25a6b1a6=1&ref=opendemocracy.net) to bid for the lucrative contract, without the right terms and conditions, any alternative could become even further embedded into the NHS. 

The Microsoft outage was the latest reminder of the risks of relying on a small number of technology providers, following the [Google outage](https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026/oct/20/power-outage-google-datacentre-london-widespread-disruption?ref=opendemocracy.net) last month and the [Amazon Web Services outage](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cev1en9077ro?ref=opendemocracy.net) a year prior. 

The Conservatives and Liberal Democrats have each told the government that the incident must be a “wake-up call” about the nation’s lack of digital resilience. But unless the government translates that warning into procurement reform to improve market competition, immediate turning points appear unlikely.

The [Milburn Review](https://www.opendemocracy.net/tag/milburn-review/) is a highly ambitious piece of work that starts with the right principle: young people want to work. They’re capable and have aspirations. [NEETs](https://www.opendemocracy.net/tag/NEETs/) – that horrible term for 18- 24-year-olds who are not in education, employment, or training – have not failed; they have been failed by the system.

Yet [the report, which was published this week and whose recommendations the government is considering](https://www.opendemocracy.net/milburn-review-scrapping-pip-young-adults-risks-pushing-unpaid-carers-into-poverty/), manages to almost entirely overlook the fact that young women often face barriers to work that are directly linked to their gender.

Every day, we at Young Women’s Trust hear from young women who desperately want to work but are unable to do so due to a lack of childcare or mental health needs that employers are unwilling to accommodate. Others tell us they spend long, repetitive days producing hundreds of job applications, which disappear into the void of AI-based recruitment portals with no reply. It’s no wonder that so many say they’re losing hope for the future.

Young women make up nearly half of all NEETs, and the vast majority are deemed ‘economically inactive’, meaning they are not in a position to work or apply for jobs. For a third, this is because they are caring for children, compared with just 6% of young men. Quite apart from the fact that raising children is far from ‘inactive’ – it is both hard work and economically productive – the Milburn Review made little mention of the specific needs of these young women.

The 267 pages of recommendations contain next to nothing on the importance of having accessible, affordable childcare that fits around the hours that young women actually work. Many are seeking employment in social care or hospitality, sectors where workdays rarely fit the standard 9-5 offered by most childcare providers. 

Similarly, if employment schemes and new training opportunities are to genuinely work for young women, they must offer flexible hours so that young mums and carers can fit them around childcare – another fact overlooked by the report.

We’re seeing entry-level jobs that give young women their first step on the career ladder disappear fastest. Milburn’s proposal to reduce employers’ National Insurance contributions for young people in the retail and hospitality sectors may go some way to addressing this, as may the recommendation to open up more entry-level jobs in the NHS and the public sector – typically large employers of women. But we also need to see more done to open up young women’s access to the male-dominated sectors, such as defence and construction, that are backed for growth. 

Young women tend to be overrepresented in insecure and precarious work, leaving them with little power and dependent on their managers deciding whether or not to offer them additional shifts. Such power imbalances enable workplace sexual harassment, discrimination and violation – all of which we know to disproportionately affect young women.

It’s unsurprising then that our research has found that insecure work can affect young women’s mental health and lead to them being pushed out of work, or deciding to leave. Each time this happens, it can cause a further knock to their confidence that makes it harder to obtain employment. A vicious cycle. 

This is particularly worrying given young women are already more likely to have common mental health problems than any other demographic, and a third of those we support tell us that their mental health has prevented them from applying for a job. We’re glad, then, to see quick-access mental health support with a fast track for unemployed young people as a cornerstone of Milburn’s recommendations. 

It’s essential that [Andy Burnham](https://www.opendemocracy.net/tag/andy-burnham/)’s government focuses on quality, secure work that young women can sustain – not just any work at any cost. Milburn’s suggestion that ministers dilute plans to clamp down on zero-hours contracts will ring alarm bells for young women who need job security if they are to thrive. 

There’s no doubt that the Milburn Review is laudable, ambitious, and potentially transformative. But it needs to be so for *all* young people; it needs a gender lens. Work works differently for young women and young men. The barriers they face when it comes to finding and staying in work are different, so the solutions must be, too. 

Measures put in place to tackle the increase in the number of young people who are NEET must be assessed for their impact on young women and men separately, with outcomes measured by gender. Only then can we ensure that no young woman is left behind because of barriers that exist purely because she is a woman.

Among his most notable recommendations is a suggestion that ministers should scrap the two main disability benefits for 18- 24-year-olds in England and Wales: the [Universal Credit](https://www.opendemocracy.net/tag/universal-credit/) health payment (UCH) and the [Personal Independence Payment](https://www.opendemocracy.net/tag/PIP/) (PIP).

Unlike UCH, which is means-tested, PIP is paid regardless of a claimant’s employment status, and acts as a “passport” that opens up access to other benefits and entitlements. These include Carer’s Allowance and the carer’s element of Universal Credit, both of which are available to unpaid carers looking after a PIP recipient.

Unpaid carers are usually family members whose ability to take on paid work is limited by their caring responsibilities. Helen Walker, the chief executive at Carers UK, noted that removing PIP from young adults will not remove the need for this care, but could push some households into financial difficulty if their carers also lose access to financial support.

“Many unpaid carers have given up employment, reduced their working hours or sacrificed career opportunities to provide care,” she said. “If a young person’s PIP entitlement ends and their parent or other unpaid carer consequently loses Carer’s Allowance, households could face two simultaneous reductions in financial support.

“Any reform of disability benefits must protect both disabled young people and the unpaid carers who support them. The need for care does not disappear simply because the benefit system changes.”

Under Milburn’s plans, most unemployed young Disabled adults would receive a new benefit at the same rate as the basic non-disabled Universal Credit payment. Some would also be eligible for a new Additional Cost Allowance, effectively a replacement for PIP, designed to contribute to individual disability-related costs that are “significant, well established and ongoing”, rather than being paid at a set rate. 

Only a small number of very severely Disabled young adults would be able to claim a new long-term disability benefit. Walker urged the government to publish a comprehensive impact assessment report setting out the consequences that the potential changes would have on unpaid carers.

“The government must clarify whether new disability benefits proposed to replace PIP will provide a qualifying route to Carer's Allowance and the Universal Credit carer element,” she said. “We also need reassurance that carers currently receiving Carer's Allowance because of a young person's existing PIP award will retain entitlement during and after the transition.

“It is unclear how the assessment processes for PIP and the proposed Additional Cost Allowance will determine eligibility, and what implications this will have for access to Carer's Allowance.” 

While the government says it is still considering Milburn’s recommendations, it has so far welcomed the report’s findings. In an initial response this week, prime minister [Andy Burnham](https://www.opendemocracy.net/tag/andy-burnham/) said: “Our direction is already clear: a fundamental overhaul of how we support young people.” 

Yet carers’ benefits aren’t the only entitlements that the proposals would put at risk. 

A person receiving the enhanced mobility element of PIP – paid to those whose illness or disability causes the most severe problems getting about – can choose to exchange part of their benefit income for a car, wheelchair-accessible vehicle, or powered wheelchairs and mobility scooters under the Motability Scheme.

This and other transport-related support could also be threatened by removing PIP, said Julia Modern of Inclusion London, a charity campaigning for equality for Deaf and Disabled people. 

“A young person not meeting very strict NHS eligibility for a wheelchair may no longer be eligible for a Motability wheelchair or a wheelchair-accessible vehicle in exchange for their PIP mobility component. A young person facing inaccessible public transport may no longer be eligible for the concessionary travel or Blue Badge, which lets them get to work or college.”

“Three-quarters of people receiving Universal Credit Health are already living in deprivation,” Modern continued. “Removing PIP and UC Health for 16-24-year-olds would push them further into deprivation and away from work, and would have knock-on effects in many areas of life where these benefits act as a passport.”

Councils, many of which are already in financial difficulties, may also lose out as a result of the proposed changes. Under the current adult care system, local authorities often take some of PIP claimants’ benefit income to cover social care charges, such as one-to-one home care and use of day centres.

“While we think that no one should have to pay for social care, under the current funding system, councils will be left with significant gaps if they are no longer able to take PIP from young people,” added Modern. 

“Milburn very clearly signals that he intends the government to make similar cuts to UC Health and PIP in adult disability benefits in the future, and wants his youth cuts to be a model for them.

“But the additional employment support that he proposes is an investment that would eventually pay for itself through reduced benefits claims and increased tax receipts. The government does not have to decimate financial support for Disabled people and push us further into poverty, to invest in more accessible employment for those who need it most.”

The Department for Work and Pensions told openDemocracy that the government will carefully consider all the Milburn Review’s recommendations and issue a full response in the coming weeks.
### As winter closes in on Gaza, the UK must offer Palestinians a route to safety
URL: https://www.opendemocracy.net/flooding-gaza-uk-government-burnham-offer-palestinians-asylum-route/
Last updated: 2026-11-19T16:06:09.000Z
Across [Gaza](https://www.opendemocracy.net/tag/gaza/), families are trying to keep floodwater out of their tents. Parents are salvaging soaked mattresses and blankets, children are exposed to freezing conditions, and those who have lost almost everything are watching their remaining possessions disappear beneath the water. 

Some 226,000 Palestinians have been affected by the flooding, with more than 40,000 shelters damaged and over 9,000 beyond repair, according to [preliminary United Nations estimates](https://www.ochaopt.org/content/humanitarian-situation-report-13-november-2026?ref=opendemocracy.net). Thousands of families have been left without basic protection. 

These people face another winter without adequate shelter, healthcare or essential supplies. [The World Health Organisation warns of rising respiratory illnesses](https://www.unognewsroom.org/story/en/3323/un-geneva-press-briefing-13-november-2026?ref=opendemocracy.net), while sewage-contaminated floodwater threatens a further public health emergency. 

This is not simply a natural disaster. It follows years of bombardment, displacement and destruction by Israel, as part of what [Amnesty International](https://www.amnesty.org/en/documents/mde15/8668/2024/en/?ref=opendemocracy.net), the [UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry](https://www.un.org/unispal/document/israel-has-committed-genocide-in-the-gaza-strip-un-commission-finds-16sep25/?ref=opendemocracy.net), and the [International Association of Genocide Scholars](https://genocidescholars.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/IAGS-Resolution-on-Gaza-FINAL.pdf?ref=opendemocracy.net) have declared to be a genocide. 

Their findings demand more than expressions of concern. They demand action to protect Palestinian lives – including from the British government, which has already acknowledged that its response to Gaza has fallen short. That acknowledgement matters, but it must lead to meaningful change.

In a speech to the [Labour Party Conference](https://www.opendemocracy.net/tag/labour-party-conference/) in September, foreign secretary [Ed Miliband](https://www.opendemocracy.net/tag/ed-miliband/) described the [suffering in Gaza as a stain on the conscience of the world and Britain](https://www.jewishnews.co.uk/ed-miliband-suffering-inflicted-on-gaza-by-netanyahu-is-stain-on-conscience-of-the-world/?ref=opendemocracy.net), echoing prime minister [Andy Burnham](https://www.opendemocracy.net/tag/andy-burnham/)’s assessment that Labour had not done enough and pledging to move beyond condemning injustice towards action. On the same day, [Shabana Mahmood](https://www.opendemocracy.net/tag/shabana-mahmood/) announced [the reopening of the UK Resettlement Scheme](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/uk-resettlement-scheme-reopens-for-new-referrals??ref=opendemocracy.net), which Labour paused in December 2024\. The home secretary confirmed that Palestinian refugees would be among those offered sanctuary in Britain.

As director of Reset, a UK-wide national charity for the community-led welcome of refugees, I celebrated this announcement. We have spent years advocating for expanded safe routes, including reopening the Resettlement Scheme and introducing named sponsorship. But there is a profound difference between promising sanctuary and making it accessible.

At Reset, we hear directly from Palestinians in Gaza and neighbouring countries. They contact us desperately seeking help, asking whether there is a way to reach safety in the UK and whether the government's announcements mean they might finally have somewhere to turn.

We also hear from people in Britain trying to bring Palestinian friends and family members to safety before it is too late. People are willing to open their homes and help those they care about escape danger. Behind every enquiry is someone searching for protection, or someone terrified for the lives of people they love. 

The willingness to help exists. The need for protection is urgent. What is missing is a way to bring the two together.

Following Russia's invasion of Ukraine, Britain rightfully established emergency arrangements that enabled hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians to seek safety here. Despite challenges, those schemes demonstrated that protection pathways can be established quickly when the government commits the resources and political will. Palestinian lives deserve that same urgency.

The government should build on its commitment to support Palestinians by launching an emergency humanitarian admission route for those facing immediate danger in Gaza, including people with urgent medical needs and those with family in the UK. This should involve working with international partners to secure safe evacuation and onward travel, expanding medical evacuation arrangements so more patients can access urgent treatment alongside their immediate families, and restoring and widening refugee family reunion. 

Community Sponsorship can play an important role. Reset has supported more than 250 community groups to welcome over 1,200 refugees to the UK since 2016, including through sponsorship and labour mobility pathways for nurses. We know that safe, practical routes to protection are possible when the government, communities and organisations work together.

But responsibility cannot rest solely with charities and volunteers. The government must ensure these routes are properly resourced, accessible and supported by practical arrangements to bring people to safety.

Crucially, offering protection must never justify the permanent displacement of Palestinians from their homeland. Palestinians have the right to remain in Palestine, return to their homes and live in safety and dignity. Israel must allow the unhindered entry and distribution of humanitarian aid into Gaza, including food, medicine, shelter and essential supplies. The international community must ensure the protection of civilians and support the rebuilding of Gaza, so Palestinians can live safely in their homeland rather than being forced to leave it.

But protecting the right to remain must not mean denying the right to seek safety elsewhere. No Palestinian should be forced to leave their homeland to survive. Equally, those facing immediate danger should be able to seek protection without surrendering their right to return.

The UK has already made arrangements for Palestinians, including bringing seriously injured children from Gaza for medical treatment with their immediate families and enabling some students to continue their education here. These measures matter but remain limited against the scale of the emergency.

At Reset, we will continue working with the government, civil society and communities to strengthen refugee protection. We know Britain has the experience and communities willing to welcome people seeking safety.

As winter begins in Gaza, families are waking to flooded shelters, freezing conditions and an uncertain future. They have already endured more than anyone should be expected to bear. Britain cannot acknowledge their suffering, recognise that its response has fallen short, promise sanctuary and then leave those seeking safety without a way to reach it. 

For Palestinians facing these conditions, sanctuary is not a question for another year; it is a question of survival today.

### ‘Will it be settled before I die?’: Miners seek urgent fix to pension promise
URL: https://www.opendemocracy.net/will-it-be-settled-before-i-die-miners-seek-urgent-fix-to-pension-promise/
Last updated: 2026-11-18T12:47:10.000Z
The growing resentment among many former miners over the government’s continued refusal to set out a timeline to release £1.2bn from their pension fund could lead to Andy Burnham’s first rebellion in the Commons, openDemocracy understands.

A meeting between chancellor John Healey and the chair of the Mineworkers Pension Scheme (MPS) trustees last week failed to result in any concrete steps toward transferring the remaining funds to former miners. Instead, the pair agreed to work together to resolve the matter “within the coming weeks”.

But for many miners and their families, who expected the money to be released at last month’s Budget and paid out by Christmas, this is not good enough. 

“As a widow of a miner who worked underground for many years and died of a mining-related illness, pneumoconiosis, I am so angry this surplus is not being released to the MPS trustees,” Bernadette France, a longtime activist from the Women Against Pit Closures movement, told openDemocracy.

“How many miners have to die? I am nearly 80; will I expect to get this settled before I die? There is no justification for it to be delayed,” she added. “The members’ money built this surplus; every penny belongs to them. As a Labour government, do the honourable thing and get it settled.”

Labour MPs representing coalfield constituencies are still pushing the government hard to speed up the process. openDemocracy understands they believe they have found a way to force a debate on this in the coming weeks if the issue is not resolved. 

Kate Osbone, the party’s MP for Jarrow and Gateshead East in the north-east of England, said: “I have been clear that the remaining £1.2bn in the Mineworkers’ Pension Scheme Guarantor’s Fund belongs to former miners and their widows, and I was deeply disappointed that it was not released at the Budget.

“While this Labour government has already taken significant steps to address this historic injustice, including returning £1.5bn to members, there is still more to do. I have met with ministers and the Chancellor to discuss this. Alongside fellow Coalfield MPs, we have called for the remaining funds to be released without further delay.

“I will pursue all parliamentary processes and keep fighting until all the remaining funds are with the people they belong to.”

**‘They built the wealth of our country’**

After British Coal was privatised in 1994, the Treasury agreed to guarantee workers’ pensions in exchange for 50% of any investment surplus. As the funds didn’t fall into deficit, the Treasury never paid into them, but still gained access to the reserves. The National Union of Mineworkers estimates that miners have lost out on more than £4.4bn as a result.

Former chancellor Rachel Reeves released one of the MPS’ funds in 2024 and the sole fund for the British Coal Staff Superannuation Scheme, whose members were generally better-paid, non-mining staff, last year. 

The Guarantor’s Fund is now the final pension pot to be paid out. After assurances from ministers, miners, campaigners and coalfield MPs believed Healey would release it last month – a move that would not cost taxpayers – and were left furious when his Budget failed to set out a timetable for doing so.

Dozens of members of the scheme have already died in the three weeks since the Budget, the MPS told openDemocracy. Many fear they will not live to see their hard-fought campaign for pension justice finally achieve its full aims.

Coalfield MPs have since been lobbying hard both in Parliament and behind the scenes to secure the release of the funds, and have threatened to rebel against the Finance Bill if the matter is not resolved urgently.

This pressure resulted in a meeting between Healey and Gary Saunders, the chair of the MPS Trustees, last week. The meeting took place around midday on Thursday, but the statement agreed by both parties was not released until almost midnight that night.

“The chancellor and Mr Saunders had a full discussion about the issue,” the statement said. “The chancellor has agreed to work with MPS Trustees and their advisers to find a way to resolve this issue within the coming weeks.” 

The government has continually said it will release the funds eventually. But many miners – who say they have heard similar promises from politicians in the past – are hesitant to take this in good faith, especially as no explanation has been offered for the last-minute U-turn. 

Neal Seargent, a former miner from Barnsley, told openDemocracy: “We were very disappointed that at the 12th hour, the agreement the MPS had with the government was pulled and no one will say why, or by whom. We need transparency from the government. 

“I’m not sure how many of the original miners that started the campaign for pensions justice are left – I know of at least three that are no longer with us. I run a Facebook group for my old workmates, and almost all we get now are posts about who has died recently.”

As openDemocracy reported, MPs believe the cash was not released due to a “blunder” by the Treasury the night before Healey’s speech to Parliament. Speaking after the Budget, the prime minister told ITV News that the money “does have to be scored on the public balance sheet and that is part of the challenge that we’ve got”.

Yet reindustrialisation minister Blair McDougall confirmed last week that the fund’s release will not require any changes to accounting rules. 

Jon Trickett, the Labour MP for the constituency of Normanton and Hemsworth in West Yorkshire, has been among the miners’ most vocal advocates. He told openDemocracy: “I will always stand by the miners; they built the wealth of our country. I will do everything possible to get the matter resolved, including raising the issue in parliament to force the government to fulfill their promises in weeks, not months. 

“There is an urgency about this which is clear from the correspondence I am receiving from the former miners, many of whom are angry and feeling let down. I hope the government will be as good as its word and resolve the Guarantor’s Fund imminently.”
