## This week in history

**The fall of the Berlin Wall • 9 November 1989**

On 9 November 1989, after weeks of mass protest across East Germany, the Berlin Wall fell. Within months, communist governments across Eastern Europe had collapsed. The moment felt briefly like the dawn of a new era. What followed was more complicated: rapid privatisation, the impoverishment of working-class communities, the rise of oligarchs, and eventually the authoritarian backlash visible across the former Eastern Bloc today.

This week's archive piece examines how the vacuum left by the fall of the Berlin Wall allowed reactionary neo-Nazi subcultures in the former GDR to mature into modern electoral movements like the AfD.

### ‘Coining it in the City’: What Starmer’s Aides Did Next
URL: https://www.opendemocracy.net/coining-it-in-the-city-what-starmers-aides-did-next/
Last updated: 2026-11-13T21:16:04.000Z
Soon after Morgan McSweeney left Downing Street this February in the wake of the Peter Mandelson scandal, he told the BBC he was ["committing to being out of politics"](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ce8j2e38zzgo?ref=opendemocracy.net) for the next few years. By August however, the chief architect of Keir Starmer’s ill-fated tenure as Prime Minister had established his own firm, McSweeney Advisory, which will offer strategic advice on politics.

McSweeney isn’t the only Starmerite alumni to set up their own ‘one-man-band’ advisory firms, openDemocracy can reveal. 

After pledging to reform lobbying and clean-up money in politics, the so-called Starmer-project has spawned a mini-cottage industry of consultants and advisors, that includes Baroness Martin, a former top adviser to Starmer’s chancellor Rachel Reeves and Starmer’s former communications’ director Ben Nunn. 

The irony is not lost on Labour veterans.

“They waged a dirty tricks campaign to take control of the party, then wasted a massive opportunity. Meanwhile we’re still here, in government, fighting for working people and trying to clean up the mess they left, while they swan off to coin it in the City,” as one staffer said, adding that these advisers are now being rewarded “not for failure, but for doing what their corporate backers wanted the whole time”.

Transparency activists and anti-corruption activists, meanwhile, describe the current lobbying rules as “pitiful”, with past research estimating that the current framework captures less than 1% of the actual lobbying which takes place in Westminster.

## **Value Added Exemptions**

Advisory firms often fall outside the narrow legislative definition of ‘consultant lobbying’. Rather than contacting ministers directly on behalf of their clients (which could trigger transparency legislation), these firms skirt the rules by offering paid-for-advice to their clients on how to interact with the government, or how to pursue their policy policy goals based on the deep knowledge the advisors have acquired over years spent in party politics and in government.

Campaigners have warned that the current lobbying rules also mean that small firms of this type are well-suited to make use of a loophole which means that, even if they do carry out work which meets the narrow definition of consultant lobbying, they still may never have to register or declare their clients. 

This loophole in the Lobbying Act, known as the so-called ‘VAT exemption’, means a company or individual is not required to register as a consultant lobbyist – no matter how much actual lobbying they do which would otherwise meet the statutory definition – if they are not a VAT registered business.

In the past, this has meant that MPs have been let off for breaching lobbying rules, because they are not VAT registered businesses, or that major lobbying firms, like the now-defunct Global Counsel, have not been required to register clients that have been billed through their overseas subsidiaries. 

MPs and campaigners have also highlighted how this exemption means relatively small businesses whose turnover is less than the VAT threshold of £90,000 are not required to register. In practice this means that an individual lobbyist who sets up a company to serve one or two large clients could still carry out a significant amount of paid lobbying without ever needing to register. 

Such flaws in the Lobbying Act are so self-evident that even industry representative bodies for the lobbying industry itself are in favour of a stricter, more comprehensive system to regulate the industry.

Senior campaign lead at Spotlight on Corruption Kamila Kingstone told openDemocracy: “The fact that even powerful and influential consultant lobbyists can get away with not putting their name on the lobbying register highlights the pitiful state of the UK’s lobbying rules. 

“Experts have repeatedly pointed out that the VAT exemption is a massive loophole, but successive governments have repeatedly ignored it.”

## **A McSweet Deal**

Senior advisers that leave government to take up private sector roles must get sign-off from the Civil Service Commission, which assesses potential conflicts of interest and imposes conditions on their employment – though in practice the commission has no formal powers to investigate or enforce these rules. 

When openDemocracy reached out to McSweeney, he said his firm offers “strategic advice and analysis on political developments, geopolitics, democratic security and related issues”. 

“My work involves helping organisations understand political and geopolitical developments, not seeking to influence government decisions on their behalf,” he said. 

Rachel Reeves’ top adviser throughout her time as shadow chancellor and in government has also set up shop as a corporate adviser, establishing Katie Martin Advisory earlier this year, despite sitting in the House of Lords as a serving peer. 

The now-ennobled Baroness Martin of Brockley had as much influence over and insight into Starmerism's economic platform as any other adviser in government. She also led on business engagement, developing relationships with City firms and other major Treasury stakeholders. 

In addition, Baroness Martin has taken up a senior advisory role with Peel Hunt, an investment bank she met with several times in office, and will support the bank to develop relationships with ministers, while sitting as a peer in the House of Lords. 

According to correspondence published by the Civil Service Commission, Baroness Martin "will advise Peel Hunt's leadership on brand and positioning to expand their presence in the UK" but will also advise on "how to strengthen relationships with officials, ministers and regional leaders in government". Baroness Martin told the commission she "would not facilitate these relationships personally" and confirmed her role "will not involve contact with, or lobbying of, government".

Baroness Martin met with Peel Hunt formally twice in government and acknowledged she had likely met representatives of the bank a further “two or three times at events”. She was also involved in conversations about London IPOs, a policy area she acknowledged Peel Hunt "had an interest in". Her new job includes supporting the bank's "emerging work with the London Stock Exchange to encourage more companies to launch on the UK stock market".

Alongside her advisory work Baroness Martin has also joined the board of ThinkLabour, the organisation formerly known as Labour Together; the Commission approved the unpaid role on 8 October. She sits on the board alongside veteran finance lobbyist Mike Craven, founder of public affairs agency Lexington. 

Beyond McSweeney and Baroness Martin, few figures have been as close to the Starmer project for as long as Ben Nunn. He was Starmer's communications director in opposition, then Reeves'. He left the party to work for [Lexington](https://morningstaronline.co.uk/article/f/labour-party-becomes-lobbyists-party?ref=opendemocracy.net) for a time, then returned in November 2025 to replace Baroness Martin as Reeves’ chief of staff, staying until the project’s collapse in July.

He is now sole director of Arlington Road Consultants, a political advisory seemingly named after the "Arlington Road" group that plotted to oust Jeremy Corbyn and install Starmer as Labour leader. 

Earlier this month, the Mail on Sunday reported that Nunn and Reeves had met two City firms days before the Budget, to discuss "the political advice the pair could offer". Sources told the paper that both chief executives had met Reeves several times while she was Chancellor. The Conservative chairman, Kevin Hollinrake, has asked the independent adviser on ministerial standards to investigate.

In response to the Mandelson scandal, Starmer’s No10 commissioned the Ethics and Integrity Commission (EIC) to produce the latest in a long series of independent reviews into lobbying reform which reported back earlier this year.

Starmer’s administration did not act on the EIC’s recommendations, though they came not long before he was ousted by Andy Burnham, whose administration is yet to commit to any reform.

Kingstone and other campaigners have urged the government to look seriously at the recommendations put forward by the EIC, including to broaden out the statutory definition of consultant lobbying to capture a much wider range of activity. 

She said: “The government needs to accept the Ethics and Integrity Commission’s recommendations to require all lobbyists to have to register on a comprehensive transparency portal - whatever their tax arrangements - so that the public can see who is meeting the government, who they are representing, and what they are discussing”

McSweeney told openDemocracy: “I do not provide lobbying services, nor do I intend to.” 

“I therefore have no plans to register as a consultant lobbyist, as that is not the business I conduct. The suggestion that my company is well-placed to exploit a loophole in lobbying legislation is misleading. I have no intention of using any such loophole.”

openDemocracy contacted Baroness Martin and Ben Nunn with questions about the nature of their work, but had received no response at time of publication.
### The Right Words in the Right Order
URL: https://www.opendemocracy.net/the-right-words-in-the-right-order/
Last updated: 2026-11-13T15:56:33.000Z
“*This piece was first published in the* [*Ideas Letter*](https://www.theideasletter.org/?ref=opendemocracy.net)*.”*

Cultural elites and educators of the Global North are now in an advanced state of panic surrounding reading, literacy, and the humanities generally. University professors find to their dismay that students either cannot or will not read at the length that was once expected. Enrollment in humanities degrees in the US has been falling ever since peaking around 2010\. The recently published OECD PISA scores (from an international test for 15-year-olds) included [troubling evidence](https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/2026/09/pisa-2025-results-volume-i%5F5265bfb1.html?ref=opendemocracy.net) of a collapse in reading ability across the OECD, with scores peaking around 2012, and then falling off a cliff since—a drop equivalent to 1.5 years of learning.

Reading for pleasure is also cratering, especially among boys and men, with major consequences for the [nonfiction book market](https://dearheadofmine.substack.com/p/the-nonfiction-book-market-is-collapsing). Commentators are now [writing](https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/2026/08/reading-crisis-postliterate-age/687618/?ref=opendemocracy.net) darkly about a new era of “[post-literacy](https://jmarriott.substack.com/p/the-dawn-of-the-post-literate-society-aa1)” or a return to one of “orality,” in which video replaces text as the central medium of knowledge-sharing, individual expression, and public argument.

Two technologies loom large in this cultural panic. The first is the smartphone, whose mass adoption in the early 2010s is often blamed, by Jonathan Haidt among others, for destroying attention spans and threatening young people’s mental health – a charge that intensified in the early 2020s as algorithmically curated short-form video became ubiquitous, following the rise of TikTok. Second, Large Language Models (LLMs) became an everyday technology following the launch of ChatGPT in November 2022\. The impact on the humanities is twofold: Not only can text be generated almost automatically, but so too can its comprehension.

Every wave of industrialization provokes a countermovement: English Romanticism flourished at the dawn of the first industrial revolution, and the Arts and Crafts movement emerged with the second. It is unsurprising, and largely welcome, that literacy is now the subject of its own defensive movements which seek to celebrate the craft of reading and writing. Some of this has been forced on universities at speed: The rapid normalization of AI-generated coursework essays has driven the return to in-person, handwritten assessment methods. But some has been more pedagogically motivated, such as the recent announcement by the University of Chicago Law School that all digital devices would be banned from classrooms for the new academic year in order to avoid “stunting intellectual growth.” Columbia’s Literature Humanities and Contemporary Civilization sections followed suit.

Amid this countermovement, a new agonistic ethic of literacy has emerged, which not only celebrates the craft of reading and writing, but emphasizes its difficulty. Some literature professors have come out fighting, arguing that reading *should* be a struggle that students *must* confront. In *The Atlantic*earlier this year, Walt Hunter [made the case](https://www.theatlantic.com/ideas/2026/02/youth-reading-books-professors/685825/?ref=opendemocracy.net) for refusing to “meet students where they are.” In a *New York Times* op-ed, [Matt Dinan suggested](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/17/opinion/higher-ed-dostoevsky-attention.html?ref=opendemocracy.net) that professors perform their own struggle with great texts before their students. Every time an AI engineer or executive brags about the imminent bypassing of reading or writing, social media becomes awash with humanists arguing that the purpose of text lies precisely in the labor it requires. On this view, inefficiency is what gives literature its worth, which at its best is a Herculean translation of human experience from subjectivity into text, and then from text into another subjectivity.

LLMs have upended assumptions about reading and writing faster than any other technology, outstripping even the rise of short-form video. So intense is the disruption that there is a risk that the wider crisis of the humanities is seen entirely through a panicked post-2022 lens. A polarization sets in: on one side is the frictionless machinery, which makes reading and writing instantaneous, and on the other a romanticism about how the humanities were before the arrival of LLMs. We are in danger of misrepresenting the pre-2022 world. The question deserves to be asked: when exactly was the age of literacy that educators and humanists are seeking to defend or revive?

---

The OECD’s Programme for International Student Assessment, whose most recent scores have added to the literacy panic, was launched in 1997, following multiple attempts to produce a common measurement of literacy. Earlier efforts had been trialed by bodies such as UNESCO and the US Educational Testing Service, dating back to the 1950s. What gave the PISA initiative momentum was a wider ideological shift, derived from Third Way neoliberalism, that placed learning and literacy at the heart of social and economic progress.

As the education scholar [Gert Biesta](https://www.gertbiesta.com/?ref=opendemocracy.net) has argued, over the 1980s and ’90s the very idea of “education” was displaced in favor of an ideal of “learning.” Education implies a teacher, a subject, and a purpose; learning is something an individual does. What Biesta termed “[learnification](https://www.taylorfrancis.com/books/mono/10.4324/9781315634319/good-education-age-measurement-gert-biesta?ref=opendemocracy.net)” meant that the transmission and application of knowledge became a priority across society and the economy in order to produce more active, independent, and prosperous citizens. Not only was “learning” (unlike “education”) something that could occur anytime and anywhere, but evidence of it would be found in practical applications, that is, the ability of individuals to achieve their goals. Pedagogy became anchored in cognitive science, so as to instrumentalize it in the service of economic ends.

One aspect of the turn towards learning was a fixation upon literacy as a measurable cognitive capacity. The literate individual in the “learning society” was one capable of using information to execute tasks successfully. The more complex the information and the task, the more literate the individual needed to be to complete it. On this basis, PISA compared literacy levels across dozens of nations. In 2000, the OECD offered a definition of “reading literacy” that few humanities professors would recognize: “Understanding, using and reflecting on written texts in order to achieve one’s goals, to develop one’s knowledge and potential, and to participate in society.” This is one of the measurable capabilities that are now reported to be in decline. Academics in literary studies would resist such a utilitarian vision of reading, and make the case for interpretation and textual analysis as worthwhile in themselves. 

Other forms of “literacy” soon followed: media literacy, financial literacy, political literacy. As literacy rose in economic and political significance, it lost its association with litera*ture*. While progressive neoliberalism may have delivered better outcomes for disadvantaged children, it’s questionable whether the “learning society” represented progress for the humanities themselves once economic growth dried up after the financial crisis. In England, English was the most popular subject for A-levels (final high-school exams) in 2010, but has since dropped out of sight, falling from [83,000 students in 2013 to 54,000 a decade later](https://www.bera.ac.uk/blog/decline-and-fall-students-perspectives-on-a-level-english-at-16?ref=opendemocracy.net).

Parents, teachers, and professors will have some idea as to why this is, and the reason is more than simply a matter of harsher economic imperatives. Over the past forty years, the shift from a world of “education” to one of “learning” and “literacy” has narrowed what it means to understand a text, whether that be Coleridge or a train timetable, and blurred the distinction between those two. Once everything is about successful task execution, questions of meaning and interpretation are approached via disaggregation, breaking texts down into ever smaller bits, where they can be processed with varying levels of executive skill. Text becomes a form of code to be “broken” and then converted into different code. This is a considerable distance from the agonistic ideal of literacy that we see in our post-2022 world, and yet it has been on the march since the 1980s.

A few months before the launch of ChatGPT, I wrote an [essay](https://www.lrb.co.uk/the-paper/v44/n04/william-davies/how-many-words-does-it-take-to-make-a-mistake?ref=opendemocracy.net) for the *London Review of Books*reflecting on my experience homeschooling my then-nine-year-old daughter during lockdown while, at my university, dealing with the rising tide of plagiarized student essays (a problem that, in its conventional form of copying, has now evaporated). My daughter’s literacy exercises required her to read and rewrite the same short chunks of text, day after day, with the expectation that eventually this would be done correctly, but providing no facility or confidence to approach writing as a space of creativity or meaning. It struck me that the way “literacy” was being taught to children was connected to the difficulty students, taught in the same way, had in sustaining a commitment to their own original authorship, both of which were greatly exacerbated by the enforced pivot to online learning.

In both cases, language was being treated as a mere technology for completing a task or satisfying a tester, not as a route to self-expression or understanding. Once literacy is reduced to the correct ordering of words to produce sentences, it becomes unclear why one would care whether the order is one’s own. It is also unclear why one would choose to study *human* languages and literature, if they are taught and learned no differently from math or computer science, as a matter of right and wrong answers.

We have been inhabiting a world of post-human literacy for far longer than the present paeans to reading and literature recognize. The current crisis of the humanities has a history that is obscured by the panic surrounding LLMs, and the slightly longer-standing one about smartphones. Neoliberal “learnification” and literacy testing did considerable violence to the humanities by subjecting them to the rationality of measurable task execution. If young people in 2026 feel intimidated by language, and assume that a machine will use it “better” than they can, we need to ask how and why language became something to be evaluated statistically in the first place. The origins of the crisis lie even further in the past.

---

In the 1940s, the problem of communication was rethought in two parallel traditions. Both, in different ways, asked how one agent could transmit a message to another in a world of noise and chaos. Cybernetics, as pioneered by Norbert Wiener, provided a means of studying and modeling control systems, whether in humans, nonhuman organisms, machines, or combinations of the three. In this first tradition, language (such as that of a military command or a persuasive advertisement) came to be treated as a tool for influencing behavior. Meanwhile, information theory, as developed by Claude Shannon, offered a mathematical theory of communication. The information contained in a message could be calculated quantitatively, in terms of the improbability of a certain set of signs being placed in a given order, regardless of the meaning. 

In the years that followed, these two traditions would provide the foundations for both the development of digital computing and the cognitive turn in psychology. These developments were closely related, as the French cognitive scientist Jean-Pierre Dupuy [has detailed](https://sts.stanford.edu/publications/origins-cognitive-science-mechanization-mind?ref=opendemocracy.net). Cognitivism modeled the human mind and brain as information-processing systems, along the lines that Shannon had laid out, in a deliberate analogy to digital computers. Cognitive processes of learning and communication could be studied in humans in the same terms as in machines, once psychology abandoned humanist problems of understanding, interpretation, and meaning. Evidence of learning was to be found in effective communication, that is, in putting words and other symbols together in the right order.

Communication of this nature requires no human subject capable of mining their subjectivity, interpreting meaning, or empathizing with an author or speaker. Instead, it is achieved through pattern recognition and mathematical calculation, precisely the techniques that machines can execute on a larger scale and at greater speed than human brains. Shannon’s probabilistic approach to information means that messages sit on a spectrum, between a probability of one (in which nothing new is communicated) and zero (in which there is just pure noise). It is on this premise that LLMs are able to complete sentences for us, predicting which words will likely appear next. The cognitive revolution—which would come to reshape pedagogy in the late twentieth century—used these post-human methods and theories to radically affect how human cognition and communication were conceived.

The temptation for humanists and cultural theorists is to recoil from this mechanization of mind, understandably given what has happened to the study of literature, history, and languages over the past two decades. But recent intellectual histories have troubled such comfortable romanticism. Bernard Geoghegan’s fascinating [Code: From Information Theory to French Theory](https://www.dukeupress.edu/code?ref=opendemocracy.net) tells an overlooked story of how in the mid-twentieth century the project of reducing communication to probabilities overlapped with the structuralist ambition to ground cultural analysis in a general science of signification.

Structuralism, as advanced in the 1950s and ’60s by Claude Lévi-Strauss and Roland Barthes, shares various family resemblances with information theory. Both sought to grasp communication as such, through studying the internal relationships in symbolic systems. Both opened doors to post-humanism, in which the question of subjectivity and interpretation could be simply set aside in favor of attention to networks of signs. Barthes’s famous 1967 essay “[The Death of the Author](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The%5FDeath%5Fof%5Fthe%5FAuthor?ref=opendemocracy.net)” liberated a generation of humanities students to abandon the question of intended meaning and interpretive depth in favor of intertextual and intratextual analysis. This appeared after Michel Foucault’s *The Order of Things*, which had concluded by dreaming that “man” might soon be erased, “like a face drawn in sand at the edge of the sea.”

In different ways, information theory and structuralism both extend a project of decoding in all directions, reading society at large as a system of signs and texts, and dissolving the distinction between literature and society, or between computation and society. While structuralists adopted a veneer of Parisian radicalism, promising to disrupt power by decoding it, Geoghegan’s argument is that the endpoint was conservative, neutering political resistance by restricting it to a form of literary studies. The dual prongs of information theory and cultural theory that appeared in the 1950s to be advancing separately were increasingly conjoined from the late twentieth century onwards, first as “literacy” became something to be measured on the basis of task execution (a form of communication, as Shannon would see it), and then in the age of platform capitalism, as vast cultural archives became technically computable as information. The “digital humanities” represent the consummation of a flirtation that could be dated back to the postwar period. “Culture,” “society,” and “information” are now all available to the same disciplinary analysis: the one performed by algorithms.

This insistence that the humanities are no longer distinguishable from mathematics is the premise of Leif Weatherby’s audacious and daunting [Language Machines: Cultural AI and the End of Remainder Humanism](https://www.upress.umn.edu/9781517919320/language-machines/?ref=opendemocracy.net), a post-2022 theory if ever there was one. For Weatherby, LLMs bring us face to face with a brutal reality that we have been inhabiting since at least the 1940s, but which we prefer to duck by clinging to some cultural ideal of humanist exceptionalism (“remainder humanism”). LLMs demonstrate the core truth expressed by both information theory and structuralism: Language and communication exist independently of what we think of as human minds. Our difficulty in even speaking of LLMs in non-anthropomorphized terms signals how caught up we still are in a pre-structuralist worldview, in which meaning and signification are things that only humans are capable of. The LLM, much as Geoghegan anticipates, represents a fusion of probabilistic and linguistic technique that is no less mathematical for being cultural, and no less cultural for being mathematical.

---

Placed in this longer intellectual history, the present crisis appears to be a failure to grapple with much slower and deeper transformations in the status of text in society. The current panic surrounding screens and AI may be rooted in the tangible harms these pose to the intellectual development of children and students. But where this panic generates romantic ideals of the humanities as a form of “craft work,” it obscures what literacy, reading, and communication have actually meant for the vast majority of people. Whether they intend to or not, the most impassioned defenders of the humanities often sound like they want to return not only to a pre-2022, or even pre-2010, world, but to one before the mid-twentieth century, before the drift to post-humanism began. 

What might an alternative stance on literacy look like? It is a worthwhile goal to separate culture from computation within the school or the university. Such an agenda would need to also take aim at the Edtech industry, which has elevated “learnification” to new heights, profiting from the development of feedback systems that close down the space for experimentation, error, and creative nonsense. A depressing aspect of the plagiarism cases I discussed in my 2022 essay (but also students more generally) was that many students seemed to view writing as a series of traps, which they were certain to fall into sooner or later. In order to eliminate risk, they wanted to know in advance how an essay should be structured, what should be in it, and how it should be expressed. The threat posed by LLMs is not so much that they remove the difficulty of reading and writing (as the agonistic humanists would have it), as that they remove the playfulness, the uncertainty, and the intriguing mistakes.

What needs reviving is not some classical ideal of “Man,” but, as Weatherby argues, poetry. Textual generation, he writes, “puts poetry on one end of a spectrum bookended on the other by ideology.” Where we feel compelled to use the *correct* words in the *right* order, for fear of consequences, we are victims of ideology. LLMs allow us to witness our own ideological constraints, showing us how our culture has been streamlined, disciplined, and constrained into certain forms of expression. Poetry, by contrast, is the exploitation of the improbable, based on the assumed freedom to put words in an order that wasn’t expected and hasn’t been done before. The point is not that only humans can write an improbable sentence; machines can too. It is that a student should be free to try one, and to get it wrong.

Literacy, in its current guise, is deeply ideological. Reading has become a cognitive processing habit, necessary to support the kinds of “symbolic analysts” (elite knowledge workers, able to work back and forth between numbers and narratives) once deemed core to post-industrial capitalism. Given that many of those same jobs now appear most at risk from the AI revolution, there is an opportunity to liberate symbolic analysis from the demands of the knowledge economy, and turn English classes into rare places of freedom.

---

**William Davies** is a writer and researcher based in London. He is an Open Society Fellow for 2026-27\. His writing is available at [Williamdavies.blog](https://williamdavies.blog/?ref=opendemocracy.net).

### Is it time to break up the UK?
URL: https://www.opendemocracy.net/is-it-time-to-break-up-the-uk/
Last updated: 2026-11-13T07:33:22.000Z
Is it time to break up the UK? In his new book, “Abolish Westminster”, long time openDemocracy writer and editor, Adam Ramsay makes just that case.

The following is an edited excerpt of an interview between Ramsay and openDemocracy’s Editor-in-Chief Aman Sethi openDemocracy’s *In Solidarity* podcast. [Click here to listen to the podcast in full.](https://www.opendemocracy.net/podcasts/abolish-westminster-with-adam-ramsay/)

  
**Adam, let’s just start with the title: What is Westminster?**

When I say Westminster, what I mean is the whole British political constitutional system. Westminster is actually just the name of a place. It's the name of the physical place that has that big building that was built in the 19th century, but it's also a metonym to refer to what I mean by the whole political system.

I mean the parliamentary system, but also in the executive, which is called Whitehall. I mean the judicial system. I mean the way we organize money in Britain. So I mean the whole of the British constitution needs to be replaced.

**You've been a journalist for many years. Give us a sense of the journey that led you to this conclusion. What was the question that was animating you that you were like, “The answer is ‘Abolish Westminster’.”**

I'm Scottish. People wouldn't guess that from my accent, but I am. And so in Scotland, this isn't really an original analysis. In the Scottish left, people have been saying for, you know, you could argue two centuries, but certainly for many decades, that achieving social justice or democratic socialism or a more progressive world or whatever you want to call it, through the old imperial British state is almost impossible.

The great Scottish writer, who's a long-term friend of openDemocracy, Neil Ascherson, famously said in the 1980s that trying to get democratic socialism through the British state is like trying to get milk from a vulture. And so in that sense, the argument, the broad argument isn't new in Scotland, but when I was first at openDemocracy more than a decade ago, suddenly there was a Scottish independence referendum, and so I found myself trying to explain to oD readers and also just other people in England and outside the UK, you know, why is it that the Scottish left, who don't really care much about flags or nations, are in favor of independence? You know, which is not an obvious position the left might take.

In some places, that's seen as a more conservative position. To which the answer was always, "Well, look at the British state. Why would anyone with progressive politics want to be governed by this institution? 

So the great Scottish writer Tom Nairn wrote for us occasionally and I got to know him. And so I was very influenced by that kind of intellectual world that made the case that, you know, this is a system that's built to run an empire. It's not very good at democratically managing the affairs of an archipelago in the North Atlantic.

**What you do in your book, which I enjoy, is you break it down into a set of components. Could you give us a sense of why you chose the components you did?** 

The traditional way to write a book about the constitution of a country would be to say, well, there's three bits of it. There's the legislature, so Westminster. There's the exesecutive, so in Britain wthat's Whitehall, and there's the judiciary. And that's how the American Founding Fathers or the original French constitutionalists thought about it.

But people who've written about the British constitution have often said, "Well, it doesn't really work like that. There's a whole other bit to it." Which — he's a terrible man, but very interesting thinker — Walter Bagehotsaid that there's the efficient bit of the constitution, by which he means all those bits we just talked about, and then there's the dignified, which he kind of meant was the monarchy and the House of Lords, and all of these bits of the constitution, which as he saw it, were kind of designed to secure consent from the masses so you didn't have to give them actual democracy.

[Abolish Westminster | With Adam RamsayFrom Andy Burnham’s northern devolution to the electoral rise of Reform, Britain's political consensus is coming apart at the seams. Longtime openDemocracy contributor Adam Ramsay joins Aman to discuss his book Abolish Westminster![](https://storage.ghost.io/c/3f/80/3f804bea-4b2d-4ddf-9ff0-6ec7d0afa5fa/content/images/icon/multi_solo-58348f6e-a599-44f1-abb7-4c2d634bd2bc.png)openDemocracyAman Sethi![](https://storage.ghost.io/c/3f/80/3f804bea-4b2d-4ddf-9ff0-6ec7d0afa5fa/content/images/thumbnail/In-Solidarity-Thumbnails-51880d10-46ad-4545-9ea7-744867a6a48f.jpg)](https://www.opendemocracy.net/podcasts/abolish-westminster-with-adam-ramsay/)

He talked about the power of the princes, , and making people feel romantically attached to it through the monarchy so that they didn't get, so that we don't get, a proper say in how it's run.

And then also the sort of sense of national identity fits in there as well, right? Like what does it mean to be British or Scottish or English or Welsh, and why do those things butt against each other? Where does Ireland fit in? 

And that, that kind of leads to the final section of the book, which is about the union.

**Where I found myself in lingering disagreement through parts of the book was your sense that this is unique to Britain. Because if you, if you look around you, there seems to be a broader sense that politics is broken everywhere, that the state form itself seems to be creaking. What makes you feel like there is something very specifically a British problem here, as opposed to a general problem with the kind of post-war nation state?**

I think these things are both true, right? So I have stood on street corners in almost every country in Europe, from Ukraine to Spain, and asked people how they feel about politics. And I can tell you that in almost all of them, they will tell you they don't like it very much. So, yes, absolutely, this is a structure of feeling that goes right certainly towards the Western world.

But what's also true is that polling consistently shows that Britain has the lowest level of trust in politics in the Western world, alongside maybe Italy.

I just do think it's kind of objectively true that we have a worse state system than others. And I go through in a lot of detail what I think is so bad about it in Britain.

Now, that doesn't mean to say that you're wrong. There's a general crisis of representative democracy. You could say that's been caused by neoliberalism. If you privatize all the decisions to the market, then people suddenly say, "Well, why does politics have no power?"

But I do think that Britain has a particularly bad form because we have the world's oldest constitutional system, the kind of only layover from the medieval era. And I think that also had terrible consequences around the world because of our overseas territories and the way they kind of provide the plumbing for liquid finance globally.

**Reading your book, I was consoled that I'm not the only one who conflates Englishness and Britishness, and it seems to be a general problem, at least in your eyes. Talk me through this.**

Being Scottish, or for that matter Welsh, often feels a bit like you're sitting in the passenger seat of a car with a driver who's having a nervous breakdown. England kind of controls the direction of the British state and has found it very, very hard to get over losing the empire. Scotland also lost its empire, I don't want to imply Scotland was a colony. The UK came together when the Scottish and English ruling classes united to go and conquer the world and do terrible things. But for various reasons, which we can get into in detail if you like, Scotland has generally been a bit better at getting over that loss.

England is still kind of totally losing its mind over the fact that it used to run the world, and now it doesn't anymore. That's a big problem if you're Scottish in particular, 'cause you keep watching the English do totally bizarre things electorally, and it's very upsetting 'cause they're done to you, too. 

**From the very apt metaphor of, you know, being in a passenger seat and watching the driver have a nervous breakdown, how does that actually translate into, let's say, the nuts and bolts of being Welsh or Scottish? And while you're answering that, I think one of the things I'm also really interested in, is that it's also not working for the English. The English are perhaps the primary hostages of Westminster.**

The really obvious point is that the most remarkable fact about British electoral politics is that England has consistently voted Tory for 200 years.

The Tories are obviously not in government now, but they've been in government and elected by England,more consistently over 200 years than any other political party in the world. Scotland in that period has, with a couple of exceptions when there were moments of governance of national unity, essentially never voted for the Conservative Party.

Wales has almost never voted for the Conservative Party. Scotland and Wales for 200 years consistently voted first for Liberals and then the Lib- dems then the Labour Party, and now in Scotland, mostly the SNP. Um, and so what it feels like is you keep voting for broadly center-left governments and you keep getting Conservative governments.

So if you're sat by the North Sea and you kind of, obviously not literally but metaphorically, look across to Nordic countries, which spent the 20th century consistently voting for center-left governments and as a result got proper social democracies, and in Scotland you voted the same way for the same thing, and instead what you got was neoliberalism.

That's pretty upsetting.

So then the question is, well, why does England consistently vote Tory? Because if you look at opinion polls on individual issues, English people are almost as left-wing as Scottish and Welsh people. They want to tax the rich more. They want more equality. They're broadly as socially liberal as we are on most issues. But the big exceptions to that are monarchy and empire. 

So, you know, what's the difference? English people are more prone to monarchy worship. They're more prone to longing for Empire. 

**Devolution is quite part of the zeitgeist at the moment with the new prime minister. What is your take on Burnham and devolution?**

I think the most important thing to understand about devolution is that it's always temporary. That's a lending of power. And as soon as the core finds it politically expedient to interfere, it will. 

Devolution constitutionally is about retaining the legal right, \[00:16:10\] the constitutional power at the core, but lending power down. And obviously, I think Andy Burnham's right that, you know, I think it's true when he says in theory he wants to devolve more power, but obviously he's always going to be tempted, and anyone after him is gonna be tempted when it's politically expedient, as he has done himself, to interfere with that.

In a normal grown-up constitutional system, it works the other way. You know, local government has its own power granted by the Constitution, and the central government can't interfere.

**I want to end with your analysis of where British politics is going now. We've seen the rise of Reform and Restore. What I understand from talking to people around me is that this is not a kind of periodic eruption that one sees, but this seems to be something new and different.** 

**A significant amount of your book talks about how the establishment and the Tory establishment, to a sense, has retained a vice-like grip, do you see this as the grip loosening? How do you read this current moment of political flux and, and everything that emerges from it?**

On the question of how to understand Reform and restore, I do think it's a new phenomenon. I said earlier that the most remarkable fact about English electoral politics is how consistently people voted Tory. You know, the Tories were and are the party of the institutions, the party of the establishment.

You go right back hundreds of years, they are the party of the monarchy and so people voting Tory, fundamentally what they were saying was, "We basically have faith in the institutions of the British state to get us through the current crisis.We have- we trust the ruling class to carry on governing us." 

And so shifting from voting Tory to voting Reform is a kind of complex way of saying, "We don't quite trust the institutions anymore." 

Now, you look at what Reform are actually saying, they're not saying, "We are gonna have, you know, we're gonna put working-class people in power."

What they are saying is all of these kind of semi-democratic reforms that have happened since the 1970s, you know, since the end of empire, have been terrible., And we're gonna go back to, basically British state as it was some point, you know, maybe the end of the 1960s, 1950s.

It's not kind of people losing faith in the institutions as a whole, but it's people saying, "We don't like them as they are now, and we want to go back to an imagined version of what they were like probably before anyone alive now can really remember or, or very many people alive now can remember."

This is an imagined era. And of course, that era, the reason people liked the state at the time, people in Britain liked the states, is it was accruing vast wealth from the empire. You know, of course, it's great being at the imperial court. You get lots of plunder. And so a vote for Reform, in a sense, is saying, "We don't like what the institutions become, so we don't trust the Tories anymore 'cause they're the party of the institutions as they are now.

There's a younger generation who might have been on the right historically, who look at all of this and think it's a bit mad, and they probably are quite against institutions. You know, there is a new common sense in the country that basically the whole political system's broken. And some of those people are drawn to Reform because they see them as anti-system.

The other thing that's true right now is that as we speak, the Tories have just re-overtaken Reform in the polls, and Labour's back up in the polls.

Now the polls are showing a kind of reemergence of two-party politics for now. 

The kind of establishment breathing its sigh of relief has made a mistake because the fundamental problems of the system are still there. Andy Burnham is not going to achieve what he wants to achieve. And I don't think that 'cause he's dishonest, I think it's because the British state is set up to stop him from achieving it.

**The final section of your book is called Break Up the UK, where you suggest a radical rewiring, restructuring, breakup of theUK into its constituent parts.** 

If you're in England, the idea that you would abolish Westminster sounds kind of absurd, and it's a kind of ridiculous radical slogan. And sure, you might like it in theory, but what does it mean in practice? Like, you know, when can you, how can you tangibly achieve that?

If you're here in Scotland, we've literally had a government that's in favor of ending Westminster rule over Scotland for most of this century. Like, the SNP has been repeatedly reelected because about half the population wants independence, and that number is growing as generations unfold. Um, if, you know, a majority of young people now in Wales also want independence.

Similarly, Northern Ireland. I think Northern Ireland is a particular situation because people there feel very trapped.The Good Friday Agreement was a \[00:28:55\] necessary way out of civil war. But I spent a lot of time there talking to voters about how they feel about politics, and what they always say is, "We need to get beyond the politics of them and us, but I have to go and vote for us.” 

And Britain has no capacity to constitutionally innovate out of that situation in Northern Ireland, where I think the Republic does. In each of these cases, there's a very good reason for each of the other nations, by which I mean Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland, and I talk a bit about Cornwall, to want to leave.

And where does that leave England? Well, England can either choose to carry on with its absurd empire state system, or it could say, "Well, this is an opportunity for a democratic revolution here too, and we could also write our new constitution." 

I think the most likely way that England is going to achieve serious, deep constitutional change is when the rest of us leave you on your own.
### Flatlining emissions won’t save us from climate crisis – and neither will COP31
URL: https://www.opendemocracy.net/cop31-flatlining-emissions-wont-save-us-from-climate-crisis/
Last updated: 2026-11-12T15:45:42.000Z
Go back three months, and there seemed little happening on the climate breakdown front, despite the approaching COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey. With that conference now underway, it may appear that progress is being made, particularly given hopeful signs of action following two elections in recent weeks. 

First, Brazil’s progressive incumbent president, [Luiz Ignácio Lula da Silva was re-elected](https://www.opendemocracy.net/ten-days-of-elections-around-the-world-may-shape-future-of-climate-debate/) for a record fourth term and is expected to continue his policy of curbing the loss of one of the world’s main carbon sinks, the Amazonian rainforest. 

Then, in the United States, Republican candidates were trounced as the Democrats took overall control of both the House and the Senate. It was a grim verdict on Donald Trump’s first two years in office and good news on the climate issue. Trump’s “drill, baby, drill” view on fossil fuels was knocked back along with his status, sparking an immediate burst of investor support for the renewable energy market.

Some further glimmers of hope came this week at COP31 itself, not least the news that carbon emissions for this year are forecast to flatline – partly due to China, the world’s biggest emitter, continuing its strong state-supported move away from fossil carbon.

But for experienced climate analysts, the overall picture still looks bleak. 

While flat-lining emissions represent progress, they must fall by as much as 10% a year in the immediate future if climate breakdown is to be avoided. This seems unlikely while the transition to renewables remains dangerously slow due to a formidably well-resourced fossil carbon lobby. 

What’s more, COP31 has also delivered bad news: 2026 will likely be the second year (after 2024) in which global temperatures exceed the recommended maximum rise of 1.5℃ above pre-industrial levels. 

As the UN head, António Guterres, put it on the second day of the conference: “It is long past time to stop treating the transition away from fossil fuels as taboo or intractable. Now, here at COP31, we must move from discussing the transition to organising it, financing it, and delivering it.” 

What are the chances of that happening? For now, they are low, despite the expansion in renewables, but there is one element that gets too little attention: devastating climate events, which tell us what to expect as the world heats up. Two in particular from recent years stand out.

One came just weeks ago, when a climate-linked catastrophe caused a huge loss of life in southern Tibet and Nepal at the end of August. Survivors told the UN that, following a massive glacier collapse, a “wall of water more than 100 metres high, travelling at 180 kilometres per hour, which devastated 60 kilometres of valley”. More than 1,500 people were killed, 5,600 missing, and more than 100 bridges, 20 hydropower dams and 23 schools destroyed.

It was a tangible expression of climate injustice, said [senior UN official Jorge Moreira da Silva](https://news.un.org/en/story/2026/10/1168651?ref=opendemocracy.net). Nepal emits just 0.08% of global greenhouse gas emissions yet is disproportionately affected by climate disasters.

For a few days after the tragedy, while it was still making headlines, some people made the link with climate breakdown. Then the climate narrative drifted away in the face of other global threats and COP31 looked unlikely to make much difference.

The other climate disaster came years earlier, in September 2023\. Storm Daniel dumped the equivalent of half a year’s rainfall in a single day over the upland catchment that feeds into the Wadi Derna river running through the heart of the city of Derna, on the coast of northern Libya.

A massive surge of floodwater overwhelmed the Bu Mansour Dam 12 kilometres from the city. This, in turn, caused floodwater to hit the Al-Bilad Dam, just over a kilometre outside Derna, which also collapsed. The result was a huge wall of water hitting the city with little or no warning. Many thousands of people were killed in a matter of minutes, washed out to sea, their bodies lost. In the immediate aftermath, the city’s mayor put the death toll at 20,000, but later estimates ranged from 11,000 to 24,000\. 

The disaster was compounded by more than 15 years of insecurity and neglect across Libya in the wake of one of the several failed Western wars of the post 9/11 era. This was the Anglo-French military operation to terminate the Gaddafi regime in 2011, from which Libya has still not recovered despite its wealth of resources.

In different ways, the Nepal and Derna disasters were pointers to the near-term future, with similar disasters and worse well-nigh certain. Most so far have been in the Global South, and the wider impact of climate breakdown will certainly be far worse for poorer communities right across the world. 

While parts of Europe and North America have experienced devastating wildfires and floods in recent years, none so far has had a loss of life on the scale seen in Derna or Nepal. It may take a catastrophe – or even several catastrophes – of the same magnitude hitting a major Western city, such as an intense heat dome or super-hurricane in New York or Los Angeles, to finally wake people up to the reality of climate breakdown and trigger structural policy change.

What all this adds up to is two trends working in parallel but, in a sense, in opposite directions. One is climate breakdown getting steadily worse and leading to multiple catastrophes; the other is a world slowly moving to a decarbonised economy to prevent it. 

The positive news is that the huge and very welcome developments in renewable energy systems make that second trend possible. The bad news is that it may take numerous disasters to make that happen, so the more we do to prevent them the better, from citizen and community action through to global summits.
### Seeking justice for abuse shouldn’t require bravery
URL: https://www.opendemocracy.net/russell-brand-seeking-justice-for-abuse-shouldnt-require-bravery/
Last updated: 2026-11-12T11:30:14.000Z
In the wake of Russell Brand’s sentencing, survivors of rape and sexual violence are being encouraged to speak to the police. The lead detective from London’s Metropolitan Police stood outside the court to praise the investigation and promise other victims considering coming forward that they would be listened to, supported and treated with care and compassion. 

This does not reflect the experience of many women who engage with the criminal justice system after traumatic experiences of violence. Often, they are left re-victimised and profoundly mistrustful of a process that they are told is there to support them and bring perpetrators to justice. This is particularly the case for Black and minoritised women, whose communities are subject to the discriminatory policing that we know is rife. 

We at Rights of Women support thousands of these women in England and Wales every year, providing legal advice and working with them to protect their rights. We see that trust in the police and criminal justice processes is vanishingly low. Many women are fearful of the police and the systems they feed into, having been shown time and again that, far from protecting them from violence, powerful institutions are often complicit in it. 

When women report crimes committed against them, they’re too often disbelieved, disrespected and ultimately discouraged from seeking accountability. Instead of offering survivors a trauma-informed service, the criminal justice system regularly perpetuates problematic attitudes: shifting blame, distorting reality and ultimately re-victimising survivors. 

Those survivors who make it through the investigation process, in the tiny number of cases where the man who abused them is charged and goes to trial, are unlikely to find solace in the courtroom. Brand’s trial highlighted how survivors are undermined and discredited using rape myths, such as problematic and offensive assumptions about how a victim of sexual violence should behave, which persist despite recognition that they are damaging and grounded in a fundamental misunderstanding of trauma.

It goes without saying that a defendant is entitled to a robust defence, put forward by a lawyer who will advocate for them fearlessly. In any criminal trial, the evidence of a witness will be tested, and rape trials will very often involve questions around consent or reasonable belief in consent. What a defendant saw and heard, and how this affected his understanding of consent, may be an important issue to be explored. But this does not require reliance on stereotypical suggestions that a victim should have fought back against her rapist or told someone about what happened sooner. 

There is a legitimate question to be explored about whether, how and when a judge should speak to a jury about rape myths. Of course, judicial directions cannot undo the assumptions that have shaped how sexual violence is understood, both during a trial and more widely. Nor can they address the serious social injustices that have enabled violence against women and girls to become so entrenched in our society. The responsibility for challenging these assumptions around sexual violence cannot continue to fall to women, many of whom are already required to recount deeply traumatic experiences under intense scrutiny when they have been harmed. 

If we are serious about encouraging survivors to come forward, we must be honest about what awaits them when they do and what support is available to them. A prosecution that results in conviction is not the only measure of whether the criminal justice system has served a survivor. To be treated with dignity and respect, a standard that should constitute the bare minimum a survivor can expect, is still lauded as a radical approach by police responding to sexual violence – perhaps so radical that many police forces still decline to meet it. 

Women who come forward and report violent crimes have undoubtedly demonstrated enormous courage. Their bravery is often praised by the very institutions that perpetuate misogynistic cultures requiring their bravery. Women should not have to be brave to seek justice and safety. 

Instead of calling for courage from survivors, those in power must give women reason to believe that coming forward will not exacerbate the harm they have already experienced and deepen their trauma. The police may promise survivors that they will be listened to, supported and treated with care and compassion. But those promises mean little until survivors see and experience a criminal justice system that delivers on them.
### The UK must back global bans on AI weapons – before it’s too late
URL: https://www.opendemocracy.net/the-uk-must-back-global-bans-on-ai-weapons-before-its-too-late/
Last updated: 2026-11-12T10:01:59.000Z
Defence spending is supposed to keep us safe, while infrastructure spending should improve our lives. But manipulation by war and tech profiteers is driving a surge of public investment with the exact opposite result: consuming essential resources and poisoning our environment, as well as countless places overseas, to build deadly and unpredictable tech. 

In London, the [largest factory](https://isembard.com/uk/newsroom/southwark-launch/?ref=opendemocracy.net) since the Second World War is being set up in Southwark, where ‘precision’ manufacturing giant Isembard will act as a machine shop for defence-tech giants including US firm Anduril, whose founder Palmer Luckey once[ crowed](https://www.defenceconnect.com.au/air/15953-no-moral-high-ground-in-losing-autonomous-systems-war-says-luckey?ref=opendemocracy.net): “I love killer robots.” 

This is just the tip of the iceberg in the UK’s military AI expansion, in which many of the most violent harms are well documented: from the[ targeting](https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/sep/11/naza-directors-film-israeli-intelligence-rachel-szor-yuval-abraham-?ref=opendemocracy.net) and killing of civilians (particularly[ children](https://www.unicef.org/syria/documents/children-and-armed-conflict-un-secretary-general-annual-report?ref=opendemocracy.net)), to hacking risks and the[ clear link](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/privacy-international%5Fautonomous-weapons-systems-are-closer-to-activity-7521950155110006784-fDi3?ref=opendemocracy.net) between AI weapons and surveillance at home. It’s unsurprising, then, that [90% of Britons want the government to lead on the global regulation of AI weapons](https://autonomousweapons.org/ai-weapons-poll-uk/?ref=opendemocracy.net), according to a recent survey by the non-profit Future of Life Institute.

Yet in defiance of this, the UK is [rumoured](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/beatrice-fihn-1351bb11%5Fafter-10-years-of-discussions-a-draft-proposal-share-7521882954617282560-l1Yb?ref=opendemocracy.net) to be joining the [US, Russia, and Israel](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/06/autonomous-weapons-ai-russia-us-binding-rules?ref=opendemocracy.net) to lobby against a last-ditch attempt to put the brakes on the uncontrolled development of military AI and lethal autonomous technologies at the[ seventh annual review conference](https://meetings.unoda.org/ccw-revcon/convention-on-certain-conventional-weapons-seventh-review-conference-2026?ref=opendemocracy.net) of the UN’s Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons in mid-November. 

Faced with the risks and encouraged by a long list of war-tech profiteers, the response of these governments is escalatory: a bid to acquire more expansive data-driven war machines before opponents do. But even outside the most violent worst-case scenarios, autonomous weaponry affects local lives and lived environments long before it appears on a battlefield.

We are currently researching the full[ life cycle of military AI’s impacts](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1NiZy8R5NZulR87IA0BSOXDUnXQmx4bCiTivNX46IsQ8/edit?usp=sharing&ref=opendemocracy.net), going beyond the dangers of war to look at the waste, damage and suffering caused by the resource extraction, manufacturing, data (computing), and post-deployment requirements of military AI systems, such as ‘combat clouds’, targeting software and automated strike-drones.

We have found the military AI buildout is already having catastrophic consequences for livelihoods and habitats in Britain and across the world, and accounts for an underacknowledged amount of the bandwidth generated by the data centres being thrown up across the country. 

The meteoric data centre expansion in and around Greater London is a key example, where digital infrastructures are being pitted against the needs and wellbeing of local residents while contributing to rising carbon emissions and ‘data heat islands’. In Slough, data centre buildout is worsening housing inequalities, raising the cost of and access to electricity, and eating away at urban green spaces, according to Slough Against Data Centres, a resident-led campaign group. 

The ecological impacts of computation, of course, go beyond AI warfare, but the militarisation of data is a key way the UK hopes to gain an economic edge in an intensifying global arms race – despite[ little evidence](https://transitionsecurity.org/buying-the-dip/?ref=opendemocracy.net) that either military or digital expansion translates into more jobs for Britons. 

Outside the UK, the picture gets worse. Militarised AI not only requires data but a wide range of digital infrastructure and component hardware that cut across a complex network of global supply chains, where a scramble for raw materials is escalating risk worldwide. 

In Taiwan, semiconductor production threatens marine life and the local water supply, forcing rice farmers out of work. In the Democratic Republic of Congo, scarred by decades of devastating conflict, people suffer from backbreaking labour and long-term exposure to chemicals and heavy metals in the mines that supply copper, cobalt and coltan to the AI arms race. 

It’s a similar story in Ghana, where toxic pollution drives chronic health problems in one of the world’s largest and most hazardous e-waste scrapyards. Millions of tonnes of discarded digital and military technologies are dismantled, burned or melted in chemical baths every year.

Ecologically vulnerable societies are ill-equipped to survive crisis and conflict. Far from protecting us, the military AI industry’s resource grab is creating both a more dangerous Britain and a more dangerous world. Due to the secrecy of digital supply chains and weapons production, it is difficult to understand the full extent of the damage.

Then there is AI-powered warfare itself, which, far from the precision and distance promised by its sellers, is making the battlefield bigger, messier, and more brutal. 

In Iran, the health, environmental and economic impacts of oil facility fires, asbestos-heavy construction debris and atmospheric fallout will continue long after US military bombing campaigns have ceased – supercharged in their intensity by AI targeting systems such as [Palantir’s Maven](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cdrm52g4pl2o?ref=opendemocracy.net). 

Similarly, when the artillery eventually falls silent in Ukraine, what will remain is a huge expanse of drone and other debris littering a vastly contaminated landscape with lithium batteries, fibre-optic cables and unexploded ordnance. In Gaza, the film *NAZA*, among numerous other investigations, has exposed Israel’s use of algorithmic mass killing: an increasingly automated, software-driven attack not just on Palestinians and their housing, education and healthcare, but also on their farms, forests and other ecosystems, water, waste and sanitation infrastructure. 

The only answer to all of these harms is a shared commitment to pull back from the brink. Even at the height of the Cold War, rival powers agreed to limit nuclear warheads, and established systems for controlling the proliferation of particularly destructive or unpredictable weapons.

Such is the momentum we now need for military AI. This is a question of human and planetary health versus short term returns to a handful of defence-tech billionaires. 

A majority of UN member states and their populations now support legal controls on autonomous weapons. The existing UN process should be the beginning, not the end, of a global drive to prevent the moral and political, as well as human and ecological, consequences of automated warfare from coming to pass – before it’s too late. 

*This commentary draws on a new report by Dr Nico Edwards titled ‘The Ecological Bootprint of UK Military Digitalisation,’ supported by Scientists for Global Responsibility, the War &* Geos *project at Newcastle University, and LEX International. Read the full report online* [*here*](https://lexinternational.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Report-Ecological-Bootprint.pdf?ref=opendemocracy.net)*.*
### It takes a village to ‘Abolish Westminster’
URL: https://www.opendemocracy.net/abolish-westminster-adam-ramsay-book/
Last updated: 2026-11-10T11:28:23.000Z
My book *Abolish Westminster* was published by Faber this week. And it would have seemed remiss of me not to stop by my old home to note how much of an impact openDemocracy had on the thinking and research which went into it.

The book runs through what I see as the six clusters of institutions which make up the British state, explaining why I think each functions to bend power back to the powerful. 

I start by looking at the executive - Whitehall - and some of the most significant departments of state. Much of my understanding of how executive power in Britain was inherited from the monarchy - which sent me down a path of research for the book - came from working with and editing oD’s founder, Anthony Barnett, over the years, and from getting to know and interview his crowd of intellectuals who came together around the social upheavals of 1968.

My understanding of the ideological blindness of the Treasury came, to a significant extent, from years as an openDemocracy editor, publishing frustrated economistscs raging against its doctrines. My chapter on the cabinet office was inspired by direct experience my then colleagues here had in investigating the response to Covid. Dan Trilling, another former oD editor, helped me understand the Home Office, and British policing.

It was while I was working for openDemocracy that I learned where the relevant registers of interests and lists of meetings of meetings for different powerful people are hidden away, and how to craft a freedom of information request in such a way as to get at least some chance of securing at least the tiniest scraps of information.

Much of my sense of the utter dysfunction of the Houses of Commons and of Lords - the deep corruption combined with infuriating culture - was developed through years covering British politics for openDemocracy. Working for a left wing platform during the Corbyn years gave me a ringside seat as the institutions of the British state bludgeoned a progressive movement into the ground.

Publishing some of the country’s top lawyers contributed to my scepticism of the legal system, as did editing and talking with Anthony about the broader constitutional problems with the British judiciary, and it was my investigations (with Peter Geoghegan) into the dark money behind Brexit which led me to Britain’s offshore havens, helping me to understand their importance as bastions of oligarch power from which democracy around the world is being drowned.

The late, and much missed Rosemary Bechler’s long form thoughts on what she called “The Monocultural National Us” were vital to my understanding of the various nationalisms of these islands, and, because of his association with openDemocracy and friendship with Anthony, I was lucky enough to get to know Tom Nairn, the great thinker about nationalism, before he died. His analysis is central to the section on British identity, and the monarchy; and to my attempts to argue against the habit among English progressives of identifying as British rather than English. 

My time at openDemocracy started almost exactly a year before the 2014 Scottish independence referendum, and my first year there was largely spent trying to explain to English progressives why their equivalents in Scotland were largely planning to vote yes. The time I had to develop my thinking and arguments during that period, and also roughly annual trips I took to Northern Ireland to report for openDemocracy, fed directly into the final section of the book, where I argue that the best way to secure radical constitutional change across the islands is to break up the UK.

I’m grateful to openDemocracy readers, who made my decade at this website possible. And I’d be delighted if you bought the book, and checked out my journalism and campaigning project [abolishwestminster.com](http://abolishwestminster.com/?ref=opendemocracy.net). Let me know what you think.

**Adam Ramsay’s book Abolish Westminster is published by Faber now, and available for** [**ordering online**](https://linktr.ee/abolishwestminster?ref=opendemocracy.net)**, or in all good bookshops. Adam edits the new website** [**abolishwestminster.com**](http://abolishwestminster.com/?ref=opendemocracy.net) **He’s a former special correspondent, editor and UK editor of openDemocracy.**

In this episode of *Change My Mind*, we’re joined by Dr. Kate Devlin, Professor of AI and Society in the Department of Digital Humanities at King's College London and co-lead of the Responsible AI UK program. Drawing on her early background in archaeology and her extensive research into human-computer interaction, Dr. Devlin explores the emotional bonds we form with chatbots and the unacknowledged corporate practices driving the AI boom. 

Plus, she opens up about her own profound shift in perspective: why she abandoned her belief in the absolute objectivity of the scientific method, realizing that controlled lab experiments fail to capture the messy reality of how humans actually engage with technology in the wild.

**What you’ll learn:**

- **The AI Companion Boom:** Why the rise of large language models has led millions of people to form deep attachments to non-judgmental AI boyfriends and chatbots.
- **The "Dirty Secret" of AI:** Why the most urgent threats aren't super-intelligent robots, but the massive environmental drain of data centers and the exploited human labor propping up the supply chain.
- **The Death of Pluralism:** How the widespread use of a few homogenous language models flattens human knowledge and erases diverse, marginalized voices.
- **The Silicon Valley Spin:** Why tech executives stubbornly claim their platforms are "neutral tools" despite building them with specific values, and the cynical optics of AI companies lobbying the Vatican.
- **Lessons from Northern Ireland:** How growing up in a mixed Catholic-Protestant family during the Troubles shaped her understanding of polarization, power dynamics, and the fragile success of the peace process.

## This week in history

**The Newport Rising • 4 November 1839**

On 4 November 1839, thousands of working-class Chartists marched into Newport, South Wales, in what would become the last mass armed uprising on mainland British soil. Demanding the democratic freedoms set out in the People’s Charter - including universal male suffrage, the secret ballot, and the right of ordinary people to sit in Parliament - the crowd was fired upon by soldiers outside the Westgate Hotel, leaving at least 22 dead. The bloodshed at Newport shattered the polite myth that British democracy was a gift from enlightened elites and remains a stark warning for our own era that democratic rights, once won through working-class sacrifice, must be continually defended.

[The Great Charter of LibertiesLooking at the distance between the Westminster parliamentary system and those to whom elected representatives are ultimately accountable, the Chartists had a point – in fact, at least six points.![](https://storage.ghost.io/c/3f/80/3f804bea-4b2d-4ddf-9ff0-6ec7d0afa5fa/content/images/icon/multi_solo-ea7d5d76-779d-4e69-8a6c-0ab2992f1cd9.png)openDemocracyMalcolm Chase![](https://storage.ghost.io/c/3f/80/3f804bea-4b2d-4ddf-9ff0-6ec7d0afa5fa/content/images/thumbnail/oDMeta-f94360a6-c7d0-48fc-9380-be604090050f.jpg)](https://www.opendemocracy.net/en/great-charter-of-liberties/)

Devolution is back at the center of the political zeitgeist, pitched as the sensible middle ground between a decaying Westminster and the breakup of Britain. But what if the entire constitutional architecture—from Whitehall and the House of Lords to the City of London and British offshore tax havens—cannot actually be fixed?

In this episode, Aman sits down with author and longtime openDemocracy contributor Adam Ramsay to unpack his book, *Abolish Westminster*. Drawing on decades of Scottish socialist critique and years spent investigating dark money in British politics, Ramsay argues that attempting to squeeze social democracy out of the British constitution is, in the words of Neil Ascherson, "like trying to get milk from a vulture."

They explore why England has voted Conservative for two centuries while the Celtic fringe voted center-left, how devolution remains a fragile "lending of power" that the core revokes at will, why Reform UK is weaponizing imperial nostalgia, and why breaking up the union may be the only catalyst capable of forcing England to build a modern democracy of its own.

- **What is "Westminster", really?** Why treating Westminster as just a parliament misses the real machinery of the British state: an unwritten, medieval constitution combining executive prerogative, Walter Bagehot’s "dignified" monarchy, and overseas tax havens acting as the global plumbing for liquid finance.
- **The myth of English left-wing divergency:** Why polling reveals that English voters share the same progressive economic instincts as Scots and the Welsh, yet consistently vote to protect class deference, the monarchy, and imperial memory.
- **The limits of Burnhamism:** Why Andy Burnham’s first Budget failed to end neoliberalism—and how his intervention over council alliances with the Greens exposes devolution as a conditional loan from the center rather than true local self-governance.
- **Post-imperial identity & immigration:** The unresolved racial politics of Britishness versus Englishness, how media oligarchs use race to distract from billionaires, and why the UK political class remains unable to process the end of empire.
- **Deconstructing Reform UK:** Why Farage’s insurgent project isn't an anti-establishment working-class revolt, but a reactionary attempt to return to the pre-1970s imperial state.
- **The democratic case for dissolution:** Why Wales and Scotland wanting out is a rational reaction to decades of unrepresented Tory rule, and why an English republic will only emerge once the Celtic nations walk away.
