### Ten days of elections around the world may shape future of climate debate
URL: https://www.opendemocracy.net/ten-days-of-elections-around-the-world-may-shape-future-of-climate-debate/
Last updated: 2026-11-06T16:11:40.000Z
In the wake of the US midterm elections, the sheer size of the electoral opposition to Donald Trump is still sinking in. It will take weeks if not months for a full analysis of the results to emerge but they are already having a global impact, with US tech companies losing $3.2trn in value since the vote on Tuesday. 

Remember, though, the political focus barely two weeks ago was not just about the US midterms but how they related to three more elections across three continents, in Serbia, Brazil and Israel. In each case, there was uncertainty over the outcome but a recognition that it could have an impact stretching way beyond its borders.

Two of the elections came on the same day, 25 October, in Serbia and Brazil, and the third was in Israel just two days later. The first two were general elections in which the populations as a whole could cast ballots, but in Israel voting was restricted to seven million Jews and the two million Palestinians residing in Israel, with five million Palestinians living under Israeli control in Gaza and the West Bank excluded. 

In Serbia, the Serbian Progressive Party (SBS) had been in power for 14 years and was dominant across much of society, including the media and economy, and with plenty of influence across the legal system. Its increasingly autocratic leader, Aleksandar Vucic, had long allowed persistent favouritism and a high level of corruption coupled with organised crime, and in the past two years a substantial community of student activists had demonstrated repeatedly against the SBS and Vucic, giving rise to an opposition Student List of candidates when it came to the election.

While the students had no clear leader, by the time of the election they were reportedly neck and neck in the polls with the government. When the election came, the Student List romped home, winning 53% of the votes, to the SBS’s 39%.

What comes next is uncertain as the List’s newly elected parliamentarians seek to establish a stable if inexperienced government. Critics fear that a combination of years of corruption coupled with the power of organised crime will ultimately dominate but that is by no means certain; many thousands of students, supported by hundreds of thousands of others, see the future very differently.

As the political environment in Serbia evolves, one thing remains certain, it has seen mass protest transform itself into a potential government. That will be watched uncomfortably by quite a few Western states, not least France, with its continuing country-wide street protests, and the UK, where over 4,000 pro-Palestine supporters have been arrested in recent years.

Mass action also applies to Brazil, where the progressive incumbent, Luiz Ignàcio Lula da Silva, failed to lead at the first round of the election, initially having fought a lacklustre campaign. The favourite to win the run-off was his right-wing opponent Flàvio Bolsonaro, a key Trump ally and the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, now imprisoned for his role in an attempted coup after losing the 2022 election.

The prospect of defeat led to a country-wide campaign of mass rallies by Lula’s supporters, with huge crowds gathering in cities right across the country. That was paralleled by far greater use of social media, an element that had not previously been prominent in Lula’s previous approach to campaigning. 

Since the return to democracy in Brazil over 40 years ago, no candidate losing the first stage of a presidential election had reversed the result in stage two, yet Lula’s renewed campaign did just this, turning a two million voting deficit in the first round into a substantial lead in the second three weeks later, having gathered around 10 million extra votes.

Much of the change was due to internal politics, but it is at the global level that the result is of note. During his recent four-year term, Lula had made much of the need to slow the rate of destruction of the rainforest, which makes up one of the most significant global sinks of carbon. If Bolsonaro had won that would have been reversed, which would have been music to the ears of Trump and his supporters, as well as to climate change deniers across the world. 

As toIsrael, there are two main outcomes. First, Binyamin Netanyahu’s Likud-led coalition lost its majority, but Gadi Eisenkot’s Change bloc also fell short. Second, Palestinian Arabs allowed to vote did so in much greater numbers than usual, with a turnout of just under 80%, largely because of a determination to prevent Netanyahu contriving to cling on to power. 

Overall, Arab-led parties won 19 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, including 11 for members of the Joint List alliance – enough to hold the balance of power. Ten days after the election, the Joint List announced it would support Eisenkot as prime minister, following in the footsteps of the other Arab group, Ra’am. Israeli president Isaac Herzog is now thought likely to invite Eisenkot to form a government.

The election itself, though, displayed thoroughly uncomfortable attitudes among Jewish Israelis during the campaign. Politics concentrated substantially on domestic issues, including the demands for accountability over the 7 October Hamas attack, with little attention given to the terrible war waged in Gaza by the Netanyahu-led government and the repeated violence perpetrated by Jewish settlers across the occupied West Bank. It was as if over 80,000 Palestinians killed or missing were best ignored.

Not all Jewish Israelis took this position, but a majority appeared to. This, coupled with Netanyahu’s decades of experience in the Israeli government and his capacity for personal survival, suggested that any sustained political stability based on trust would be difficult to achieve. What remained though, was the transformation among Palestinian Israelis and their determination to vote and put Netanyahu out of office.

The fourth of the elections, the United States mid-sessionals for both houses of congress, was the one that sprung by far the greatest surprise. That the Republicans lost was not unexpected, it was the massive size of the loss that counted.

Given Trump’s past behaviour, if a modest shift in votes had given the Democrats the House but not in the Senate, Trump and his team would have carried on if somewhat tarnished. That was not to be. The extent of the failure was so great that it undermined the entire Trump machine and with it the vast numbers of supportive officials brought on to the Federal payroll in the past two years.

That has three implications. One is at the international level, where Trump will no longer maintain his status and influence. There is a risk of hitting out where he thinks he can, but the extent of the failure in these elections means a minimal risk of Trump trying to cry foul in 2028\. Times have changed and it won’t wash.

The second is that the last two years have been hugely profitable for the Trump camp but not just for them. Wealthy elites across the entire country have made millions if not billions and will be singularly unhappy at the great gravy train being derailed. Work will already be underway in the Heritage Foundation, the think tank that authored the Project 2025 blueprint for the second Trump administration, and other right-wing think-tanks to adjust to a different era. 

Finally, on some key domestic issues with global implications, Trump’s abject failure is very good news. Of all the disastrous policies of the Trump years, it is [climate denial and the curbing of the renewables revolution that have been the most dangerous](https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/05/democrats-midterms-triumph-renewable-energy-industry-donald-trump?ref=opendemocracy.net). Within a day of the election result, though, the financial press was reporting a surge in the value of renewable energy outfits, not just in the US but across the world. 

Trump is still in the White House and his supporters will still be in the system, but their power is already ebbing away. Taking a global view, the combination of Lula’s re-election in Brazil and Trump’s failure leading to a re-energised environmental movement give the world a rare day of good news.
### How a tech start-up lobbied to put delivery robots on UK pavements, and won
URL: https://www.opendemocracy.net/starship-technologies-delivery-robots-uk-pavements-silicon-valley-lobbying/
Last updated: 2026-11-10T09:17:58.000Z
Lisa Johnson can’t stop talking about the Highways Act of 1835\. By her own admission, she’s brought up the law “once or twice, a day, over the space of four years”. 

As she has told politicians and LinkedIn followers alike, Johnson believes the legislation is blocking Starship Technologies, the tech start-up where she is vice-president of global public affairs, from unleashing its automated delivery robots on England’s pavements. 

But she may not have to worry for much longer. In September, chancellor John Healey announced “new sandboxing powers” to let businesses “safely test frontier technologies, from pavement robots to drones to lifesaving medical treatments”. The move comes despite concern from unions, campaign groups and members of the public over the risks to pedestrians, privacy (delivery robots are typically mounted with around 12 cameras), and the livelihoods of the country’s hundreds of thousands of couriers.

Now, openDemocracy can reveal that the expected law change follows an intense lobbying effort by Starship Technologies, the industry leader, which has offices in Estonia and San Francisco but has concentrated its expansion efforts in the UK. Johnson, who is married to Angela Rayner’s top adviser and has close personal ties to senior figures in the Labour Party, led a years-long charm offensive resulting in back-to-back meetings with senior government officials. 

Yet Starship’s battle to put its robots on pavements in the UK goes beyond a company using its political connections to get its way. 

openDemocracy’s review of government emails obtained under Freedom of Information law, interviews with experts and campaigners, and site visits to observe the robots in operation reveal Starship has followed a familiar Big Tech playbook: privately lobbying and publicly railing against regulations, while rapidly deploying unproven and not-yet-legal technologies. Companies such as Uber, Amazon, Meta and Alphabet have used elements of this model to reorder the world to their advantage – to the detriment of communities, workers, small businesses, and the environment.

In the process, England’s pavements have become the site of a dangerous experiment, says Living Streets, a charity promoting pedestrian safety. A US tech company hoping to profit from replacing couriers with robots has made UK pedestrians – including children, the elderly, parents with prams, and people with mobility or sight vulnerabilities – its unwitting “human testers”. In a sign of what could be coming, tech companies have successfully lobbied authorities in the US city of Philadelphia to classify their delivery robots [as “pedestrians”](https://edition.cnn.com/2026/10/31/us/philadelphia-woman-delivery-robots-cec?ref=opendemocracy.net), giving them similar rights to human users.

The Highways Act bans “carriages” from pavements, said Tanya Braun, a director at Living Streets, but it is unclear if Starship’s robots count as carriages. “We have had a number of MPs write questions to ministers about this; the answer just tends to be, ‘it’s a legal grey area,’” she explained. “But there are robots operating in towns and cities across England. So while there is no legislation and no legal framework, these robots are still being allowed to operate on our pavements.”

Weeks after Braun and I spoke, Starship accused Living Streets of “selectively editing” a video showing one of its robots colliding with Emily Green, an 18-year-old wheelchair user. The company said it will report the charity to the regulator if it fails to correct the record.

“Starship claim I moved into their robot’s path but dropped kerbs are placed there for the benefit of wheelchair users and I don’t have the luxury of not using them,” Green told [The Times](https://www.thetimes.com/uk/technology-uk/article/robot-delivery-crash-video-disabled-person-staged-m8lhcx29t?ref=opendemocracy.net) last week. “A Silicon Valley tech giant using a legal grey area to privatise pavements for profit should not take priority over my safety and mobility.”

## **Aim for Mars, hit Leeds**

Starship’s origins lie in a 2013 competition to design a NASA rover to collect dust samples from Mars. Estonian computer programmer and Skype co-founder Ahti Heinla entered his design but was ineligible for the prize as he was not a US citizen. Still, seemingly inspired, he launched his own robot fleet on Earth the following year. 

The company told openDemocracy its decision to make robots that run on pavements, rather than roads, was rooted in “sustainability”. “It makes little environmental sense to transport a 2lb meal in a two tonne car,” it said, adding: “Pavements also lead straight to people’s front doors, so a delivery can be completed without a van, a parking space or an engine.”

The London borough of Greenwich became the first place in the world to temporarily trial Starship’s robots in 2016, and the company officially launched in the UK in partnership with Co-op two years later. Today, the company says it operates in 27 locations across eight countries, including in partnership with Uber Eats in six English towns and cities. openDemocracy understands Co-op no longer works with Starship.

Starship told openDemocracy its robots have completed more than 11 million trips globally. “The unit economics are clear: our robots deliver groceries at a cost $3-4 lower per delivery than traditional courier fulfilment,” Heinla said in a press release earlier this year, [adding:](https://www.starship.xyz/press/starship-technologies-doubles-down-on-grocery/?ref=opendemocracy.net) “The opportunity in grocery is generational.” The company, which does not disclose revenue figures, has raised about $281m over multiple funding rounds, [according to Tracxn](https://tracxn.com/d/companies/starship-technologies/%5F%5FM8hQlunMFlSbhbXsrUi2%5Fsx7SBNbYMiSML6DvzoI67o/funding-and-investors?ref=opendemocracy.net#funding-rounds).

In North America, pavement delivery robots have been banned in [Chicago](https://interestingengineering.com/videos/chicago-bans-delivery-robots?ref=opendemocracy.net), [Toronto](https://policyoptions.irpp.org/2025/01/sidewalk-robot-delivery-safety/?ref=opendemocracy.net), [Ottawa](https://www.ctvnews.ca/ottawa/article/robot-delivery-services-banned-on-ottawa-streets-city-says/?ref=opendemocracy.net), and [much of San Francisco](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2017/dec/10/san-francisco-delivery-robots-laws?ref=opendemocracy.net) after complaints from residents and disability rights advocates. But here in the UK, Starship is expanding operations – although it says it is hindered by there being both too much and not enough regulation. While Johnson has focused her ire on the Highways Act, Heinla has [complained](https://www.thetimes.com/uk/technology-uk/article/soon-there-will-be-thousands-of-delivery-robots-on-british-streets-8mtzg0537?t=1735819122117&ref=opendemocracy.net) that the lack of a national law governing robots is forcing his firm to negotiate with individual councils. 

![](https://storage.ghost.io/c/3f/80/3f804bea-4b2d-4ddf-9ff0-6ec7d0afa5fa/content/images/2026/10/Delivery-Robot_1_1.gif)

In 2020, while Labour was still in opposition, the company began courting the party’s senior figures, treating newly crowned leader Keir Starmer to a demonstration from one of its robots at a Co-op in Milton Keynes. Fast-forward four years, and Starmer, then the prime minister, invited Starship to a breakfast he hosted with tech firms in Estonia in late 2024.

Over the following nine months, Johnson, who began her career as an assistant in the office of Labour MP Jon Trickett in the 2000s, became a regular feature at government events. She appeared as an expert witness at a meeting of the Science, Innovation and Tech Committee; met with Starmer and then-tech secretary Peter Kyle in Downing Street for London Tech Week; and hosted a fringe panel discussion at the Labour Party Conference. 

On each occasion, Johnson raised the need to update the Highways Act, to seemingly little appetite from ministers. “The PM remembered his last trip to meet the robots years ago as an opposition shadow minister,” she wrote on LinkedIn after her trip to No 10\. “We might have mentioned regulations still haven’t changed…”.

Publicly, Starship was threatening to exit the UK market. Privately, it wasn’t giving up. Emails obtained by openDemocracy show that in September last year, Ryan Case, Starship’s public affairs and corporate communications manager for Europe, emailed a junior minister in the Department for Transport (DfT) seeking “a call with you to go over where things are in terms of regulation for personal delivery devices”. 

For three weeks, Case received no reply. 

Then, on 6 October, The Times published a glowing account of Starship’s robots, drawing solely on a report paid for by Starship and written using its “data, expertise and insight”. The report claimed that “expanding robotic deliveries could yield a £125m increase in grocery spending and generate a productivity gain equivalent to 300,000 working hours saved”. 

Johnson sent a link to The Times article to another transport minister, Simon Lightwood, asking again for a meeting. “We would greatly appreciate the chance to discuss government plans for the sector and how clearer regulation might be achieved,” she said. “Starship would be more than flexible around your diary, and be happy to meet either in London or at the DfT in Leeds if that were helpful.” 

She needn’t have bothered. As The Times landed on desks across Westminster earlier that day, the government had finally bitten; Lightwood had written to Case inviting Starship in for a chat two hours earlier.

On 28 October, Johnson finally got her meeting with the government. Twenty-four hours later, she got her second meeting with the government.

In the first, she and Starship founder Heinla, who happened to be in town – “a lovely addition to the meeting”, according to the civil servant tasked with scheduling it – sat down with Lightwood in Parliament. 

Johnson knew Lightwood well; just three months earlier, he’d watched her marry Nick Parrott, Angela Rayner’s longtime chief of staff. The wedding was a veritable who’s who of the Labour government and Leeds local governance, with [Politico](https://www.politico.eu/newsletter/london-playbook/the-ballroom-where-it-happens/?ref=opendemocracy.net) reporting that it was attended by at least six serving or former members of Starmer’s cabinet, including Rayner, business secretary Jonathan Reynolds, and ex-transport secretary Louise Haigh (now Burnham’s most senior minister), as well as at least 16 junior ministers and backbench MPs, and a handful of parliamentary private secretaries. Also present were Starmer’s political director, Claire Reynolds; several members of the House of Lords, including former Labour deputy leader Tom Watson; West Yorkshire mayor Tracy Brabin; Leeds City Council leader James Lewis, and Leeds Council executive member Helen Hayde.

An internal DfT briefing sent to Lightwood ahead of the meeting and seen by openDemocracy reveals that months earlier, Starship wrote to another minister, Jim McMahon (also present at Johnson’s wedding), seeking an amendment to the English Devolution and Community Empowerment Bill “to include additional regulation-making powers that would effectively allow the legalisation of pavement robots”. This would effectively hand decisions on whether or not to permit the robots over to local councils.

The briefing advises Lightwood that pavement delivery robots would be “out of scope of the Bill”, explaining: “The government’s view is vehicles should continue to be regulated by central government consistently across Great Britain.” Yet this week the government rejected openDemocracy’s request to see the correspondence between McMahon and Starship, claiming it is “not in the public interest” because it relates to “live policy” decisions.

The day after Johnson sat down with Lightwood, she returned to Westminster for a face-to-face with Tom Layfield, a special adviser in the Department for Transport, organised and attended by Woburn Partners, a lobbying firm founded by two former Labour advisers. Special advisers are not required to declare their meetings with businesses, meaning the public had no way of knowing this took place. 

This year, the government appointed Johnson to sit on its inaugural Robotics Advisory Group, tasked with shaping the UK’s policy on robots.

Starship told openDemocracy: “Like any company working in an innovative and fast-growing sector, we want the law to keep pace with today’s technology and with how people now shop and consume. As one of the pioneers of robot delivery, we’ve been open about this from the start. 

“Over several years, we’ve engaged with government, parliament and policymakers on a cross-party basis on these issues, through meetings, consultation responses and giving evidence to select committees.”

## **Robot hunting in West Yorkshire**

“You’ll be waiting a while to see one in action,” the man behind me laughs. 

I’m in a greengrocer in Headingley, a buzzy neighbourhood not far from Leeds’ city centre, home to a large student population. I travelled here this morning to see Starship’s robots at work, a goal that increasingly feels like saying you went to London because you really wanted to spot King Charles.

I was excited to see two stationary robots – at knee-height, they’re bigger than I expected – within minutes of getting off the bus, but realised after hanging around staring at them for a while that they weren’t budging. Continuing up the high street, I asked in a couple of takeaways – national chains and independents – whether they use the robots for deliveries, but was met with blank stares. “The white robots? There’s some parked up there on the corner?” The servers shook their heads slowly, making me feel like I suggested they try delivering fried chicken via carrier pigeon. 

The two student-age boys serving in the greengrocer appear similarly perplexed when I ask if they see many robots going past. I’m starting to think the robots are some kind of inside joke, when the customer behind overhears. He says I’m unlikely to see any around here – confusing, given Starship has been active in this area for 10 months – but suggests I try Adel, the leafy north Leeds suburb that became the first place in the city to get the robots in November 2022, as part of a partnership with Co-op. 

“No, we don’t use them anymore,” a woman in Adel’s Co-op tells me. What? Since when? She shrugs. “Maybe a few weeks ago.” She’s not sure why they stopped, but thinks it could be to do with the A-road directly outside the shop, busy even at this time on a Monday afternoon. “The robots couldn’t cross it,” she says. “You could only really order if you lived on this side.” There’s a bad joke in there somewhere, but the problem was seemingly bigger than this fairly major flaw; the woman thinks even the people on this side of the road realised a human delivery was quicker.

It’s a similar story in a Greek takeaway in Hyde Park, back on the edge of the city centre. Human couriers, “who can take three orders at once”, are quicker and more efficient than robots, which “can only do one at a time”, says the man behind the counter, who visibly thaws after reassurance that I don’t work for Starship. Plus, he adds, with “the robots, you have to go outside and load them up”, which just isn’t possible when he’s busy behind the counter. Humans will come in to collect the orders.

Across the street, I finally have a breakthrough. A cafe that does use robots! But, says the woman at the till, translating for an older man in the kitchen whom I take to be the owner, “probably only once a month”. Is it their decision to mostly use couriers instead? No, no, she says, translating again, “He thinks the customer decides how it’s delivered.” 

I step outside and ponder this, and that’s when I see it: a Starship robot, in motion, rattling along the pavement towards me. 

![](https://storage.ghost.io/c/3f/80/3f804bea-4b2d-4ddf-9ff0-6ec7d0afa5fa/content/images/2026/10/Delivery-Robot-drop.gif)

I follow the robot closely, watching without interfering. I am David Attenborough; this is my seal cub. I will let orcas tear it apart if need be. That’s nature, baby. We reach our first hurdle: a road crossing. But it’s almost rush hour now, and the pavements are full; a pedestrian also looking to cross presses the button. The robot notices the green man before I do. How did it do that? No time to question it; it’s off. I follow it around a corner, where it literally bounces off a large porthole – I hope the recipient hasn’t ordered a carton of eggs – before pausing to recalibrate itself. 

At another junction, this time without a traffic light, the robot takes a full 35 seconds to psyche itself up to enter an empty road. “Naturally risk-averse, they will take time to assess the route ahead and the road to understand if there’s traffic coming before deciding if it’s safe to cross,” says the Starship website. 

The robot comes into its own as it turns into the nearby park. “Our robots travel on sidewalks at the speed of a walking pedestrian,” says Starship. That may be, but away from the *sidewalk* and without the threat of cars, it speeds up to its maximum four miles per hour. I have to power-walk in an obvious effort to keep up – if I knew a single soul in Leeds, I’d be mortified – desperate to get there in time to talk to whoever’s food it is delivering.

Luckily for me, an orca emerges. A whole pod, actually. The teenage boys descend, surrounding the robot. They kick it, pull at its flag-bearing antenna, and obstruct its path. One sits on it. The robot bucks around, trying and failing to throw him off, a futuristic mechanical bull. “I’m recording you now,” the robot pleads in an American accent that makes the teenagers laugh harder. They do back off, though; I’m not sure if it was the robot’s threat of surveillance, boredom, or the watching adults, myself included, but they retreat, and the robot continues on its way. It looks relieved somehow.

At the other end of the park it becomes clear that this robot is not making a delivery at all; it’s returning from one. It parks up alongside three of its mates, flag still askew – a war wound.

It’s around this point that I realise the only way I’m going to see a robot deliver any food is if I order it myself. My best bet, I think, is to order from the one cafe that has told me it definitely uses the robots. I am exactly 0.5 miles away; Starship says its robots carry out deliveries of up to four times this distance. I order a panini I don’t really want, and Uber Eats prompts me to opt in to “autonomous delivery”, promising: “We’ll try to match you with a robot delivery” and “If a robot delivers your order, you’ll save on tip”. It feels icky, but I agree in the name of science. 

Fifteen minutes later, I’m assigned a definitely human rider named Mohammed. Disappointed, I message him saying he doesn’t need to bother fulfilling the order; he can just eat the panini if he likes, and I’ll still tip him for it. “Thank you, dear,” he replies, clearly confused; I have fundamentally misunderstood Uber Eats’ business model. 

Mohammed brings me the panini. It’s pretty good, to be fair. 

## **Red flags and grey areas**

When the UK government set out to regulate the use of motor vehicles in the Locomotive Act of 1865, it ruled that any “self-propelled vehicle” had to be accompanied by a team of at least three: a driver, a stoker to tend to the engine, and a flagman. The latter, generally a young boy, was required by law to walk at least 60 yards (around 55 meters) ahead of the vehicle, waving a red flag – or, at night, a red lantern – to warn pedestrians and horse riders of its presence. 

It would be 31 years before a car could legally travel on British roads without the need for this walking escort. 

The Red Flag Act, as the law came to be known, is remembered as an example of a government over-regulating and restricting technological advances to appease an anxious public (and a lobbying effort by horse-drawn carriage and railway operators). 

More than 160 years later, critics have accused the Starmer and Burnham governments of the opposite: under-regulating amid pressure from tech firms – leading ministers to turn a blind eye as a nascent technology is trialled on our streets, despite being technically illegal. 

This “legal grey area” creates confusion over liability in the event of an accident, said Living Streets’ Tanya Braun. “The trouble is, because nothing is legal at the moment, if anything happens, who does someone get in touch with? Something happens to them, or their car, or their personal belongings; who do they get in touch with? If they contact Starship, is Starship seriously going to just pay them out?”

Asked about this, Starship told openDemocracy: “Safety is our number one priority and incidents are incredibly rare, but of course as with any form of transport accidents do happen on occasion. Starship is responsible for our operations and our fleet – liability always rests with us. We hold comprehensive insurance. Any incident would be dealt with through our insurance process.”

Yet a legal battle in the United States may offer further insight. Trudy Perez, a 73-year-old car park attendant, is suing Starship after allegedly suffering permanent impairment and a spinal fracture when she was knocked down by one of its robots while working at Arizona State University in 2023\. 

Perez says the robot suddenly changed direction, knocking her off her feet – an account that appears to align with the [campus police department’s review of footage](https://npr.brightspotcdn.com/de/1c/c1056ed442fbb413a67da29c9771/23-2385.pdf?ref=opendemocracy.net) from two nearby CCTV cameras. “The robot suddenly reverses and strikes the victim, causing victim to fall down on her back,” the police report says. “The robot then moves westbound several feet, then suddenly reverses again back toward victim, who is still laying on the ground, the robot stops before striking the victim again.”

![](https://storage.ghost.io/c/3f/80/3f804bea-4b2d-4ddf-9ff0-6ec7d0afa5fa/content/images/2026/10/Delivery-Robot-egged.gif)

[Arizona state law](https://www.azleg.gov/legtext/54leg/2R/summary/S.1305TPS.DOCX.htm?ref=opendemocracy.net) requires delivery robot operators to ensure, among other things, that their devices have a general liability insurance policy of at least $100,000 and are actively monitored by a human operator. Perez’s lawsuit claims Starship failed to operate in a reasonably safe manner; that its robot, which was still being tested, was defective; and that an unnamed Starship employee tasked with monitoring the robot was negligent. Starship’s attorneys, meanwhile, argue her injuries were caused by her own negligence, a third party, and were pre-existing. 

Starship told openDemocracy it does not comment on ongoing litigation, and Perez’s lawyers declined to be interviewed before her case is heard by a jury next year. But when told that the robots are on the brink of being legalised in the UK, the law firm said: “Given what we’ve learned, we wouldn’t feel comfortable with these robots roaming our streets.”

The British government did not respond to our questions about whether there is legislation or other safeguards in place to set out liability in the event that a pedestrian is involved in a collision that was the fault of a pavement delivery robot.

Starship’s robots have already been observed in near-collisions on pavements across England, including by academics analysing how people respond to delivery robots. “We often saw pedestrians enacting very subtle, fleeting, but fluid changes to their embodied ways of traversing the street to somehow accommodate robot behaviour,” researchers noted in [a paper published at the 2024 International Human-Robot Interaction Conference](https://dl.acm.org/doi/epdf/10.1145/3610977.3634936?ref=opendemocracy.net).

In what they described as one of “many such instances” from their 12 hours of fieldwork in Milton Keynes and Northampton, the researchers saw a pedestrian forced to steady themselves to avoid falling after a Starship robot “brakes abruptly”. 

![](https://storage.ghost.io/c/3f/80/3f804bea-4b2d-4ddf-9ff0-6ec7d0afa5fa/content/images/2026/11/data-src-image-c766b13e-d372-4cb1-ad87-fea999b5e3f5.png)

**Research by Hannah R M Pelikan, Stuart Reeves, Marina N Cantarutti*

“Robot mobility can be illegible to members of the street, unaccountable to the situation (there was no street-readable obstruction here), and therefore difficult to anticipate”, the research paper said. This can cause “potential dangers to members of the street, with the robot itself turning into an obstacle, ironically – it turns out – as part of its own obstacle avoidance routines”.

Stuart Reeves, a co-author of the paper and an associate professor at Nottingham University, told openDemocracy that “for the most part, interactions \[with the robots\] come off fine, but there’s always kind of issues and problems that occur every now and then”. It is not clear whether these occasional issues pose particular risks to pedestrians with disabilities, he said, describing this as “a big gap in our knowledge” due to a lack of research.

Starship said it has “worked with charities on inclusive flag and robot design, robot behaviour and cane detection” and offers “decommissioned robots to guide dog-training centres”. It added: “We work closely with disability groups to both provide a good service to Disabled residents and operate sensitively around those with disabilities. Our customer surveys show around 25% of our regular customers have a disability or live with someone else who does.”

But for Lily Higgitt, a project coordinator at Living Streets’ Leeds branch, the robots are “dressed up as helping Disabled people”, while enabling their ostracisation from society. 

Over coffee, Higgitt explained that she worries about the long-term effects of further isolating some people with disabilities in their homes and removing what could be one of their key points of contact with the outside world. “You’re replacing a small interaction they have with a person in a day,” she said, “replacing that interaction with a machine, not even a human face.”

While Higgitt is “not necessarily anti-the robotic technology”, she doesn’t see the point in it. We already have better answers to the issues it purports to solve, she said: humans can deliver food and medicines to other humans, using bikes and e-bikes to reduce deliveries by emission-producing cars. 

In short, she sighed, delivery robots are “just another solution looking for a problem”.

## **Rise of the machines**

Starship Technologies is in the habit of hiring executives who built their careers on the front lines of the fight for workers’ rights.

Lisa Johnson spent almost 13 years working for trade unions, including nine years at GMB, the UK’s third-largest union; her colleague, Ryan Case, spent more than eight at Unite, the second-largest union. This work may now appear at odds with warnings from unions, delivery drivers and customers about their current employer’s impact on the labour market. 

In an email to the government seen by openDemocracy, Johnson said investing in the robots would “create 555 new, high-skilled jobs”. This claim was repeated in a debrief Starship sent to ministers after its initial meeting with the Department for Transport. 

What Starship failed to mention is the scale of the potential job losses it could contribute to. There are an estimated [295,000 active delivery drivers employed in the UK, around 120,000 of whom are thought to operate in the gig economy](https://pegasuscouriers.co.uk/2025/01/how-many-delivery-drivers-in-the-uk-and-is-there-still-a-shortage-normal/?ref=opendemocracy.net) – many of them delivering food via app-based platforms such as those used by Starship robots.

“I know that there are like political discussions and nuances around delivery riders and e-bikes and stuff,” Higgitt told openDemocracy, “but people that do those jobs do tend to be quite vulnerable, so I think taking those jobs away is like, it feels really bad.”

![](https://storage.ghost.io/c/3f/80/3f804bea-4b2d-4ddf-9ff0-6ec7d0afa5fa/content/images/2026/10/Delivery-Robot-Sudden-stop.gif)

Asked about this, Starship said: “Robot delivery is part of a multi-modal delivery mix to meet the growing demand for quick-commerce. Robots are one part of the solution to creating a sustainable delivery system that is affordable, fair and environmentally friendly. We’re proud of the jobs we create in the UK – our robot fleet needs humans to look after it. We employ robot technicians, operations managers and field assistants, and we hope to employ more as delivery continues to scale.”

But at school pick-up time in Leeds, these corporate claims came up against a tough critic: an eight-year-old girl snacking on chocolate-covered raisins.

I’d just stopped her family outside a supermarket to ask their opinions on the robots. Her mum said she’d never used them, and doesn’t “really like their presence”; when I asked why, the young child jumped in forcefully, shouting: “Because they steal people’s jobs!” 

She seemed embarrassed by her sudden outburst, shyly offering me a handful of raisins. Smiling, her mum explained that her daughters “go to school around here, and lots of the dads are delivery drivers, and they feel a bit threatened or intimidated by the robots”.

Starship told openDemocracy that council surveys in Leeds and Cambridgeshire “show real positive sentiment” towards robot delivery, which “adds a little fun to your groceries or takeaway”. “People love the robots,” it said. “Kids dress as robots for Halloween.” 

But on the edge of Leeds city centre, there’s a generation of children who, if Starship and other companies like it get their way, will grow up in a world of robots. Those kids aren’t wearing cute delivery robot costumes; they’re fearing for their parents’ jobs.
### Lula Won. The Markets Want a Third Round
URL: https://www.opendemocracy.net/lula-won-the-markets-want-a-third-round/
Last updated: 2026-11-06T12:29:29.000Z
On Sunday, October 25, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won Brazil’s presidential runoff with [51.8 percent of the vote](https://resultados.tse.jus.br/?ref=opendemocracy.net). His rival, Flávio Bolsonaro, is the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, [sentenced to twenty-seven years in prison](https://www.scrippsnews.com/us-news/us-to-issue-flavio-bolsonaro-and-family-visas-after-he-defied-a-travel-ban-and-left-brazil?ref=opendemocracy.net) for plotting a coup. The next day, the financial markets punished no government policy. They punished the vote. The Ibovespa, the São Paulo stock index, [fell 13.9 percent](https://www.riotimesonline.com/brazil-stocks-close-down-13-9-percent-lula-win-2026/?ref=opendemocracy.net) after the first automatic halt in trading since March 2020, and the real lost more than 8 percent against the dollar. Wall Street rose that day. The shock was Brazilian, and its cause is no mystery.

Three weeks earlier, when Flávio led the first round, the same index had [jumped 7.7 percent to a record](https://en.mercopress.com/2026/10/26/brazil-s-real-plunges-more-than-8-and-s-o-paulo-stocks-slump-after-lula-s-victory?ref=opendemocracy.net). The bet had a name and a program, and it lost at the polls. Since then the dollar has eased, but stocks kept falling: [16.6 percent in three sessions](https://www.campograndenews.com.br/economia/dolar-a-vista-volta-a-recuar-e-encerra-pregao-cotado-a-r-5-34?ref=opendemocracy.net). The panic of a few days now threatens to set fiscal policy for four years.

## The third round

The markets are not alone. On election night, Flávio refused to concede and vowed to seek the annulment of the runoff. His pretext was a two-hour extension of voting that his own campaign had requested for seventeen municipalities. Only [35,521 votes](https://www.opovo.com.br/noticias/politica/eleicoes/2026/10/26/no-2-turno-apenas-35-mil-votos-foram-registrados-apos-17h.html?ref=opendemocracy.net) were cast after 5 p.m., less than 0.03 percent of the total. On Monday, his right-wing Liberal Party (PL) [recognized the result](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/27/bolsonaros-party-accepts-result-after-trump-suggests-vote-was?ref=opendemocracy.net). Donald Trump, who in 2025 [imposed a 50 percent tariff on Brazilian goods](https://www.occrp.org/en/news/trump-threatens-50-tariffs-on-brazil-over-bolsonaro-trial?ref=opendemocracy.net) over what he called a “witch hunt” against Jair Bolsonaro, said “it looked like another rigged election.”

Then Flávio fled. On the Monday after the election, Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes had ordered him to surrender his passports within twenty-four hours, [citing the risk that he would leave the country](https://www.gazetadopovo.com.br/republica/pf-confirma-flavio-bolsonaro-deixou-brasil/?ref=opendemocracy.net). Flávio is under investigation for corruption and money laundering, including over the funding of a biopic of his father. In a video, he said he had [“never thought of leaving.”](https://www.infomoney.com.br/politica/flavio-bolsonaro-viaja-para-os-eua-apos-derrota-na-eleicao-diz-agencia/?ref=opendemocracy.net) On Tuesday the deadline passed, the Federal Police canceled his passports, and he [left for the United States](https://www.scrippsnews.com/us-news/us-to-issue-flavio-bolsonaro-and-family-visas-after-he-defied-a-travel-ban-and-left-brazil?ref=opendemocracy.net) with his wife and daughters, defying the travel ban. A State Department official said Washington would issue the family visas. By Wednesday he was [in Miami](https://www.metropoles.com/mundo/fugido-do-brasil-flavio-bolsonaro-esta-em-situacao-regular-nos-eua?ref=opendemocracy.net) on an Italian passport, and his allies said he would ask his patron for political asylum. His father, too, left for Florida after losing to Lula in 2022.

The fronts converge. Flávio calls the social package of the campaign’s final weeks vote-buying. The markets call the same measures fiscal risk. The losers want to annul the result in the courts. The Faria Lima, the São Paulo avenue that serves as Brazil’s City of London, wants to undo it in the budget. Its spokesmen now ask Lula to carry out the program that lost: the *tesouraço*, Portuguese for a giant pair of scissors, taken to the social chapter of the 1988 Constitution. This is the third round.

## The program that lost

It is worth recalling the losing side’s agenda. Flávio’s economic coordinator, Daniella Marques, [promised to cut R$190 billion](https://www.gazetadopovo.com.br/eleicoes/2026/daniella-marques-diz-que-plano-de-flavio-bolsonaro-preve-corte-de-r-190-bi-em-gastos/?ref=opendemocracy.net) from public spending, about $36 billion or £27 billion, 1.5 percent of GDP. Months earlier, the press had reported [campaign studies](https://www.correiobraziliense.com.br/politica/2026/04/7403233-flavio-avalia-reajuste-de-gastos-sociais-pela-inflacao-e-mais-privatizacoes.html?ref=opendemocracy.net) on limiting increases in pensions and in the constitutional floors for health and education to inflation. The campaign denied it. Voters rejected the program anyway.

It is now coming back through the Finance Ministry. Two days before the vote, Finance Minister Dario Durigan [said](https://www.cnnbrasil.com.br/economia/money/macroeconomia/durigan-diz-que-e-impossivel-resolver-problema-fiscal-por-completo-em-2027/?ref=opendemocracy.net) that no one could “sell the market” a fix in the first year. Two days after it, following the crash, he [promised](https://www.cnnbrasil.com.br/economia/money/macroeconomia/durigan-diz-que-vai-propor-ajustes-fiscais-para-perseguir-centro-da-meta/?ref=opendemocracy.net) to pursue the center of the fiscal target “formally.” His bill would scrap the tolerance band around the 2027 surplus target, which means up to [R$36.6 billion](https://investirecocaresocomecar.com.br/meta-fiscal-2027-centro-durigan/?ref=opendemocracy.net), about $7 billion or £5 billion, of extra tightening. It would also widen his power to freeze spending. It is doubtful that the surplus matters much even to the markets. They stood by Jair Bolsonaro after what he did to the public accounts in his failed bid for reelection in 2022.

## Austericide and betrayal

Brazil has seen this movie twice before. The first time was recent. Between mid-2024 and mid-2025, the Finance Ministry tightened the budget, and its own [Secretariat for Economic Policy rated the stance contractionary](https://static.poder360.com.br/2025/12/Boletim-RFE-2024-1o-Semestre-de-2025.pdf?ref=opendemocracy.net). Meanwhile the Central Bank [raised its policy rate, the Selic, from 10.5 to 15 percent](https://www.bcb.gov.br/controleinflacao/historicotaxasjuros?ref=opendemocracy.net). In Datafolha polls, the share of voters rating the government good or excellent [fell from 36 to 24 percent](https://www.intercept.com.br/2026/10/02/governo-extrema-direita-acelera-colapso-democracia/?ref=opendemocracy.net). The electoral turnaround came only when the government loosened its grip in the final stretch of the campaign.

The second time was 2015\. Dilma Rousseff won reelection promising to protect jobs and wages, then handed the Finance Ministry to a banker with her opponent’s program. The economy shrank by more than 3 percent in 2015 and again in 2016, revenue fell with it, and the deficit grew. Rousseff lost the voters who had elected her and was left at the mercy of a Congress that removed her on the pretext of budget maneuvers. An electoral betrayal does not calm the markets. It opens the way to a coup.

None of this was forced by necessity. Under Fernando Haddad, the Finance Ministry governed as if the balance of forces that toppled Rousseff were a law of nature. Brazil borrows overwhelmingly in its own currency and holds large foreign-exchange reserves, yet it runs [one of the highest real interest rates in the world](https://www.infomoney.com.br/economia/com-selic-em-1345-brasil-tem-maior-juro-real-do-mundo-set2026/?ref=opendemocracy.net). Compared with what international finance demands of emerging markets with far thinner buffers, Brazil’s macroeconomic policy has been more royalist than the neoliberal king. What is contained by decision can be released by struggle. The campaign to end the six-day working week proved it. A movement born on social media pushed a [constitutional amendment](https://en.mercopress.com/2026/10/15/brazil-approves-a-40-hour-week-and-two-days-off-ten-days-before-the-runoff?ref=opendemocracy.net) through Congress ten days before the runoff, against the employers’ lobby.

The fiscal framework will be revised anyway. The Treasury’s own [projections](https://static.poder360.com.br/uploads/2026/07/RPF-jun26-1.pdf?ref=opendemocracy.net) show its targets cannot be met from 2028, even with the largest spending freeze the law allows. The question is who pays. It could be pensioners, through the end of the link between benefits and the minimum wage. It could be health and education, through their constitutional floors, or the poor, through another freeze of the Bolsa Família cash transfer, or public investment. Any of these would look like a betrayal to the voters who fought to reelect Lula. The presidency could then pass in 2030 to a right-winger more palatable than the Bolsonaros, such as São Paulo’s governor, Tarcísio de Freitas, [reelected in the first round](https://www.correiodamanha.com.br/nacional/sao-paulo/estado-de-sao-paulo/2026/10/324290-tarcisio-e-reeleito-governador-de-sp-com-6265-dos-votos-no-1-turno.html?ref=opendemocracy.net) with 62.7 percent.

## Britain’s Healey moments

British readers know this script. In 1976, with sterling falling, a Labour chancellor, Denis Healey, [turned back at the airport and went to the IMF](https://www.chathamhouse.org/publications/the-world-today/2016-12/britains-big-bailout-december-15-1976?ref=opendemocracy.net). The $3.9 billion loan came with significant spending cuts, and three years later Margaret Thatcher was in Downing Street. Last week, another Labour chancellor named Healey delivered what one fund manager called [“the boring Budget that bond markets demanded.”](https://www.trustnet.com/news/13487487/credible-uneventful-boring-how-the-experts-reacted-to-healeys-first-budget?ref=opendemocracy.net) A year ago, Andy Burnham said Britain had to get beyond being [“in hock to the bond markets.”](https://www.ajbell.co.uk/news/articles/uk-chancellor-takes-aim-burnhams-hock-bond-markets-comment?ref=opendemocracy.net) Before taking office, he said he had [“never said you can just ignore the bond markets.”](https://www.inkl.com/news/andy-burnham-s-change-in-tack-on-fiscal-rules-and-bond-markets-is-understandable?ref=opendemocracy.net) John Healey kept the fiscal rules, a [£15 billion buffer](https://live.euronext.com/en/financial-news/british-markets-take-healeys-first-budget-their-stride?ref=opendemocracy.net) and the promise of [“no tax rises on wages or dividends.”](https://www.lbc.co.uk/article/what-in-budget-2026-john-healey-5HjdkZM%5F2/?ref=opendemocracy.net) He doubled the surcharge on bank profits, and the gilt market took it in its stride.

The comparison has limits. Britain’s gilt market has already brought down a prime minister, in 2022, while Brazil’s problem is the price of its debt more than its size. But the question is the same on both sides of the Atlantic: whether a government elected to change course answers first to its voters or to the bond market.

## A Congress worse than 2015

The Congress that takes office on February 1 may be even more hostile than the one that removed Rousseff. Bolsanaro’s rightwing PL will have [the largest bloc in the lower house](https://www.gazetasp.com.br/politica/camara-tera-121-deputados-do-pl-e-70-do-pt-confira-como-ficaram-as-513-cadeiras-por-partido-e-os-mais-votados-das-eleicoes-de-2026-no-brasil/?ref=opendemocracy.net), 121 of 513 seats, against 70 for Lula’s Workers’ Party (PT). In the Senate, the right will hold [49 of 81 seats](https://www12.senado.leg.br/noticias/materias/2026/10/25/fim-da-eleicao-define-composicao-do-senado-em-2027-com-13-partidos?ref=opendemocracy.net), exactly the three fifths needed to amend the Constitution. The PL [wants Rogério Marinho](https://www.congressoemfoco.com.br/noticia/122994/valdemar-diz-que-pl-quer-eleger-rogerio-marinho-presidente-do-senado?ref=opendemocracy.net), the rapporteur of the 2017 labor reform, to preside over the Senate, and it [claims 49 of the 54 votes](https://www.cnnbrasil.com.br/blogs/caio-junqueira/politica/pl-rejeita-acordao-e-defende-impeachment-de-moraes-e-dino/?ref=opendemocracy.net) needed to impeach Justice Moraes. Before this Congress, a government that abandons its voters loses both its social and its parliamentary base.

## What to do now

The markets want short-term signals, and some make sense. Lula should name his economic team soon, because uncertainty over who will run the Finance Ministry weighs on prices. But a name is worth its program. A minister who announces more austerity will calm the Faria Lima for a week and repeat the mistake of 2024.

On Monday, the Treasury [bought back R$14.8 billion in bonds](https://exame.com/invest/mercados/por-que-o-tesouro-esta-comprando-de-volta-os-proprios-titulos-apos-a-eleicao/?ref=opendemocracy.net), about $2.8 billion or £2.1 billion, to steady the debt market. On Tuesday, the governor of the Central Bank, Gabriel Galípolo, [said it could intervene in the currency market](https://ac24horas.com/2026/10/27/dolar-cai-quase-1-e-ibovespa-recua-apos-tombo-eleitoral/?ref=opendemocracy.net) if it saw dysfunction. Those are the right tools. The Central Bank should not answer panic with higher rates. With the Selic at [13.75 percent](https://www.bcb.gov.br/controleinflacao/historicotaxasjuros?ref=opendemocracy.net), raising it on November 4 would make the public debt dearer and squeeze families who spend [28.7 percent of their income](https://www.bcb.gov.br/estatisticas/estatisticasmonetariascredito?ref=opendemocracy.net) servicing debt. Public banks can do the rest. Before the first round, Banco do Brasil [cut its rate on personal loans from 7.43 to 5.86 percent a month](https://gazetabrasil.com.br/economia/2026/10/14/juros-do-emprestimo-pessoal-caem-para-855-ao-mes-aponta-procon-sp/?ref=opendemocracy.net), still close to 100 percent a year.

There is another lever. The 3 percent inflation target is set by the National Monetary Council, where the government holds two of three votes. A 2024 decree signed by Lula requires [thirty-six months’ notice](https://www2.camara.leg.br/legin/fed/decret/2024/decreto-12079-26-junho-2024-795845-publicacaooriginal-172205-pe.html?ref=opendemocracy.net) to change it. Another decree can lift that lock. A less austere target would lower the interest rate needed to meet it.

## A new Transition Amendment

The medium-term signal matters more, and the question is who writes the revision of the fiscal rules: this Congress, before it rises on December 22, or the next one, from February. In December 2022, before Lula took office, an outgoing Congress passed a [Transition Amendment](https://www.migalhas.com.br/quentes/379051/pec-da-transicao-e-promulgada-pelo-congresso?ref=opendemocracy.net) to the Constitution in a few weeks. It opened R$145 billion above the 2023 spending cap, about $27 billion or £20 billion at today’s rates, to pay for the Bolsa Família. Lula needs a new one. Public investment and capital injections into state companies and the BNDES development bank should leave the spending limit. Real increases in the minimum wage and in the Bolsa Família should be guaranteed. And spending should no longer be tied to revenue. Once in the Constitution, these rules could be undone only by three fifths of both houses, voting twice.

The same fiscal target can be met by defending the interests of the majority, through tax justice, or those of the minority, by cutting social spending. A government elected by a popular uprising against the Bolsonarist threat cannot choose the path favored by the richest Bolsonaristas. Income tax changes published by December 31 apply from January. A [2025 law](https://www.courthousenews.com/brazil-enacts-tax-reform-with-new-exemptions-minimum-rate-for-top-earners/?ref=opendemocracy.net) already exempted earnings up to R$5,000 a month, about $940 or £700, and set a minimum tax of up to 10 percent on incomes above R$600,000 a year, about $112,000 or £85,000\. What remains lightly taxed is well known: part of dividends, exempt in Brazil from 1996 until this year; the “interest on equity” that companies deduct as a cost; and tax-exempt investments concentrated at the top.

Brazil does not have a debt crisis. It has a crisis of the cost of debt. In the twelve months to August, interest [cost R$1.18 trillion](https://agenciabrasil.ebc.com.br/economia/noticia/2026-09/contas-publicas-tem-deficit-de-r-10-bilhoes-em-agosto?ref=opendemocracy.net), about $221 billion or £166 billion, 8.9 percent of GDP. The primary deficit was 0.6 percent. Flávio has gone to Florida. The markets that bet on him lost, and the bill for that bet should not be paid with the promises that reelected Lula. The ballot box has spoken. The markets cannot play a third round.

*Pedro Paulo Zahluth Bastos is a full professor at the Institute of Economics of the University of Campinas (Unicamp), Brazil.*
### ‘Nice face of the devil’: Google whistleblower on AI, Gaza, and breaking NDA
URL: https://www.opendemocracy.net/nice-face-of-the-devil-google-whistleblower-on-ai-gaza-and-breaking-nda/
Last updated: 2026-11-07T09:47:43.000Z
The day Google DeepMind research engineer Sofia Liguori returned to work following the birth of her first child was the day her activism began. 

The 32-year-old was part of the London-based frontier AI lab’s sustainability-focused Impact Accelerator team, tasked with identifying new ways the technology can be used for good. These range “from pathogen detection and crop resilience to medical countermeasure acceleration”, according to a [LinkedIn post](https://www.linkedin.com/feed/update/urn:li:share:7521951056101216257/?ref=opendemocracy.net) advertising new roles in the team. 

Liguori’s own project focused on how AI could optimise electricity power flow to allow the national grid to use less energy and reduce overall carbon emissions. She told openDemocracy she now refers to her work as “building the nice face of the devil”.

“I felt so hypocritical that we were just talking about all these good things and not even mentioning Project Nimbus”, she said, speaking to openDemocracy from her home in south London, a Palestinian Keffiyeh scarf draped on the wall behind her. 

Project Nimbus is a [$1.2bn deal ](https://www.timesofisrael.com/israel-signs-deal-for-cloud-services-with-google-amazon/?ref=opendemocracy.net)that Google and Amazon Web Services signed with Israel to build data centres in the country and provide public entities with cloud-based data storage in 2021\. The [contract](https://www.timesofisrael.com/israel-signs-deal-for-cloud-services-with-google-amazon/?ref=opendemocracy.net) stipulated that neither company could shut down their services in Israel or deny them to particular government entities.

Google has said its work with Israel is “not directed at highly sensitive or classified military workloads relevant to weapons or intelligence services”, as a spokesperson told [Time](https://time.com/6964364/exclusive-no-tech-for-apartheid-google-workers-protest-project-nimbus-1-2-billion-contract-with-israel/?ref=opendemocracy.net) magazine this year. Yet training materials leaked to The Intercept in 2022 revealed the [full suite of Google Cloud AI tools](https://theintercept.com/2022/07/24/google-israel-artificial-intelligence-project-nimbus/?ref=opendemocracy.net) are available to Israeli state departments, including the Ministry of Defence, for face detection, object tracking and “sentiment analysis”. 

The ministry could have used these tools to [identify](https://www.nytimes.com/2024/03/27/technology/israel-facial-recognition-gaza.html?ref=opendemocracy.net) and [surveil](https://ccrjustice.org/home/press-center/press-releases/google-s-aiding-israel-s-genocide-against-palestinians-exposes?ref=opendemocracy.net) Palestinians across the West Bank, East Jerusalem, and Gaza, including since 7 October 2023, according to reporting in the New York Times and the Centre for Constitutional Rights. Israeli military officials have said they have killed [70,000 people](https://www.timesofisrael.com/idf-believes-70000-gazans-killed-in-war-as-claimed-by-hamas/?ref=opendemocracy.net) in Gaza since the Hamas attack on October 7 2023 that killed approximately [1,200 Israelis](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/live/cq2e9kyzer2nt?ref=opendemocracy.net). 

As she sat at home with her new baby, Liguori said she “watched a live-streamed genocide for a year, knowing that my company was complicit”. She added: “If we accepted this modus operandi, we were basically legitimising what has been tested in Gaza to become the standard.”

Returning to work in August last year, she said she implored her colleagues: “If our aim is AI for good, trying to stop genocide is one of the ultimate goods we can do, right?”

Ultimately, having been unable to convince executives to end Google’s role in Israeli military actions, Liguori left the company this year. In recent weeks, she has acted as a whistleblower, speaking out despite being subject to the strict lifetime non-disparagement agreement signed by Google employees.

Liguroi had always been prepared to be fired for her activism, but, she said, the real risk of “being sued by Google is different”. The tech giant’s parent company, Alphabet, is consistently ranked as the third or fourth most valuable globally, with a reported market worth of around $3.5trn. 

This week, she was delivered some good news: a Google executive told the company’s UK staff that it will not enforce the NDA’s clause against workers who criticise the company after leaving. Speaking to openDemocracy after the news was announced, Liguori details what it took to get Google to back down.

## The final straw

Liguori, whose background is in theoretical physics and reinforcement learning for video games, told openDemocracy she never set out to work with frontier AI models and knew “nothing” about Project Nimbus when she joined Google DeepMind in May 2023\. 

After becoming increasingly aware of the project’s impact in Gaza while on maternity leave, Liguori sent her immediate colleagues a letter urging them to take action shortly after she returned to work in August last year.

“This team is full of mothers,” she wrote. “I am not going to describe how it feels to become a mother for the first time while watching snipers targeting children, children dying of starvation, and all the rest of the horrors. What’s happening is lacerating my heart, really.”

The letter, which openDemocracy has seen, continues: “How can we do AI for good, and not even talk about Project Nimbus? How can we do AI for good in a company that is officially recognised and listed \[as\] complicit in the ongoing genocide in Palestine?”

Liguori also asked to discuss Nimbus in a team meeting. When her request was denied by a senior manager, she began sharing links to news articles about the project in internal channels. If they contained the word “genocide”, she said, they were deleted for “violating internal policies” prohibiting “aggressive language”. 

Two months after her return to work, documents were leaked to Israeli-Palestinian publication [+972 Magazine](https://www.972mag.com/project-nimbus-contract-google-amazon-israel/?ref=opendemocracy.net) and Hebrew-language outlet [Local Call](https://www.mekomit.co.il/ps/157869/?ref=opendemocracy.net) revealing that Google and Amazon had agreed to use a secret code to “effectively sidestep legal obligations” and [tip off the Israeli government](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2025/oct/29/google-amazon-israel-contract-secret-code?ref=opendemocracy.net) if they were ever ordered to share Israeli data shared on their cloud services with law enforcement authorities any where in the world.

Then, in late April 2026, it was announced that Google had signed a [contract with the US Department of War](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/apr/28/google-classified-ai-deal-pentagon?ref=opendemocracy.net) that would allow the Pentagon to use Google’s AI for “any lawful government purpose”, including mission planning and weapons targeting. 

That was the day Liguori decided enough was enough. The [petition](https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/2026/04/27/google-employees-letter-ai-pentagon/?ref=opendemocracy.net) she and over 600 colleagues had sent to CEO Sundar Pichai opposing the partnership had fallen on deaf ears. 

“I really believe there is a value of infighting from the inside,” she said, “I tried to stay and do activism and raise awareness”, but the mental toll was becoming too great. “I reached a level of disgust with my company that was just incompatible with me continuing to stay there.” 

Liguori used a combination of sick and holiday leave to cease undertaking work for Google, officially [resigning](https://stay-human.sofialiguori.com/?ref=opendemocracy.net) on 20 October. 

“I no longer believe that our technology will have a net positive impact on society. I think there’s a fantasy world where AI can help decarbonise grids, cut waste, protect ecosystems, and benefit humanity,” she wrote in her publicly posted [resignation letter](https://stay-human.sofialiguori.com/?ref=opendemocracy.net). 

“But it’s not this world, and it’s not this type of general-purpose AI we are racing to develop.”

## The growing revolt inside Google DeepMind

Google hasn’t always been so resistant to employee dissent. 

Back in 2018, after 3,000 employees signed a [petition](https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2018/apr/04/google-ceo-drones-ai-war-surveillance?ref=opendemocracy.net) seeking a policy that would stop Google and its contractors from “ever building warfare technology”, the tech firm [announced that it would no longer be renewing its contract with the Pentagon](https://www.cityam.com/286848-google-backtracks-over-controversial-military-drone-project/?ref=opendemocracy.net) on controversial military drone Project Maven. 

Shortly after, the company [published its AI Principles](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/products/ai-principles/?ref=opendemocracy.net), a set of internal guidelines that prohibited the use of its technology for AI weapons or for human rights abuses.

But weeks after Donald Trump’s second term began in January last year, the Silicon Valley-based company appeared to have a change of heart, with the AI principles [updated](https://deepmind.google/blog/updating-the-frontier-safety-framework/?ref=opendemocracy.net) to remove references to weapons or surveillance. 

“We believe democracies should lead in AI development, guided by core values like freedom, equality, and respect for human rights,” Google DeepMind chief Demis Hassabis and research labs senior vice president James Manyika wrote in a [blog post](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/products/responsible-ai-2024-report-ongoing-work/?ref=opendemocracy.net) announcing the updated policy.

Soon after, Google announced that Gemini would be used for both classified and unclassified purposes at the AI factory of [Lockheed Martin, ](https://www.googlecloudpresscorner.com/2025-10-29-Lockheed-Martin-and-Google-Public-Sector-to-Bring-Generative-AI-to-On-Premise-Infrastructure-for-National-Security?ref=opendemocracy.net)a US weapons company that primarily builds military aircraft, missiles, satellites, and defence technology for the US armed forces. 

Then, in June of this year, a [partnership](https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/partners/google-cloud-and-palantir-announce-annalytics-partnership?ref=opendemocracy.net) between Google and US military contractor [Palantir](https://www.opendemocracy.net/palantir-is-turning-the-nhs-into-a-tool-for-mass-surveillance/) was [expanded](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260604907574/en/Palantir-Announces-Availability-on-Google-Cloud-Marketplace-Including-Two-Way-Integrations-between-BigQuery-and-Foundry-and-Deep-Connectivity-between-Gemini-and-AIP?ref=opendemocracy.net) to integrate Palantir platforms across Google Cloud and Google Cloud Marketplace. 

“You never know then how your technology will be used in Palantir’s systems,” Liguori told openDemocracy. “Workers need to know what the technology they are building on will contribute, and we want the right to abstain on ethical grounds”.

Since then, a number of UK Googlers have left the company on ethical grounds, but were gagged from speaking about the firm by strict NDAs. Feeling strongly that the public needed to know about Google’s dealings with Israel, Liguori said she decided to breach her own NDA to publish her [resignation letter](https://stay-human.sofialiguori.com/?ref=opendemocracy.net), knowing that Google could retaliate. 

But this week Google told its staff in the UK that it will not take legal action against those who criticise the company or its AI products after leaving. “We’ve always encouraged an open dialogue about safety and responsibility,” a Google spokesperson told [The Washington Post](https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/2026/11/03/google-deepmind-staff-protest-lifetime-ban-criticizing-company/?ref=opendemocracy.net). “Recently, we’ve updated our terms for new hires, which included removing the post-termination aspect of non-disparagement clauses.”

Liguori sees the move as a win that “happened because of collective action”. After an employee’s attempts to raise concerns about the clause through internal channels did not lead to any change, DeepMind members of the United Tech and Allied Workers (UTAW) coordinated with the [No Tech for Apartheid](https://www.notechforapartheid.com/?ref=opendemocracy.net) campaign group and whistleblowing non-profit [Psst to ](https://psst.org/?ref=opendemocracy.net)pressure Google from multiple directions, Liguori told openDemocracy. 

It’s only because of this support network that Liguori says she was able to “find the courage to take the risk” of a public resignation.

The concession comes as the Employment Rights Act 2025 comes into effect in the UK, allowing unions to enter workplaces across the country to [speak to workers in person](https://www.tuc.org.uk/blogs/employment-rights-act-whats-changing-30-october?ref=opendemocracy.net) about joining a union. At Google and Google DeepMind, the new law will likely support [UTAW and Unite’s drive for formal recognition](https://utaw.tech/news/google-deepmind-recognition?ref=opendemocracy.net).

For Liguori, who joked that she had considered “disappearing in the Italian countryside”, the news that she won’t face legal action for her activism has come as a “big relief”. She added: “... it’s also a sign that our collective effort had an effect, and that it's worth challenging the rules.”

Google has not responded to openDemocracy’s request for comment at time of publication.
### MPs willing to rebel if Treasury doesn’t keep new miners’ pension promise
URL: https://www.opendemocracy.net/mps-willing-to-rebel-if-treasury-doesnt-keep-new-miners-pension-promise/
Last updated: 2026-11-04T11:49:45.000Z
Coalfield MPs will force a debate on the [broken miners’ pension promise](https://www.opendemocracy.net/burnham-furious-u-turn-miners-pensions-healey-budget-treasury/) if it is not resolved within weeks, openDemocracy understands.

Labour MPs in former mining heartlands have been “lobbying hard behind the scenes” since the government quietly dropped a promise to release more than £1bn from the Mineworkers Pension Scheme (MPS) from last week’s Budget. 

Sources involved in government discussions told openDemocracy that a last-minute technical bungle within the Treasury was to blame for John Healey removing the measure, which would cost taxpayers nothing but provide more than 100,000 ex-miners with an extra £20 per week in their pensions. 

The government has now pledged to release the money “within weeks, not months” – meaning it could still reach miners before Christmas as planned – after more than 40 MPs wrote to the chancellor to complain.

Jon Trickett told openDemocracy that MPs have warned the Treasury they will table an amendment to the Finance Bill if ministers fail to meet this timeline. 

“After an apparent blunder the day before the Budget, it is clear that the Treasury didn’t understand the strength of feeling their decision would provoke,” Trickett said. “But I am hopeful that we will see justice for the miners in the coming weeks and I, along with my colleagues, will continue to fight hard for this. 

“Speaking for myself, and, I am sure, for others, I will not rest until justice is done.”

When British Coal was privatised in 1994, John Major’s Tory government struck a much-maligned deal to guarantee the two primary miners’ pensions if they ever fell into deficit. In exchange, the Treasury demanded 50% of any investment surplus.

The funds performed well enough that the government never had to pay a penny into them, but still got access to the reserves. Miners have lost out on more than £4.4bn as a result, according to the National Union of Mineworkers.

As chancellor, Rachel Reeves released one of the MPS’ funds in 2024, and the sole fund for the British Coal Staff Superannuation Scheme, whose members were generally better-paid, non-mining staff, last year. 

After months of discussions and assurances from ministers, campaigners and coalfield MPs expected Healey to release the final pot of money, the Mineworkers’ Pension Scheme, this week, freeing up £1.2bn according to MPs’ estimates.

Instead, former miners were left furious when the Budget left them without a timetable to receive the money – and no explanation for the government’s last-minute U-turn.

openDemocracy understands there was a technical misunderstanding relating to the source of the cash.

While the Mineworkers’ Pension Scheme guarantor’s fund is not taxpayer money, but a share of an investment surplus generated and held by the pension fund, the government’s claim to it still needed to be accounted for in the fiscal headroom under certain accounting standards, according to Treasury sources. 

MPS trustees who have held meetings in coalfield areas in the week since the Budget report that many members feel “distraught” and “betrayed”. The government initially offered no timeline for resolving the issue, prompting significant concern about a prolonged process.

openDemocracy understands the trustees have invited the chancellor to a meeting in his South Yorkshire constituency, home to around 2,200 MPS members, later this month. 

A trade union source said they worried the political damage had “already been done”, with miners feeling “angry they’d had something taken away that they’d been promised”. 

Gary Saunders, chair of the trustees, said: “The trustees welcome the chancellor’s commitment to resolve the issue of the Guarantor’s Fund in weeks rather than months. But our members need action within days. Every week, 100 of our members pass away. 

“For them, delay cannot be undone. The Trustees have worked with the government in good faith throughout this year, and an agreement is ready to sign today. Signing it would allow us to start making payments to our members by the end of this year. We ask the chancellor to come to the table now and resolve the issue in the coming days so that more members can receive these payments during their lifetimes.”

Opposition MPs have also pushed for the Treasury to release the funds. Reform said if it wins the next general election and the funds have still not been released, it would transfer them within the first 100 days in office.

Chris Kitchen, the general secretary of the NUM, welcomed the chancellor’s commitment to release the funds within weeks, not months. 

“We are pleased that the government has recognised the injustice and committed to resolving this, and releasing the money. Weeks are better than months, but days would be better than weeks, as time is working against our members. 

“At the budget, the chancellor rightly took the other steps to make right the historic injustice of the miners’ pensions, and we are confident he will put right this final issue.”

Healey did use the Budget to end the 50:50 split of future surpluses between the government and members, telling MPs: “For ex-mineworkers, I'm guaranteeing that every penny of the pension fund surplus now goes to miners. I know the job's not done, and I will go on to ensure the full transfer of the guarantors' fund.”

The chancellor also abolished the “standstill” rule, under which bonus pensions could be frozen if the scheme fell into deficit.
### A trilogy of John Berger pieces on the centenary of his birth
URL: https://www.opendemocracy.net/a-trilogy-of-john-berger-pieces-on-the-centenary-of-his-birth/
Last updated: 2026-11-03T18:49:26.000Z
I first got to know and work with John Berger in 1971 when he helped with the launch of 7 Days, a short-lived revolutionary weekly, by becoming a ‘trustee’. He contributed a dramatic essay on Mayakovsky, which he co-wrote with Anya Bostock. From then our friendship developed, as described in Tom Overton’s new biography. The photo above, taken by Jean Mohr, dates from around late 1977 in my flat in Covent Garden. I’m trying to show John how to unravel a roll of Sellotape while he fingers a packet of Gitanes he was not allowed to smoke. More important, for me at least, was that his example taught me how to write. 

Fast-forward two decades and he became a contributor to openDemocracy. There was no formal relationship but he was a spiritual trustee of its commitment to openness, honest argument, international solidarity and opposition to the lies of the US and UK governments headed by Bush and Blair. His interview about the decisive importance of the 2004 US election, which we run here, focuses on the terrible mendacity of the Bush administration. Bush won the election and we can see today that there is a direct inheritance from his triumph that leads to Trump.

John’s powerful and demanding *Ten Dispatches about Endurance in the Face of Walls*, is in part a response to the creation of the so-called ‘Separation Wall’ then under full construction by Israel along the West Bank.

One of the most notable of John’s achievements in the later part of his life was his commitment to the cause of Palestine and resistance to Israeli occupation and expansion. The short statement that opens our trilogy is worth thousands of words and stands today as a simple moral instruction. We must go on refuting the actions of the Israeli state and the appalling support, material and verbal, that it receives, as it seeks to crush its Palestinian neighbours in a fashion that is “viscerally racist”. It opens the three contributions.

Judging from his post-Budget interview with ITV, even Burnham doesn’t think his Budget was radical enough to meet this moment. To understand what he could have done differently, read our lead story, which features the reactions of a panel of economists, politicians, and campaigners. 

Also in this issue of the newsletter, Labour MP Jon Trickett says Burnham’s Budget has failed what he calls the “Makerfield test”. “If the policies unveiled do not work for his constituency, or constituencies like it, they do not work at all,” Trickett says, “And by that measure, the Budget has failed.” While openDemocracy’s Ethan Shone, himself the grandson of a miner, digs into what the Budget means for the ongoing negotiation around the surpluses that have accrued to the miners’ pension scheme. 

Following a report that YouTube makes millions in profits from showing advertisements against videos pushing hate speech, a group of senior advertising executives have come together to push their industry to do better, openDemocracy’s Evie Breese reports, citing research that shows that “the most lucrative videos target migrants, Muslims and Black communities, often together.” A company spokesperson told Evie that YouTube doesn’t allow hate speech on its platform (to which I thought, do they even watch YouTube?).
