### ‘Blindsided’ Burnham ‘furious’ as Treasury U-turns on miners’ pension boost
URL: https://www.opendemocracy.net/burnham-furious-u-turn-miners-pensions-healey-budget-treasury/
Last updated: 2026-11-02T13:45:08.000Z
More than a hundred thousand retired miners who expected their pensions to rise by up to 20% next month have been left with no timetable for the payment, after a last-minute Treasury U-turn that senior Labour sources say left the prime minister “furious”. 

openDemocracy understands the government may now be unable to transfer the funds it promised until next year – a delay that means thousands of miners could pass away without ever seeing the money. 

When British Coal was privatised in 1994, the government agreed to guarantee the two primary miners' pensions if the funds they had been paying into ever fell into deficit. In exchange, the Treasury demanded 50% of any investment surplus.

The funds performed well enough that the government never had to pay a penny into them, but still got access to the reserves. Miners have lost out on more than £4.4bn as a result, according to the National Union of Mineworkers.

As chancellor, Rachel Reeves released the funds for the British Coal Staff Superannuation Scheme, whose members were generally better-paid, non-mining staff. Based on assurances from ministers, campaigners and coalfield MPs expected that Healey would do the same for the Mineworkers’ Pension Scheme this week, freeing up more than £1bn according to MPs’ estimates.

But in a meeting on Tuesday, Treasury officials told the trustees the money would not be released after all, blaming government accounting rules. Senior Labour sources told openDemocracy that Andy Burnham was “blindsided” by the decision, which he and Healy “clashed” over. 

The Treasury did not directly comment on these allegations, and Downing Street had not responded to our questions at the time of publication.

Burnham made the dispute part of his Makerfield by-election campaign earlier this year, pledging to “keep fighting” to make sure “every penny reaches the people it is meant for”.

Believing the deal would be signed off at the Budget, trustees of the Mineworkers' Pension Scheme (MPS) had lined up a bonus to be added to members’ December pension payments, following months of negotiations with ministers, coalfield MPs, and the National Union of Mineworkers.

The pension boost would have been funded by the government renouncing its claim to the scheme's guarantor's fund, and would not have cost the taxpayer anything. Now, the former miners have been left with no timetable for payment. 

The MPS estimates that more than 5,000 of its members, many of whom are ageing and suffer health problems related to their former profession, pass away every year. Any delay means many more pensioners will never see the additional funds they were promised. 

The National Union of Mineworkers understands that the remaining funds can only be released at a fiscal event such as a Budget. If correct, this would likely mean the earliest money can be released will now be well into next year. 

Chris Kitchen, the NUM’s general secretary, told openDemocracy: “We're frustrated that money that could be used to mitigate cost of living pressures and benefit the country now is still locked up, doing no good for anybody.”

The Treasury would not respond to openDemocracy’s questions on what prompted the last-minute U-turn. Instead, it pointed only to remarks the prime minister made earlier this week: “Nothing's gone wrong. The commitment is in no way diminished.”

In the interview cited by the Treasury, Burnham added that the Budget “didn't give us all of the room for manoeuvre that we would have wanted”, and that the fund “does have to be scored on the public balance sheet and that is part of the challenge that we've got”.

### **‘Heard loud and clear’**

When he made his first conference speech as chancellor in Liverpool last month, Healey referred throughout to a miner's lamp that sits on a shelf in his home. “Those miners,” he said, “didn't just use their lamps to light their own steps, they shone them to help others.”

But as he drained his pint at the Two Chairmen pub in Westminster on Wednesday evening, celebrating his first Budget in traditional style, many of his Labour colleagues' inboxes were filling up with angry correspondence from those same miners. 

Labour activists canvassing in coalfield constituencies in the days after the Budget told openDemocracy the issue has already come up frequently on the doorstep, and the party’s coalfield MPs have since engaged in three days of fierce lobbying of the Treasury, both in public and behind the scenes.

On Friday afternoon, Labour whips sent the party’s MPs a briefing promising to meet with coalfield MPs “in the coming weeks” – but set out no date for releasing the money.

The briefing, which openDemocracy has seen, said that Healey, chief secretary to the Treasury Emma Reynolds and reindustrialisation minister Blair McDougall had “heard loud and clear the representations” and would work with MPs, trustees and the National Union of Mineworkers “to find a resolution”.

But this resolution may come too late for many former miners.

In a letter sent to his MP and shared with openDemocracy, a retired miner from Yorkshire asked: “Are we seriously expected to believe that an accounting problem significant enough to prevent the agreement being implemented was not identified until the final hours before the Budget?

“Many MPS members are now elderly. Some will never live to benefit from another pension increase if these delays continue,” he added. “Blaming accounting rules at the very last moment is simply not good enough.”

Jon Trickett, the MP for Normanton and Hemsworth, was among the coalfield MPs who lobbied No 10, the Treasury and the whips on the eve of the Budget. “The apparent last-minute decision by the chancellor to make changes to the miners’ pension promise has sparked anger and puzzlement in the coal mining areas I represent,” he told openDemocracy. 

“Whilst I wholly welcome the good intentions of the Prime Minister, people are telling me that it’s time to deliver what was promised, sooner rather than later. I will continue to press hard for an immediate decision. Nothing less will do.” 

In his Budget speech on Wednesday, Healey did end the 50:50 split of future surpluses between the government and members, telling MPs: “For ex-mineworkers, I'm guaranteeing that every penny of the pension fund surplus now goes to miners. I know the job's not done, and I will go on to ensure the full transfer of the guarantors' fund.”

The chancellor also abolished the “standstill” rule, under which bonus pensions could be frozen if the scheme fell into deficit.

But, unlike the release of the guarantor’s fund, neither of these measures will put extra money in former miners’ pockets before the end of the year. 

“The money in the MPS guarantors fund is not taxpayers' money,” the NUM said in a statement on Wednesday. "It is the remaining ill-gotten gains from an unfair system put in place that has penalised members of the MPS for the last 31 years.”

### **‘Second-class deal’**

The trustees say the accounting explanation is hard to square with last year’s decision to transfer £2.3bn to members of the British Coal Staff Superannuation Scheme, which covers non-mining staff from the industry and already pays higher pensions.

Gary Saunders, chair of the MPS trustees, said they were “very disappointed” that the chancellor had decided “just hours before the Budget announcement” not to go ahead, “even though a deal had been worked on extensively by both sides for months and was ready to sign”.

“What is hard to understand is how members of the MPS have been left with a second-class deal compared to the higher pensioned members in the British Coal Staff Superannuation Scheme,” he said.

Allen Young, speaking for the scheme's elected trustees, said: “One month ago, the Chancellor said that miners' lamps are a symbol of hope, but today he confirmed that there is still no light at the end of the tunnel for MPS members.”

The Treasury’s Emma Reynolds has defended the package. “This government has done more than any other government to do right by our mineworkers,” [she told *PoliticsHome*](https://www.politicshome.com/news/article/government-holding-talks-labour-mps-after-miner-pensions-backlash?ref=opendemocracy.net) after the budget. “We still have the outstanding issue of the guarantor's fund, which we're working closely with Labour MPs on.”
### Advertising industry must stop funding online hate, whistleblowing execs warn
URL: https://www.opendemocracy.net/youtube-google-advertising-must-stop-funding-online-hate-whistleblowers-warn/
Last updated: 2026-10-30T13:27:42.000Z
“The atmosphere towards immigrants is the worst it’s ever been, and people are saying they don’t know why. But *we* know why.”

Michael is a senior executive in the global ad industry. He has built a highly successful international career, forged relationships with glitzy clients with million-dollar advertising budgets, and managed partnerships that have made the big tech players a serious amount of money. 

At the same time, he has watched with dismay as loved ones in the US have been increasingly subjected to racism and hatred, partially rooted in misinformation.

Michael believes his industry is funding such hate by allowing adverts to be placed on online content pushing racist, homophobic, or misogynistic narratives. He is part of a group of advertising insiders calling on their industry to demand change from the Big Tech firms running social media sites.

“It’s the amplification of this hateful stuff online,” he told openDemocracy, speaking under a pseudonym to protect his career. “I think as an industry, we haven't done enough to actually hold our hands up and go: ‘Hey, we’re partially responsible here, because the fact of the matter is that if this content wasn't making money, it would be off most of the platforms.’”

Michael and his fellow advertising whistleblowers were convened by Inside Track, a British non-profit that builds confidential peer groups of senior professionals in powerful industries to spotlight and shift harmful cultures, norms, and incentives. 

“For years the advertising industry has told government and clients that funding hate is either unavoidable, under control or something they have no influence upon,” said Nisreen Shahin, director of Inside Track.

Michael agrees that this is untrue, telling openDemocracy: “A lot of these \[social media\] platforms could solve the problem of hate speech online in a matter of days, weeks, but they don’t because it makes too much money.”

His and his peers’ calls for change come as new research from the Global Disinformation Index (GDI), a non-profit seeking to reduce the spread of online disinformation, reveals the huge profits to be made from videos encouraging hatred towards marginalised people. 

The GDI’s researchers analysed 100 YouTube channels producing hateful and bigoted content, finding they are “on track to generate an estimated $13.3m in ad revenue in 2026”. The team also revealed YouTube is reaping large profits, retaining an estimated $6m from ads placed on hate content. 

“The most lucrative videos target migrants, Muslims and Black communities, often together”, according to the research, which used large language models to conduct sentiment analysis of the videos on these channels.

YouTube operates a high bar to classify content as hate speech. “Much” of the content GDI categorised as hateful is permitted and monetisable under [YoutTube’s own definition](https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/2801939?hl=en&ref%5Ftopic=9282436&ref=opendemocracy.net) of hate speech, which focuses on the ‘promotion of violence or hatred’. This definition, explains Clare Melford, CEO of GDI, means that groups of people including Muslims or migrants can be repeatedly referred to in a denigrating way – as criminals or as a threat – but unless there is a specific incitement of violence, YouTube is unlikely to take the content down or demonetise it. 

“We support YouTube in not taking down the content unless it is explicitly illegal, but monetisation is a privilege not a right,” she said, “and advertisers deserve control over whether their ads appear next to content that denigrates an entire group of people.”

The GDI identified a UK-based podcast channel that linked the LGBTQIA+ movement and the Quran to terrorism, which may breach YouTube’s own rules but remains monetised by the platform. The GDI estimates the channel earns around $23,000 a year from ad revenue, as well as generating around $19,000 for YouTube.

“YouTube has already written rules against this content, and it has the power to stop paying for it,” said Melford. “What nobody outside YouTube can see is whether those rules are applied.”

Back in 2017, YouTube’s owner, Google, faced a watershed moment when an [investigation by The Times](https://www.thetimes.com/business/technology/article/google-faces-questions-over-videos-on-youtube-3km257v8d?ref=opendemocracy.net) revealed that companies including Mercedes-Benz and Argos were “unintentionally funding terrorism” when their ads appeared alongside extremist YouTube videos. Major brands including Verizon and Walmart [pulled their ads](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2017/mar/25/google-youtube-advertising-extremist-content-att-verizon?ref=opendemocracy.net) from the online video-sharing platform, and Google lost millions of dollars. 

Google publicly apologised and promised to give brands [more control](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/ads/expanded-safeguards-for-advertisers/?ref=opendemocracy.net) over where their ads appear. It later unveiled a [stricter harassment policy](https://www.nytimes.com/2019/06/05/business/youtube-remove-extremist-videos.html?ref=opendemocracy.net), which introduced specific, structured penalties targeting creators who repeatedly “brush up against” or violate rules. These changes were a step in the right direction, said Melford, but stopped short of offering full transparency for where adverts end up. 

Advertisers often have limited control over where their adverts appear on social media sites such as YouTube, Facebook and X, and may be unaware they are funding content targeting marginalised groups. But as these platforms make the majority of their revenue from adverts, Michael believes the advertising industry has a responsibility to demand guarantees or withdraw their custom. 

Since Donald Trump re-entered the White House last year, all of the social media platforms run by US tech companies have rolled back on their commitments to trust and safety, while many have changed their [content moderation policies](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c4g93nvrdz7o?ref=opendemocracy.net), often ditching commitments to [fact-checking](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2025/jan/10/mark-zuckerberg-meta-factchecking?ref=opendemocracy.net). 

“I think we've just seen a reversal in the last few years,” Michael said. “In the last few years there has been no concerted effort by advertisers to go, ‘hey, we're gonna stop spending if you don’t fix this’”.

Jenny, an advertising insider in the UK who also spoke to openDemocracy under a pseudonym, believes hateful content online has exploded since companies including [X](https://fortune.com/2024/02/06/inside-elon-musk-x-twitter-austin-content-moderation/?ref=opendemocracy.net) and [Meta](https://www.aibusinessreview.org/2026/06/25/meta-ai-content-moderation-workforce-cuts/?ref=opendemocracy.net) (which owns Facebook) cut content moderation teams, replacing some with AI. 

“They've happily washed their hands of the responsibility to control this situation, and we've just carried on spending exactly as much money with them as we ever did, if not more,” she said. 

“The internet is free because of advertising; that is the single thing that is fuelling everything that we are discussing when we talk about online harms.”

Asked by openDemocracy what it would take to force big tech companies to remove all hateful content from their sites, Jenny said that “if every big player in the media industry was willing to collaborate” they could leverage their spending power.

This is not the first time the advertising industry has attempted to influence what is shared online. The World Federation of Advertisers launched the Global Alliance for Responsible Media in the wake of the 2019 mass shooting at a mosque in Christchurch, New Zealand, which was livestreamed on Facebook. 

The alliance, which established tools and frameworks to ensure “advertising dollars do not inadvertently support illegal or harmful content that damages their brands”, was [shut down](https://www.marketingweek.com/wfa-suspend-garm-x-lawsuit/?ref=opendemocracy.net) in 2024 after Elon Musk’s X announced it would bring a lawsuit against it and its members, who said they did not have the funds to fight the lawsuit. X accused the non-profit coalition of violating US competition law by creating an “illegal boycott” that would cost it “billions of dollars” in lost ad revenue.

In response to GDI’s research, a YouTube spokesperson told openDemocracy: “[Hate speech](https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/2801939?hl=en&ref%5Ftopic=9282436&ref=opendemocracy.net) is not allowed on YouTube and we rigorously remove content that violates our hate speech policy, regardless of channel size. We also enforce our strict advertiser-friendly guidelines that determine what content is eligible to monetise.”
### Big talk, small promises: Experts’ verdict on ‘underwhelming’ Budget
URL: https://www.opendemocracy.net/budget-burnham-john-healey-experts-verdict-big-talk-small-promises/
Last updated: 2026-11-04T16:22:18.000Z
“I am ready to do things my predecessors wouldn’t. I will make a break with the direction of the past 40 years and put Britain on a new path. Build a new economy and a new politics.” 

That’s the pitch Andy Burnham made to the country at last month’s Labour Party Conference.

The new prime minister promised to undo 40 years of “deindustrialisation, deregulation, privatisation, austerity and Brexit”, which, he said, have left us with “a country run for vested interests. Not in the public interest.”

This week, as chancellor John Healey delivered his first Budget, we finally got a look at just how Burnham’s government will fix Britain. Except, we didn’t really. 

As academics, politicians, and campaigners have written for openDemocracy, the Budget was something of a non-event. A few policies that will go some way to helping struggling families up and down the country, but none that will bring about desperately needed wealth redistribution. 

Below, they explain how opportunities were missed to tax banks’ huge profits and rein in private companies’ profiteering through public ownership, while money that could have lowered energy and food prices was thrown at US defence companies and domestic data centres. 

## **A Budget for markets and the wealthy**

**—Prem Sikka, Labour peer** 

John Healey needed to use his first Budget to make the economy and households more resilient. In the end, he delivered little on either front, limited by self-imposed revenue-raising constraints due to obedience to fiscal rules and a foolish manifesto promise against increasing most taxes.

The result was a chancellor left floundering, and an underwhelming Budget. 

Energy companies have escaped a windfall tax. Banks will pay a puny 3% more for 15 months, yielding £1.5bn. Tax on gambling through slot machines is to rise from 20% to 25%, far lower than the 40% the industry expected.

The commitment to spend 3% of GDP on defence by 2030 has been reaffirmed. The biggest beneficiaries will be US arms corporations, as the UK has weakened its manufacturing base. An extra £1.5bn will be allocated to social housing, to deliver around 10,000 homes in England, taking total investment in the Social and Affordable Homes Programme to more than £40bn over ten years. The waiting list for social housing is around 1.3 million households and recent governments have failed to hit the housebuilding targets. Reindustrialisation remains a distant goal.

The freeze on income tax thresholds that started in 2021 will continue – hitting the poorest hardest. Someone with an annual salary of £17,000 will pay nearly £1,000 more in income tax and National Insurance in this financial year. Gestures such as a £100 reduction in energy bills for households in council tax bands A to D, promises of absorbing gas supply standing charge into unit prices, and cuts to VAT on electricity will not eliminate the impact of fiscal drag. Millions will remain in poverty.

Middle classes will welcome the abandonment of the plan to reduce Cash ISA investment from £20,000 to £12,000\. It will do nothing for 39% of the adults with savings of £1,000 or less.

Overall, the Budget appeases markets and the super-rich. It does little to improve infrastructure or disposable income of the bottom 50%, making sustained economic growth difficult.

## **The military-industrial complex swallowed Labour’s Budget**

**— Kevin Cashman, Transition Security Project** 

John Healey[ resigned as Keir Starmer’s defence secretary](https://www.theguardian.com/politics/2026/jun/11/john-healey-resigns-defence-secretary-military-spending?ref=opendemocracy.net) in June after failing to secure the additional £28bn in military funding defence officials said they needed from government. Now, in his first Budget as Andy Burnham’s chancellor, we are seeing what his ambitions cost the rest of us.

To help fund the eventual £15bn Defence Investment Plan, Healey announced the government will cut a further £3bn across other departments, on top of £6.8bn in cuts announced by Starmer earlier this year. These spending priorities undermine Burnham’s cost of living agenda. 

Taken together, the cuts could cost roughly 15,000 net jobs, according to a newly updated version of the[ analysis](https://transitionsecurity.org/buying-the-dip/?ref=opendemocracy.net) that we at the Transition Security Project, a research centre investigating the US and UK military-industrial complexes, carried out earlier this year. Military spending supports fewer domestic jobs than the investment being cut, partly because spending on imported weapons flows overseas, especially to the United States. 

Longer-term military spending commitments imply a colossal transfer of wealth from the public to the military sector. Starmer was[ strong-armed](https://www.theguardian.com/politics/2025/jun/03/nato-defence-spending-uk-trump?ref=opendemocracy.net) by the US into raising military spending to 3.5% of GDP by 2035 – a decision that Healey has[ repeatedly](https://www.gov.uk/government/speeches/budget-2026-speech?ref=opendemocracy.net)[ reaffirmed](https://www.theguardian.com/politics/live/2026/sep/01/andy-burnham-statement-commons-prison-release-farage-healey-defence-latest-news-updates?ref=opendemocracy.net). Meeting this target would require an estimated £280bn in extra spending by 2035, or about £28bn more a year. If £15bn over four years requires these sacrifices, what will successive budgets sacrifice? 

This Budget makes the consequences for households clear. It cuts £1bn from the Warm Homes Plan – a scheme to upgrade millions of homes, cut fuel poverty and support the transition to low-carbon heating – reducing investment that would help bring down energy bills. Meanwhile, the government’s immediate support on energy bills is welcome, but[ falls far short](https://neweconomics.org/2026/10/autumn-budget-shows-right-instincts-but-not-the-right-scale?ref=opendemocracy.net) of the increase in bills expected this winter. 

These military commitments show the ambition the government should bring to tackling rising living costs, as Burnham has promised to do. The military can help, too. A new[ National Security Strategy](https://transitionsecurity.org/posturing-to-the-world/?ref=opendemocracy.net) that ends Britain’s[ complicity](https://www.lbc.co.uk/article/sending-jets-saudi-arabia-drive-up-bills-opinion-5HjdkMf%5F2/?ref=opendemocracy.net) in the[ conflicts driving up our bills](https://www.thetimes.com/business/economics/article/budget-john-healey-trade-union-defence-spending-f9hl5z07q?ref=opendemocracy.net), in favour of defence, diplomacy and de-escalation, would lower our household costs. 

The public will judge Burnham on living standards – including clean, affordable energy and reliable public services – not new fighter jets or submarines. As temperatures fall, the time to change course is now.

## **Post-industrial Britain deserves better than data centres**

**—Sacha Hilhorst, Senior Research Fellow at Common Wealth, Hallsworth Fellow at University of Manchester**

On the face of it, this Budget spoke to the everyday concerns of people across the country: high energy bills, declining high streets, powerless communities. 

These themes come up often in the former mining and manufacturing towns of the Midlands where I conduct ethnographic research. People there will approve of how the Budget hit betting shops, vape shops and big banks, in favour of breathing life into pubs and shops, and curbing rising energy bills. Passing surpluses in coal industry pension schemes on to retired miners will be popular, too. 

On a structural level, however, this was a small fiscal event. Insofar as the Budget revealed a strategic direction, it saw the government double down on defence spending and AI. Post-industrial England is already feeling the effects on both counts: in Nottinghamshire, a large data centre will be built near the former Ratcliffe-on-Soar power station, while another is proposed on erstwhile Rufford pit. Politicians seem to have run out of other ideas for these vast tracts of previously industrial land. 

Then there is the commitment to military spending at the expense of other investments. Already, there is local outrage over plans to defund infrastructure projects across the East Midlands and redirect cash to the Ministry of Defence. Military spending has smaller employment effects than other investments, so this will lead to net job losses. 

In his speech, Healey spoke with pride of the Regional Development Agencies (RDAs) he had promoted as a Treasury minister in Gordon Brown’s New Labour government. In the Midlands, flagship ‘successes’ included a site for a massive, exploitative Sports Direct warehouse and a ‘regeneration route’ that now hosts Amazon. 

If the RDAs’ history shows us anything, it is this: politicians must be far more ambitious in their policies for post-industrial areas. Devolution efforts are welcome, but we need a break with the prevailing economic system, which this budget did not offer. 

## **Burnham promised a rupture. Healey delivered tinkering**

**—Jon Trickett, Labour MP**

Chancellor John Healey said he would secure growth in every postcode. A £100 one-off energy payment is very welcome, but the energy sector has been ripping consumers off for a generation, while retail giants take advantage of their market power by driving up the cost of groceries. 

If we really want to help people in every area of the country, why not take on the privatised monopolies directly, not with a few more rules, but with proper public ownership?

Finding additional money for defence is an inevitable choice for a chancellor who helped precipitate Keir Starmer’s downfall by resigning as defence secretary. But the defence industries are concentrated in a small number of regions and will do little in terms of growth for the large part of the country.

Healey has delivered a Budget within the same fiscal constraints as his predecessors, one that simply does not shake off the cloying grip of neoliberal ideology, Treasury orthodoxy, and the usual vested interests lobbying the government. If the chancellor cannot deliver radical change at a macro-economic level, the only option is to tinker around the edges with micro-economic policy. 

But that strategy simply doesn’t transform the country in the way Burnham promised Makerfield, and Britain, he would. What is clear is that over-reliance on official institutions, which Burnham has spoken strongly against, has produced a budget that is at best mildly progressive. 

Of course, there are good things in the Budget. Healey’s pledge that every penny of the Miners’ Pension Fund will go to miners was welcome – although questions remain over when and how that will happen – as was his recognition of the need for “breathing room” from the cost of living crisis, especially by imposing a 6% levy on banks’ profits above £100m. But the truth is that this levy is less than it ought to be, and will apply for only 15 months. It does not go far enough at a time when banks make billions in super profits as many struggle.

NHS founder Nye Bevan once said socialism is a language of priorities, a mantra that any Labour chancellor should heed in a budget. That’s why it is disappointing that the chancellor is pushing ahead with plans to abandon the pensions triple lock, a move projected to save £15bn a year, while ignoring policies such as equalising capital gains tax, which could raise over £19bn a year by 2030\. Britain doesn’t have to choose between offering a decent pension and decent care. We can, and should, provide both. 

***This is an edited extract of***[ ***an article Jon Trickett wrote for openDemocracy. Read in full here.***](https://www.opendemocracy.net/budget-burnham-promised-rupture-neoliberalism-healey-delivered-gentle-tinkering/)

## **Stuck in Britain’s gas trap**

**—Ewan Gibbs, senior lecturer in economic and social history at the University of Glasgow**

Energy was the headline policy area of this year’s Budget. The cost of energy, disagreements over climate action and debates over North Sea drilling have dominated British politics since the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022 sent oil and gas prices spiralling. More recently, Donald Trump and Binyamin Netanyahu’s new war in the Persian Gulf turbocharged concerns over oil supply and affordability. 

In this context, the central measure in the chancellor’s plan to give “breathing space” to those struggling amid high cost of living is a one-off £100 “energy payment” for most households in England (those in council tax bands A-D). Devolved administrations have indicated they’ll follow suit. Along with the direct alleviation itself, Burnham’s government is signalling that it understands the pressures facing pensions and workers, as wages lag behind spiralling bills.

But £100 is paltry by contrast to the annual increases consumers are facing. It may well communicate only that the government cannot, or at least will not, meet the challenge of an energy system patently failing citizens and industry. 

The other energy measure that grabbed pundits’ attention is the scrapping of standing charges for gas customers, which is estimated to typically save billpayers £45 per annum. These monthly charges have long been in the sights of fuel poverty campaigners. Scrapping them will save most households money, especially poorer households. It’s left opponents on the back foot, with the Scottish National Party seemingly committing a vault face by shifting from calling for the measure to condemning it. The saving will be welcome and follows on the removal of VAT on electricity, but, as with the energy payment, will be marginal in the face of the energy price headwind.

A less prominent announcement was the removal of a green levy from consumer bills. The levy, which funds hydrogen projects, will now instead be covered by central government. While a relatively minor measure, it would signal a major drift in the direction of funding energy investment if it were applied across the board. Contract for Difference, the UK’s main subsidy scheme for encouraging developers to build wind and solar farms, currently makes up nearly 5% of electricity bills.

Ultimately, this Budget does not mark any significant break with the status quo. The privatisation of our energy system, especially electricity and gas utilities, along with the ‘dash for gas’ that saw energy companies abandon coal in favour of new gas power stations, was fundamental to the making of a neoliberal Britain in the 1980s and early 1990s. One consequence has been the consolidation of a pricing structure that left electricity prices dependent on gas prices. 

Since 2022, the British government has spent a net £55bn on subsidising gas prices. Today’s measures are only tinkering around the side, leaving Britain dependent on an expensive, impoverishing, inefficient and carbon-based energy system.

## **A Budget that still leaves women waiting**

**—Daniella Jenkins, Women’s Budget Group**

Healey’s Budget offers a few much-needed measures to address the cost of living, primarily by shielding households from even steeper energy bills. But many women, particularly single parents on low incomes, won’t see enough help with the scale of financial pressures they face going into this winter.

Housing was one of the clearest omissions. The focus was on supporting aspiring homeowners, but for many women the immediate challenge is making next month's rent. [Women now spend an average of 57% of their earnings on private rent,](https://www.wbg.org.uk/article/women-spend-over-half-their-income-on-rent-as-chancellor-urged-to-unfreeze-housing-benefit/?ref=opendemocracy.net) compared with 41% for men, leaving many financially exposed. While increasing funding to end rough sleeping is welcome, preventing homelessness is equally important. By failing to unfreeze Local Housing Allowance, the chancellor has missed a crucial opportunity to ease pressure on renters and protect more women from being pushed into poverty and homelessness.

The government has promised to unlock growth in every postcode and boost living standards across the UK, yet this Budget continues to overlook the social infrastructure that makes economic participation possible. Investment in care, childcare and support for families is too often treated as secondary to traditional infrastructure spending. That comes at a significant cost. Our analysis estimates that the UK [loses £113bn](https://www.wbg.org.uk/article/economy-loses-113bn-when-it-excludes-women-female-labour-mps-warn-chancellor/?ref=opendemocracy.net) in economic output because women's skills and labour are underutilised.

There were some positive steps. Extending statutory paternity pay to self-employed fathers and removing the Carer’s Allowance earnings cliff edge are important reforms that recognise the value of unpaid care, much of which is carried out by women. Yet these changes will take years to reach families, leaving many waiting until the end of the decade for meaningful support

While the chancellor did say the paternity pay was a ‘down payment’ on wider reforms to parental leave, he also needed to address the inadequacy of maternity pay, which continues to put many mothers under severe financial pressure. [Our analysis](https://www.wbg.org.uk/publication/strengthening-statutory-maternity-adoption-and-maternity-allowance-pay/?ref=opendemocracy.net) has shown that improving maternity pay would put more than £1bn in families’ pockets and deliver social and economic gains.

And while a new fund to tackle misogyny is welcome, £5m a year for three years is a drop in the ocean. It is, notably, just half the amount allocated to a single new parkway station in Cardiff.

## **While we ration heating, the ultra-rich fly tax-free**

**—Myles Cummins, climate charity Possible**

Labour’s 2024 manifesto promised action against the worst polluters and fossil-fuel giants. Yet once again, the super-rich and their climate-wrecking habits have escaped penalty, just a week or so after the government approved the Jackdaw gas field, and with approval of the Rosebank oil field remaining an alarming possibility. 

Helping business does not mean continuing to give the wealthiest few a leg up. Our small business owners do not receive anywhere near the leniency that big corporation owners continue to benefit from. 

We are left wondering, ‘How do the ultra-rich keep getting away without paying their fair share for the damage they’re doing to the environment?’ They insult us all with their private flights to luxury holiday destinations, while the poorest in our society are likely to have to ration their heating this winter. 

Yet we constantly see them being given an easy ride, paying no fuel duty at all on the kerosene fuel used for their super-expensive private jet journeys, and severely undertaxed compared to our ordinary economy or standard airline travel. The fact that air passenger duty on private jet flights increased by only the same inflation metric as tax on ordinary flights encapsulates this perfectly.

For how long can we be told nothing can be done to even slightly level the playing field between the haves and the have-nots? It’s frankly insulting that the government thinks that we can be placated by a few pounds off our grocery bill each month, while private jets continue to fly all over Europe to luxury locations at their leisure, while paying a much lower real rate of tax. 

We watch our living standards tumble and see mega-polluting jets show no sign of slowing down, and we pick up the bill for the damage being unleashed upon the climate.

It’s past time for a Labour government to do more to get the wealthiest few to start paying their fair share, particularly while ordinary people keep feeling the pinch. That’s why we’re not giving up the fight for a better, fairer system, to ensure the vast majority of us don’t have to keep on feeling like the system is stacked against us all the time. 

We need to introduce fair taxes on private jets, which would need to increase by a factor of 30 times the current rate to match the relative rate that ordinary people pay on their tickets. This would raise valuable funds (potentially £2.7bn) that could be used to actually ease the cost of living, and to help protect all of us against some of the worst harms of the climate crisis.
### Burnham promised a much-needed rupture. Healey delivered gentle tinkering
URL: https://www.opendemocracy.net/budget-burnham-promised-rupture-neoliberalism-healey-delivered-gentle-tinkering/
Last updated: 2026-10-29T11:42:00.000Z
Having spent 30 years as a Labour MP, I have long argued that tinkering around the edges with the UK’s badly skewed economy simply will not do. Andy Burnham seemed to agree when campaigning in the Makerfield by-election in June.

Back then, Burnham promised a new direction, a break with neoliberalism and the hope of a better future. He seemed to understand that the country needed a rupture with the status quo in order to address the underlying economic, political and social malaise. 

Within weeks of winning his seat, he became Labour leader and entered Number 10 without a contest, meaning there was no real space to interrogate his political programme. The Labour Party and the country took him at his word, because we had to. 

The Budget, then, is the first time Burnham’s vision has been properly tested. We should judge it by a ‘Makerfield test’: if the policies unveiled do not work for his constituency, or constituencies like it, they do not work at all. And by that measure, the Budget has failed. 

Chancellor John Healey said he would secure growth in every postcode. A £100 one-off energy payment is very welcome, but the energy sector has been ripping consumers off for a generation, while retail giants take advantage of their market power by driving up the cost of groceries. If we really want to help people in every area of the country, why not take on the privatised monopolies directly, not with a few more rules, but with proper public ownership?

Finding additional money for defence is an inevitable choice for a chancellor who helped precipitate Keir Starmer’s downfall by resigning as defence secretary. But the defence industries are concentrated in a small number of regions and will do little in terms of growth for the large part of the country.

Healey has delivered a Budget within the same fiscal constraints as his predecessors, one that simply does not shake off the cloying grip of neoliberal ideology, Treasury orthodoxy, and the usual vested interests lobbying the government. If the chancellor cannot deliver radical change at a macro-economic level, the only option is to tinker around the edges with micro-economic policy. But that strategy simply doesn’t transform the country in the way Burnham promised Makerfield, and Britain, he would. 

What is clear is that over-reliance on official institutions, which Burnham has spoken strongly against, has produced a Budget that is at best mildly progressive. 

Of course, there are good things in the Budget. Healey’s pledge that every penny of the Miners’ Pension Fund will go to miners was welcome, but it should never have been in doubt – and questions still remain over when and how that will happen.

It is also welcome that the chancellor has recognised the need for “breathing room” from the cost of living crisis, especially with a 6% levy on banks’ profits above £100m. But the truth is that this levy is less than it ought to be, and will apply for only 15 months. It does not go far enough at a time when banks make billions in super profits as many struggle.

NHS founder Nye Bevan once said socialism is a language of priorities, a mantra that any Labour chancellor should heed in a Budget. That’s why it is disappointing that the chancellor is pushing ahead with plans to abandon the pensions triple lock, a move projected to save £15bn a year, while ignoring policies such as equalising capital gains tax, which could raise over £19bn a year by 2030\. Britain doesn’t have to choose between offering a decent pension and decent care. We can, and should, provide both. 

The country needs to fundamentally rupture with the neoliberal status quo. In recent decades, the government has ceded control of the main economic levers to the Treasury, the Bank of England and the Office for Budget Responsibility, making it difficult for any government to intervene adequately in the economy. 

Indeed, the UK’s institutions have been colonised by neoliberalism. We have witnessed a long history of catastrophic forecasting failures due to Whitehall orthodoxy: from Denis Healey’s misjudged swingeing cuts in the 1976 IMF crisis to joining the European Exchange Rate Mechanism in 1990 and exiting two years later on Black Wednesday, the promotion of austerity over much of the past two decades, the blind eye turned to deindustrialisation, and most recently, the miscalculations of the Truss Budget. 

Burnham previously criticised our central institutions, arguing that top-down neoliberal economics doesn’t work. Why, then, expect the country to continue to accept the Treasury’s orthodoxy? 

His government has spoken a lot about a “radical rewiring” of the state to restore democratic control. But the Budget was always touted as a ‘safety first’ fiscal event, with the promise that a 10-year plan is on its way to address the underlying crises in our economy. My concern is that putting off big decisions until next year’s Spending Review, as the chancellor has said he is doing, suggests potential cuts down the line. 

The truth is, the UK’s economy is still constrained by tight fiscal rules, which will not deliver the urgent changes needed, especially for communities such as those in Makerfield. Indeed, I would advise that the chancellor needs to be careful to avoid the accusation that he is starting to look a lot like his much-criticised predecessor, Rachel Reeves.

### Inside the Israeli military mindset driving endless war
URL: https://www.opendemocracy.net/israel-election-netanyahu-eisenkot-military-driving-endless-war-gaza-palestine-lebanon/
Last updated: 2026-10-26T11:23:37.000Z
**Listen to this article** [Sign up for a free account to do so](#/portal/signup) 

Listen to this article. (6 min 50 sec)

15s 15s 

Audio generated with a low-energy computer, no data-centre used.

As Israel’s general election looms next week, any idea that it could usher in a government committed to ending the country’s wars has evaporated. Even before the 7 October 2023 attack by Hamas, Israeli political culture was heading to the right, and that has only [accelerated since](https://observer.co.uk/news/international/article/israels-far-right-hard-men-ride-a-wave-of-support-among-the-young?ref=opendemocracy.net). 

Today, almost three-quarters of Israelis want troops to remain in Gaza – 55% of them preferring a long-term military presence in the enclave – while almost 80% want the Israeli Defence Forces (IDF) to continue the war in Lebanon, according to polling. There is also a growing trend for young, secular left-leaning Israelis to leave the country. 

This rightward shift should boost prime minister Binyamin Netanyahu’s chances of re-election, yet he may not emerge victorious. [Recent polls](https://www.jpost.com/israel-election-2026/article-912004?ref=opendemocracy.net) suggest a bloc led by retired General Gadi Eisenkot is the favourite to win, although he is expected to fall short of the seats needed for an overall majority in the Knesset. 

Eisenkot was brought into Netanyahu’s inner war cabinet soon after the 7 October attack, but he resigned after eight months, saying the cabinet had “completely failed” on its objectives, including returning hostages, dismantling Hamas’s ability to govern, and returning evacuated residents to northern Israel.

During the latter part of his military career, Eisenkot was a supporter of the Dahiya doctrine of military control in Lebanon. This promotes responding to a paramilitary uprising with broad-based attacks on the civilian population deemed to support the uprising. That [approach has underpinned the Israeli war on Gaza](https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2023/dec/05/israel-disproportionate-force-tactic-infrastructure-economy-civilian-casualties?ref=opendemocracy.net), leading to the destruction of most of the territory. 

If he takes office now, Eisenkot may curb Netanyahu’s efforts to centralise power – such as the prime minister’s plan to limit the role of the judiciary and other institutions – but is unlikely to deliver much change on security issues. He might exercise more caution over Iran – but that is already a losing battle, at least for now, whatever Donald Trump may claim – and he will likely continue central government support for settlers across the occupied West Bank and whatever level of force the military deems necessary in Gaza and Lebanon. 

That means that regardless of whether Netanyahu or Eisenkot wins the election, what happens next depends very much on what the top brass of the IDF considers the appropriate way forward. It is here that a new analysis of IDF thinking is singularly useful – if thoroughly dismaying. 

[The “New” National Security Concept](https://www.inss.org.il/publication/new-concept/?ref=opendemocracy.net), published by the Israel Institute for National Security Studies (INSS), concludes that Israel must pursue permanent war, with no room for any long-term peace settlement. Given the disaster of 7 October, it says, there is no other way forward. 

The analysis is written by INSS’s executive director, reservist Major General Tamir Hayman, a former commander of Israel’s National Defence College and a former chief of the IDF Intelligence Directorate, although he makes clear that it is not necessarily his personal position, but an assessment of current thinking within the upper echelons of the Israeli military. 

This thinking, he suggests, is underpinned by a series of principles that can be condensed into five themes.

1. **Israel’s Jewish identity is more important than its democracy.** The country’s continued existence as a Jewish state must be prioritised at all costs, even if it means eroding its democratic values.
2. **Peace is a bargaining tool, never the end goal.** A meaningful peace agreement is unattainable as it would require constant reassessment – so any deal struck with Arab actors can only be temporary and a way to achieve other policy objectives. As Hayman puts it: “Politically, ‘peace’ is regarded as a naive concept representing the left-wing ‘peace camp’ which stands in tension with, or in direct opposition to, ‘security,’ which represents the right-wing ‘security camp.’”
3. **Arab states should not exist.** Arab states should not be seen as genuine nation-states, since most are not. The Israeli military instead sees them as “collections of tribes and ethnic groups lacking a shared history and a foundational national vision”. Undermining their stability is to be encouraged, being easier to manage than facing up to strong nation-states. Precedence must be given to offence over defence, involving preventive strikes and wars, and where that is difficult, forward defence may be necessary.
4. **War is a foundational state in which self-reliance is essential.** The decades-long pursuit of peace talks was a mistake that led to 7 October, while preventive war secures success from the start. In these preventative wars, Israel must rely on its own capabilities, as its primary ally, the United States, is a declining power that “will soon abandon Israel” due to its own “ongoing social and political shifts.
5. **The Israeli-Palestinian conflict is a permanent Israeli-Arab conflict.** The “existence of a Palestinian national movement is an inauthentic Western narrative rooted in post-colonial guilt,” Hayman writes. The struggle for Palestine is in practice an Arab attempt to destroy the State of Israel, to which there must be principled opposition. Security comes from control of the entire territory, with settlement playing an important role and, in such circumstances, “Arab inhabitants of the Land of Israel who choose to remain in the Jewish state will be granted residency rights and local self-governance”.

To repeat, Hayman’s analysis, which [should be read in full](https://www.inss.org.il/publication/new-concept/?ref=opendemocracy.net), is not necessarily his personal view, but his understanding of present Israeli military thinking. If accurate, it is easy to find fault with.

Take the suggestion that Israel’s previous pursuit of peace was a mistake that led to 7 October, and it should have instead pursued preventative war to increase security and avoid the attack. In reality, the IDF fought four preventive wars in Gaza between 2008 and 2021, killing over 5,000 Palestinians, but leaving Israel far from secure. Even now, and despite over three years of further war, the IDF cannot occupy what remains of Gaza, where Hamas remains in control. 

Despite such glaring errors, the polling cited earlier suggests the majority of the Israeli public will support the military’s view. Israel is a far more highly militarised state than most Global North nations, with the IDF far more part of society and culture than usual, not least since most Jewish Israelis have served in the force, and many are reservists. 

This means misconduct by the military – both in Gaza and beyond – is ignored or normalised in current Israeli political culture. Such misconduct may extend to the destruction of communities, imprisonment without trial, starvation, torture and the mass killing of tens of thousands of people, many of them children.

Where there is disagreement within the IDF over its conduct, it is treated as criminally irresponsible. Take Netanyahu’s response to the recent documentary, *NAZA*; the prime minister has [ordered the attorney general and the head of the security service to identify and prosecute the anonymous dissenting IDF personnel who gave interviews](https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/oct/12/naza-netanyahu-orders-identification-prosecution-interviewees-documentary-film?ref=opendemocracy.net), accusing them of harming “Israel’s diplomatic and security interests”. 

All of this means that, whoever wins the election next week, Israel has got itself into an insecurity trap from which it is difficult to see a way out. The phrase “impregnable in its insecurity” comes repeatedly to mind as a state that cannot face up to the decades-old reality of its suppression of Palestinian aspirations. 

For now, there is no end in sight – so how might change happen? Ordinary IDF soldiers may begin to feel more angst and a willingness to move out of line, while their seniors could start to recognise that endless war produces a de-civilised society. Another option is that the loss of allies such as Germany, the UK, or a post-Trump United States sways military thinking.

There could also be a shift in public opinion within Israel, especially as international boycotts take hold. The past three years have seen support for Palestinians grow markedly right across the world, and this will not just go away. Already, Israel’s overseas diaspora find themselves in a difficult position, with the country seen as little more than a rogue state across so much of the world – this will worsen if Israel continues to insist on pursuing war, as the INSS analysis suggests.

When Hamas organised the assault and killings of 7 October, it no doubt aimed to shake Israeli society to the core. It has so far failed in that aim, yet Israel has altered, like a building that is losing its foundations. In a recent article for [The Observer](https://observer.co.uk/news/opinion-and-ideas/article/israel-is-strong-scared-and-dangerously-divided-but-change-is-not-on-the-ballot-paper?ref=opendemocracy.net), former Knesset speaker Avraham Burg described Israel as a “pressure cooker, with every candidate turning up the flame.” That is not a good place for any state to be in.

Somos muchas las que vemos cómo la IA va ocupando nuestros espacios de trabajo. Puede ser un asistente muy útil, o un recordatorio de nuestra propia, e inminente, irrelevancia.

Con ese fin, recopila cientos de datos de los trabajadores, y con ellos arma un índice de “riesgo de sindicalización”, como si organizarse por un salario y condiciones dignas fuera un delito, y no un derecho duramente ganado por las y los trabajadores de todo el mundo en los últimos dos siglos.
