### Something is changing in Spain – and tenants are leading the way
URL: https://www.opendemocracy.net/something-is-changing-in-spain-and-tenants-are-leading-the-way/
Last updated: 2026-10-23T12:16:45.000Z
There are moments when a society seems to realise, almost suddenly, that what it had been putting up with for years was not natural. That the hardships faced by millions of people have causes, those responsible and, above all, alternatives. These moments are difficult to identify whilst they are happening, often lost amidst the noise of current affairs, fleeting outrage or yet another protest. But every now and then, something snaps. And what until then had seemed natural begins to feel intolerable.

Perhaps we are going through one of those moments in Spain right now.

## **From individual injustice to collective struggle**

The story of Maricarmen Abascal encapsulates many of the contradictions of our time. An 87-year-old woman, evicted on 23 September from her home of seven decades, a home that had become a business opportunity. She died shortly afterwards, on 7 October. A whole lifetime of work and memories subordinated to the profit expectations of a property investment company. What is truly disturbing about her story is that it could have been just another eviction. Another personal tragedy lost among those of thousands of people evicted every year.

But Abascal decided to fight back, joining forces with the Sindicato de Inquilinas e Inquilinos de Madrid (Madrid Tenants’ Union). She attended one of their meetings, turned her problem into a shared struggle and, alongside her fellow campaigners, began to defend something that went beyond her own home: the right of every person to build a decent and stable home, regardless of whether they are owners or tenants.

There is something profoundly political about this decision. Abascal could have faced her situation alone, seeking an individual solution to a problem that seemed to be hers alone. Instead, she decided to organise. And it was precisely that decision which elevated her conflict to a dimension no one could have imagined. An elderly woman standing up to a property development company became the icon of a trade union struggle capable of putting an investment fund on the ropes, bringing down a government and prompting a general strike, backed by every trade union in the country, to be held on 11 November.

Within 12 days of her eviction, social unrest forced prime minister Pedro Sánchez to call an early election for 29 November after Congress rejected his government's emergency measures, named after Abascal, to tackle housing unaffordability. The real estate company that owned her building also signed an agreement that would have allowed her to return home.

Her death has provoked a sadness and anger that are difficult to describe. But it also forces us to ask what has happened to make her story shake an entire country in this way. The answer cannot be found solely in outrage at injustice. There have been years of tenants organising, collective disputes, training and the building of a social force capable of transforming that outrage into a political conflict of extraordinary proportions.

The Madrid Tenants’ Union has demonstrated over recent weeks something we had forgotten for far too long: that grassroots organisations can exercise power, set conditions and wrest gains from those who seemed untouchable. The agreement reached with Abascal’s landlord, the legislative measures promoted in her name and the mobilisation of millions of people are all expressions of the same reality. When there is organisation, the balance of power shifts.

## **When survival is no longer enough**

For decades we have internalised a particularly cruel form of resignation. We have become accustomed to the fact that working does not guarantee making ends meet, that becoming independent is a privilege, and that our aspirations must always conform to the needs of the market. We have learnt to accept as individual problems the consequences of economic and political decisions that were never within our control.

Housing is probably the most obvious manifestation of this process. We have ended up accepting that an exorbitant proportion of our wages goes towards paying rent to property owners, while our chances of building a life for ourselves dwindle. And we have done so on the promise that, with enough effort, one day we would manage to escape this situation. A promise that, for millions of people, is no longer credible.

However, something is changing in the way we interpret this reality. The discontent sweeping through our cities is beginning to find collective explanations. It is becoming increasingly difficult to convince those who work, study or care for others that their precarious situation is solely down to their personal choices. And when a society begins to recognise that what is happening to it has shared causes, it also begins to understand that it can tackle them collectively.

This is one of the great achievements of the housing union movement: transforming the way thousands of people understand their problems and, above all, how they can resolve them. Union assemblies have become spaces where individual powerlessness finds collective answers. Where people who arrive convinced that nothing can be done discover others facing similar situations and realise that, together, they can begin to change the rules of the game.

## **Organising as the path to a better future**

It is important, however, to avoid an overly triumphalist feeling. Indignation does not guarantee lasting change. History is full of outbursts that seemed to herald profound transformations but ultimately fizzled out without altering the structures that caused them. The strength of the current moment will depend on our ability to turn this mobilisation into stable organisation, new trade unions, greater membership and a social force capable of sustaining struggles long after they have disappeared from the headlines.

That is why what is at stake goes far beyond housing. The difficulty in paying rent, the deterioration of public services, job insecurity and the inability to find time to live one's life are all part of the same struggle. The struggle against a society in which the needs that sustain our existence are increasingly subordinated to the private accumulation of wealth.

And it is precisely at this point that we must broaden our aspirations. Because we have spent too long discussing how to make a situation bearable that should strike us as unacceptable. Perhaps the time has come to return to a much simpler and, at the same time, profoundly radical question. Why should we settle for merely surviving when the resources needed to live better exist?

The answer has political implications. It means understanding that rights are historical achievements, that no substantial improvement in the living conditions of the majority was a gift from those who held power, and that every advance required organisation, conflict and a collective will to transform the status quo.

The general strike for housing and against the high cost of living must open up precisely this horizon: the possibility that conflicts over wages, housing, care and public services are recognised as part of the same struggle, because they are consequences of the same system. It is essential that the union movement once again takes centre stage in the debate over how wealth is distributed and who decides how we live. Because challenging how much we pay just to live is also challenging how much of our lives we are forced to give up so that others can continue to accumulate wealth.

Abascal is no longer with us. And no political victory will ever make up for that loss. But she left us something to be cherished. Her decision to attend a union meeting reminds us that great changes often begin with seemingly small gestures. That organising is a way of regaining control over our lives, and that even those who seem most vulnerable can become the driving forces behind extraordinary transformations. That the union is family, as our comrade said so many times.

Something has changed in Spain. Perhaps we cannot yet gauge its full significance, but one of the great certainties upon which our collective resignation was built is beginning to crumble: the idea that life consists, fundamentally, of mere survival. That we should be grateful to have a job, even if it barely covers the cost of housing. That aspiring to anything more than simply making ends meet is asking too much.

And when a society begins to break away from that idea, the horizon of what it considers possible also shifts. It begins to understand that a better life is a right worth fighting for. That we can aspire to more time, better wages, decent housing and an existence less clouded by fear of tomorrow.

But there is an even more important lesson to be learnt. This shift in consciousness has found a way to organise itself. Abascal found in the Madrid Tenants’ Union the means to defend her home and, alongside thousands of others, sparked a much broader debate on the right to live with dignity.

That is the strength of trade unionism, and the political opportunity before us. We can live better; we have the right to do so, and the only sure way to secure that future is by building the collective power needed to make it happen. Organise, fight and win.
### ‘Nosotros, los pueblos’: la ONU necesita una líder para la gente, no para las superpotencias
URL: https://www.opendemocracy.net/es/onu-secretaria-general-mujer-latinoamericana-independencia-sociedad-civil/
Last updated: 2026-10-22T18:26:55.000Z
Por primera vez en la historia, una mujer latinoamericana encabeza [la carrera para ocupar la Secretaría General de las Naciones Unidas](https://1for8billion.org/straw-polls-2026?ref=opendemocracy.net). Tras más de ocho décadas de liderazgo exclusivamente masculino, cobra fuerza el impulso para romper el techo de cristal en el organismo internacional creado para librar a las generaciones venideras del flagelo de la guerra.

Sin embargo, salir del festejo superficial de la representación obliga a afrontar una paradoja evidente: llegar al cargo más alto de la diplomacia global corre el riesgo de heredar un cascarón vacío, atrapado en un multilateralismo en caída libre y sin margen real frente al veto de las grandes potencias.

La próxima persona al frente de la secretaría general presidirá una ONU fragmentada y sumida en una de sus pruebas más difíciles. Rusia y Estados Unidos, que como [miembros permanentes del Consejo de Seguridad](https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/09/trump-un-chief-candidates-01115653?ref=opendemocracy.net) deberían velar por el mantenimiento de la paz y la seguridad internacionales, vulneran de forma abierta la prohibición de agresión recogida en la Carta fundacional y torpedean la labor de la j[usticia penal internacional.](https://www.icc-cpi.int/news/icc-strongly-rejects-us-sanctions-against-institution?ref=opendemocracy.net)

Mientras tanto, las grandes potencias continúan utilizando su derecho de veto como escudo para la impunidad en conflictos devastadores. Y, al mismo tiempo, la organización arrastra una asfixia presupuestaria sin precedentes ante un retroceso global de libertades civiles, derechos humanos y compromisos climáticos que no admite más dilaciones.

En este contexto de parálisis, la ONU no necesita una burócrata plegada a los designios de los Estados, sino una figura capaz de romper moldes. Quien asuma la secretaría general debe buscar su legitimidad en la representación de las necesidades y anhelos de más de 8.000 millones de personas en todo el mundo, aplicando los principios del liderazgo feminista: escucha activa, valentía, búsqueda de consensos y empatía con las víctimas de los abusos. Como recordó en 1960 el entonces secretario general de la ONU, [Dag Hammarskjöld, ante la Asamblea General](https://www.un.org/depts/dhl/dag/time1960.htm?ref=opendemocracy.net) – cuando el líder de la Unión Soviética, Nikita Jrushchov, exigió su renuncia –, no son las grandes potencias las que necesitan la protección de la ONU, “sino todos los demás”. Décadas después, en 2004, [Kofi Annan demostró esa misma independencia](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2004/sep/16/iraq.iraq?ref=opendemocracy.net) al calificar de ilegal la invasión estadounidense de Irak en una abierta desautorización a Washington.

Para blindar esa valentía frente al chantaje de los países más poderosos, resulta imprescindible plantear dos reformas operativas inmediatas que nuestra alianza global recoge directamente del debate con miles de organizaciones de base.

En primer lugar, la próxima secretaria general debe comprometerse formalmente a ejercer un único mandato voluntario. Esta decisión permitiría liquidar de entrada la cautela excesiva ante las potencias durante el primer periodo de gestión y disipar la tentación de moderar posturas con el afán de asegurarse la reelección.

Los [miembros permanentes del Consejo de Seguridad ](https://www.opendemocracy.net/en/security-council-reform-why-it-matters-and-why-its-not-happening/)ya han demostrado que utilizan su derecho de veto para bloquear las renovaciones de quienes no se someten a sus intereses: [en 1996, Butros Butros-Ghali ](https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1996-11-20-mn-976-story.html?ref=opendemocracy.net)se quedó sin un segundo mandato por el veto explícito de Estados Unidos. Renunciar a la reelección es la única garantía para actuar sin miedo a represalias diplomáticas.

En segundo lugar, la nueva dirección debe reconectar el organismo con la realidad de las calles nombrando, en sus primeros 100 días, a una persona como enviada especial para la sociedad civil. Hoy el espacio cívico está cercado: [solo 75 de los 193 Estados miembros](https://monitor.civicus.org/?ref=opendemocracy.net), que representan apenas el 7% de la población mundial, respetan las libertades de asociación, expresión y manifestación pacífica. Esta enviada especial no puede ser un gesto decorativo; debe tener el mandato expreso de meter en las salas de decisión a los movimientos que hoy enfrentan la represión en el Sur Global, visibilizar las represalias contra los activistas que colaboran con la organización y denunciar el veto injustificado de ciertos gobiernos a las ONG que intentan participar en los trabajos del organismo.

Desde su fundación en 1945 sobre las ruinas de la guerra, los pueblos oprimidos han visto en la ONU la conciencia moral del mundo.

En la segunda mitad del siglo XX, a través de líderes como [U Thant,](https://www.ohchr.org/en/stories/2025/10/remembering-u-thants-legacy-peace-diplomacy-and-human-rights?ref=opendemocracy.net) la organización abanderó las aspiraciones de autodeterminación y dignidad de las poblaciones discriminadas y colonizadas. Durante la crisis de los misiles de Cuba, a comienzos de los años 60, el propio U Thant mantuvo abiertos los canales diplomáticos con Estados Unidos y la Unión Soviética, propuso una tregua que alejó al mundo del abismo nuclear y convenció al líder cubano Fidel Castro para frenar la escalada.

Del mismo modo, Hammarskjöld ideó[ las operaciones de mantenimiento de la paz (los cascos azules) ](https://ask.un.org/faq/209615?ref=opendemocracy.net)durante la crisis del canal de Suez en 1956, yendo más allá de lo previsto en la Carta, y Annan transformó las dolorosas lecciones de Ruanda y Srebrenica en el principio de la [responsabilidad de proteger.](https://www.opendemocracy.net/es/la-responsabilidad-de-proteger-r2p-una-doctrina-golpeada-pero-aun-con/)

Quien aspire a ser la primera mujer al frente de las Naciones Unidas no puede limitarse a administrar una diplomacia de contención. Su liderazgo debe ser audaz, imaginativo y sin miedo al fracaso, dando voz prioritaria a la juventud y a los sectores históricamente excluidos.

Para recuperar la legitimidad perdida y situar de nuevo a “[Nosotros, los pueblos](https://www.un.org/de/node/126501?ref=opendemocracy.net)” en el centro del sistema internacional, la próxima secretaría general necesitará determinación ética y la audacia necesaria para desafiar las ataduras del Consejo de Seguridad.

*Mandeep S. Tiwana es secretario general de la alianza de la sociedad civil CIVICUS y ejerce como representante de la organización ante la sede de la ONU en Nueva York*.
### Amazon usa la IA para impedir que sus trabajadores se sindicalicen
URL: https://www.opendemocracy.net/es/amazon-trabajadores-ia-sindicalizacion-vigilancia-control-derechos/
Last updated: 2026-11-02T18:37:08.000Z
Garfield Hylton, un trabajador de Amazon, sabe desde hace tiempo que la empresa monitorea y registra minuto a minuto su jornada laboral. Cada producto que escanea, cada segundo que transcurre entre un escaneo y otro, cada vez que su escáner está brevemente inactivo: todo se rastrea, se registra y se utiliza para establecer objetivos y predicciones de productividad.

Pero lo que Hylton, de 62 años, no sabía hasta ahora es que Amazon también vigila la posible "disidencia" en el depósito donde trabaja, situado en Coventry, centro de Inglaterra, mediante una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) que revisa las publicaciones de sus trabajadoras y trabajadores en redes sociales y en el panel de avisos del personal de la empresa.

[Documentos internos](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1nosR5ER-VFYiw52si%5FM5kM9ZBfDXmRxJ/view?pli=1&ref=opendemocracy.net) que se publicaron en el marco de una batalla legal entre Amazon y un sindicato canadiense indican que el gigante tecnológico utiliza Atlas, una herramienta interna de predicción basada en IA, para predecir la probabilidad de que sus empleadas y empleados en los depósitos de Estados Unidos, Canadá y el Reino Unido intenten formar un sindicato, organizar una ocupación o llevar a cabo otras "acciones laborales disruptivas".

Los documentos, que parecen ser insumos de capacitación para gerentes de Amazon en Canadá, incluyen un apéndice que indica que Atlas recopila "cientos de datos", como publicaciones en foros de Reddit y respuestas de las personas empleadas a encuestas internas de retroalimentación, así como información más amplia sobre el lugar de trabajo y cualquier acción sindical previa, para asignar a cada uno de sus almacenes un puntaje de riesgo de actividad sindical de entre 100 y 900.

Cuanto menor la puntuación, mayor la probabilidad de que los trabajadores de un depósito – a quienes Amazon denomina “asociados” – se sindicalicen o tomen otras acciones que puedan afectar la productividad o la rentabilidad de Amazon. El documento indica que, para la dirección de la empresa, los puntajess más altos son “mejores”.

Esto “deja en evidencia que para ellos la sindicalización es mala”, dijo a openDemocracy Michael Newman, abogado de la firma legal Leigh Day, con sede en Londres. Newman observó que se trata de “una historia muy diferente” a la que mostraban declaraciones previas de Amazon, en las que aseguraba que no pretendía impedir que sus trabajadores se afiliaran a un sindicato.

Según el puntaje de “riesgo sindical” en la herramienta Atlas, los depósitos estan clasificados en cinco niveles. El Nivel 5 indica "ningún riesgo inmediato percibido" y el Nivel 1 "inminente actividad futura". El documento indica que esta clasificación se puede usar para "orientar las decisiones sobre personal, la planificación de recursos, las acciones estandarizadas y la responsabilidad de mitigar riesgos para la estructura laboral de Amazon".

Un portavoz de Amazon refutó la descripción de Atlas como "monitoreo o vigilancia de empleados individuales", y dijo que "se limita al nivel de actividad de un sitio/edificio". 

La empresa, agregó el portavoz, "no hace seguimiento de las opiniones, afiliaciones o membresías sindicales de empleados individuales", ni de ningún "dato personal", y Atlas no se utiliza para monitorear la disidencia, sino para "ayudarnos a comprender dónde los asociados necesitan más apoyo y para asegurarnos de que estamos abordando los problemas que plantean".

En total, 16 depósitos de Amazon en Estados Unidos, Canadá y el Reino Unido están clasificados como Nivel 1, según el documento. Dos están en el Reino Unido: un centro de distribución robotizada de pedidos de 500 millones de libras esterlinas (670 millones de dólares) en Sutton Coldfield, al noreste de Birmingham (conocido por Amazon como EMA4), y el almacén donde trabaja Hylton cerca de Coventry (BHX4).

![A survey on a screen posed to an Amazon US employee asks to what extent the reader agrees with the statement "I am optimistic about the future of AI at Amazon."](https://storage.ghost.io/c/3f/80/3f804bea-4b2d-4ddf-9ff0-6ec7d0afa5fa/content/images/2026/10/Amazon-AI-question-Facebook.jpg)

Un empleado de Amazon EEUU es encuestado sobre su opinión "acerca del futuro de la IA en Amazon" | Facebook

Hylton, cuyo trabajo consiste en recibir productos en el depósito y despacharlos a otros almacenes, está afiliado al sindicato industrial GMB. En su opinión, la cantidad de datos que Amazon ha recopilado sobre él y sus compañeras y compañeros crea un enorme desequilibrio de poder, ya que los trabajadores solo cuentan con sus propias experiencias para defenderse.

“Esto no es correcto en una democracia…, el empleador no debería interferir”, dijo Hylton a openDemocracy luego de enterarse de la herramienta Atlas a través de su sindicato. “Los trabajadores deberían tener la libertad de decidir si desean sindicalizarse”, dijo. “Si se ejerce vigilancia, se está socavando ese proceso de forma deliberada e intencionada”.

Rachel Fagan, dirigente del sindicato GMB, dijo a openDemocracy: “Estos documentos dejan muy claro que estos sitios son vigilados en busca de actividad sindical. Todo el mundo sabe que Amazon ejerce una intensa vigilancia, pero esto es más personal.

“Amazon está utilizando esta tecnología esencialmente para burlar o manipular a los trabajadores que quieren organizarse \[en un sindicato\]. En esta lucha contra Amazon, nada es equitativo; tienen toda la riqueza, toda la tecnología, todo a su disposición y lo utilizan”, añadió. 

GMB lleva mucho tiempo intentando sindicalizar a los y las trabajadoras de Amazon en el Reino Unido, y estuvo a punto de conseguirlo en Coventry en julio de 2024\. Los empleados de ese depósito fueron los primeros del país en [declararse en huelga](https://www.bigissue.com/news/employment/amazon-workers-stage-first-formal-uk-strike-calling-on-jeff-bezos-to-share-the-wealth/?ref=opendemocracy.net) contra Amazon en enero de 2023 y, seis meses después, alrededor de 2.600 votaron para deicidir si se formalizaba una sección del GMB en el depósito, que se [perdió por solo 28 votos](https://www.gmb.org.uk/news/amazon-faces-legal-challenge-after-workers-rights-vote?ref=opendemocracy.net). 

El sindicato y Foxglove, una organización sin fines de lucro dedicada a la justicia tecnológica, acusaron a Amazon de desplegar "tácticas sucias" en los días previos a la votación, para influir en du resultado. Estas tácticas incluyeron la [contratación masiva](https://novaramedia.com/2024/03/28/amazon-warehouse-in-chaos-due-to-union-busting-dirty-tricks/?ref=opendemocracy.net) de trabajadores no sindicalizados y la colocación de códigos QR en pantallas, mesas de la cafetería y puertas de los baños del almacén, que las empleadas podían escanear para cancelar su afiliación al GMB.

Foxglove y Leigh Day representan a dos trabajadores en un juicio contra Amazon por el uso de códigos QR para “cancelar la afiliación con un clic”, con el argumento de que esta herramienta fue un intento de “intimidar” a los trabajadores para que abandonaran su sindicato.

Los documentos que revelaron la existencia y uso de la IA Atlas se conocieron a raíz de otra demanda, interpuesta por el sindicato canadiense Unifor, y fueron divulgados por el medio estadounidense [Truthout](https://truthout.org/articles/amazon-is-deploying-ai-to-spy-on-its-workers-and-bust-unions-before-they-form/?ref=opendemocracy.net), ante la Junta de Relaciones Laborales de Columbia Británica, el tribunal administrativo sobre derechos laborales y sindicales de esa provincia de Canadá.

La Junta dictaminó que [Amazon violó varias leyes laborales locales](https://www.readthemaple.com/b-c-workers-just-defeated-amazon-in-court-again/?ref=opendemocracy.net). Poco antes, también había fallado que la empresa [había congelado de manera ilegal los salarios](https://www.unifor.org/news/all-news/following-a-million-dollar-ruling-against-amazon-unifor-will-seek-mediation-expedite?ref=opendemocracy.net) de los y las trabajadoras sindicalizadas en un almacén de las afueras de Vancouver.

Rosa Curling, codirectora ejecutiva de Foxglove, considera que el nivel de vigilancia detallado en el documento es "altamente intrusivo", lo que demuestra que Amazon tiene una "política muy deliberada para frustrar la organización y la sindicalización, y está utilizando todo tipo de herramientas para lograrlo".

Curling continuó: “Estamos revisando estos documentos para ver si hay argumentos adicionales que deberíamos agregar a la demanda que ya presentamos por incitación ilegal, o incluso sobre esta violación permanente del derecho de los trabajadores a sindicalizarse, que es un derecho ampliamente reconocido en las leyes británicas”.

Amazon aseguró a openDemocracy que no está utilizando el sistema Atlas en el Reino Unido. Pero no contestó nuestra pregunta sobre si emplea un sistema similar con otro nombre.

Newman, de Leigh Day, dijo: "Ahora que sabemos que Amazon utiliza Atlas, haremos más preguntas sobre qué datos se usan y cómo se obtuvieron esos puntajes". 

Amazon ya fue declarada [culpable de vigilancia "excesiva"](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/business-68067022?ref=opendemocracy.net) de sus trabajadores. En 2022, la Comisión Nacional de Informática y de Libertades de Francia, encargada de controlar la protección de los datos personales y las libertades individuales, multó a la empresa con 32 millones de euros (35 millones de dólares) por violar el Reglamento General de Protección de Datos.

El motivo de la multa fue que Amazon vigilaba la actividad de sus trabajadoras y trabajadores con tanta precisión que se activaba una alerta si permanecían inactivos entre uno y 10 minutos.

Un portavoz del gobierno británico, interrogado sobre si la herramienta Atlas de Amazon establece un nivel de control apropiado de los trabajadores, contestó: “Tanto los empleadores como los trabajadores comparten el interés de que las tecnologías de monitoreo del lugar de trabajo se utilicen de forma transparente, justa, responsable y fiable, para que puedan respaldar la productividad y la buena gestión, manteniendo la confianza en el ambiente laboral. Esperamos que todos los empleadores respeten el derecho de los trabajadores a participar en actividades sindicales legales”. 

El portavoz de Amazon agregó: “La caracterización que hace el sindicato GMB es equivocada. Esto no es vigilancia. Como cualquier empleador responsable, tenemos muchas vías para que nuestro equipo nos retroalimente, y utilizamos esa retroalimentación para identificar dónde podemos mejorar la experiencia diaria de nuestros empleados”.

“Nuestros empleados siempre tienen la opción de afiliarse o no a un sindicato. Lo que más nos importa es la relación directa entre nuestros equipos y sus gerentes: así se escucha la voz de todos, no solo la de unos pocos, y cuando alguien detecta una manera de mejorar su trabajo, podemos actuar con rapidez. En los últimos años hemos logrado avances significativos en aspectos importantes como el salario y la seguridad, y sabemos que siempre hay margen para mejorar. Ese es nuestro objetivo: mejorar cada día”.
### They were victims of domestic abuse. They ended up under arrest
URL: https://www.opendemocracy.net/domestic-abuse-victims-arrested-policing-prisons-injustice/
Last updated: 2026-10-23T14:33:44.000Z
This investigation is the first to quantify how domestically abused women in England and Wales are ending up in handcuffs, while their abusers walk free. It has taken months of research, yet there is still so much more to do. 

Our regular donors make investigations like this possible. If you haven’t had a chance yet, [please consider setting up a regular donation](https://opendemocracy.ghost.io/?ref=opendemocracy.net#/portal) and help Sian to keep exposing this hidden scandal.

Olivia\* had always wanted to be a police officer. It was, she said, “a dream job. I worked very hard at school and university to get the results and do what I always wanted to do, from being quite young."

Yet in December 2020, she was suspended from her job at a force in England, and later charged with misconduct in public office for an act she committed under immense coercion from a man she said was controlling her. 

The seriousness of the offence left Olivia terrified – of prison and, crucially, of losing her daughter Pearl\*. “I’d gone from facing a fine and losing my job, to looking at life imprisonment.” 

“It was like a nuclear bomb went off in our lives,” said her mother Sarah\*. “I saw my daughter being systematically and cruelly dismantled in front of my eyes.” 

Now, for the first time, an investigation by openDemocracy can show that Olivia is one of potentially thousands of women in England and Wales arrested for offences driven by domestic abuse and coercive control. 

Data obtained via Freedom of Information laws revealed that of more than 4,000 women arrested for three offence types commonly associated with coercive control (carrying or handling drugs, weapons and stolen goods), a fifth had been flagged as at risk of domestic abuse. 

Our investigation shows how male violence draws women into the criminal justice system where they are treated as perpetrators, not as victims. Coercive control affects decision-making, risk assessment and perceptions of available choices. Its relationship with women’s arrests challenges the assumption within the criminal justice system that all offending occurs within conditions of genuine freedom. 

Coerced offending is not the only way in which victims are criminalised. Another is via counter-allegations: where abusers accuse their victims of domestic abuse-related crimes. Data from 11 police forces revealed the devastating figure that half of women arrested for coercive control were themselves identified as potential victims of domestic abuse. 

These are not isolated incidents. Abusers are skilled at presenting their victims as perpetrators. As a result, women are [three times more likely](https://static1.squarespace.com/static/5aa98420f2e6b1ba0c874e42/t/68779ea04751767d92c5f9ba/1752669858372/Doing+his+job+for+him+full+report+FINAL.pdf?ref=opendemocracy.net) to be arrested than their male partners at a domestic abuse incident involving counter-allegations, often where they have used force to protect themselves, such as pushing him away. 

Nearly three-quarters of women in prison are survivors of abuse, and [68%](https://figshare.northumbria.ac.uk/articles/report/%5FWho%5Fis%5Feven%5Flooking%5Ffor%5Fit%5FWomen%5Fs%5FExperiences%5Fof%5FCoercive%5FControl%5FCriminalisation%5Fand%5Fthe%5FCriminal%5FJustice%5FSystem/33548542?file=68626486&ref=opendemocracy.net) of women with convictions report having experienced domestic abuse, compared to 25% of the general population. 

Yet the link between domestic abuse and women’s offending has often gone ignored within the criminal justice system.

As Olivia said, “I didn’t realise he was controlling until it was too late.”

## **Coerced into offending** 

“I loved my job,” Olivia said. “I really loved it. I worked really hard, everyone would say that.” 

“And that’s why he targeted you,” said her mum, Sarah, as the three of us talked over coffee in a hotel bar. “He identified you as someone who the job meant a lot to. And so he was able to manipulate you. He was a known master manipulator.”

Olivia met David\*, a fellow police officer, in December 2019\. The pair started talking, “and then he went from zero to 100 in his behaviour,” said Olivia. The “love bombing”, she said, “was so subtle but so effective. He did a number on me. It got really intense.” 

It didn’t take long, Olivia said, for David’s behaviour to turn angry and controlling. She alleges that he would drive past her house in his police car, and if she had friends visiting, demand to know who they were and what she was doing. He called her “all day, every day; it was truly relentless”. 

People noticed what was happening. More than one friend joked that he was her “stalker”. Her dad would ask, “who was constantly calling me non-stop”. At work, David criticised Olivia, saying that she was poor at decision-making. His comments, she said, “undermined my remaining self-confidence.” 

As well as bullying Olivia, David criticised her friends and family, isolating her from her support network, a known tactic of coercive control. “I really believed him. Looking back now, I can’t understand it.” She felt, she said, “completely isolated and alone.” 

David had warned that if she told anyone, “then he would get to know about it. When you are in that thought process, I genuinely thought that saying anything would compromise my career, my life.” She described living “with constant fear”. Not of arrest, but of him. “He said he knew people in high places in the force, which it really seemed he did, as he appeared to be immune from all accountability.”

For Sarah, it was devastating to see David’s abuse and control change her daughter. “I would think: where has my daughter gone?” She remembered how she would “ask Olivia about this David – who is he? What is his story? I noticed that he was a serious problem in the family dynamic.”

Things came to a head when Olivia learned that David was pursuing relationships with other women. She confronted him, and he responded with an angry and abusive message. It was the final straw; with Sarah’s support, Olivia ended the relationship in September 2020\. “My mum managed to make me realise he was dangerous and problematic,” she said. 

A month later, another woman reported David to the police for controlling abuse, and he was arrested and suspended from the force.

Olivia started to move on with her life, focusing on her young daughter. It wasn’t easy; the pandemic made life harder, and she became “exceptionally unwell”. But at least, she thought, she was free of David’s control. 

Then, in December, police officers arrived at Olivia’s house to suspend her from her role as a police constable.

[Hundreds of domestic abuse victims face jail for assaulting policeWomen who call police to help deal with abusive partners are being criminalised for assaulting emergency workers![](https://storage.ghost.io/c/3f/80/3f804bea-4b2d-4ddf-9ff0-6ec7d0afa5fa/content/images/icon/multi_solo-86571c4c-d179-4862-88e8-d918ec58c0c6.png)openDemocracySian Norris![](https://storage.ghost.io/c/3f/80/3f804bea-4b2d-4ddf-9ff0-6ec7d0afa5fa/content/images/thumbnail/A_female_prison_guard_in_HMP_Styal_Credit_In_Pictures_Ltd.Corbis_via_Getty-1776273170703-781de06d-1f43-443b-be78-d341857cf781.jpg)](https://www.opendemocracy.net/en/domestic-abuse-victims-criminalised-tory-law/)

Olivia learnt that while investigating the allegations against David, officers discovered messages on his phone that indicated she had breached data privacy laws earlier that summer. “I couldn’t even remember it,” she said. The abuse “had really ramped up at that point”, and the pressure to give him this information “was constant, relentless and oppressive”. At first, she told the police it simply couldn’t be accurate. “But they showed me the messages, and it was there.”

On the day Olivia committed the offence, David messaged her more than 150 times, threatening to come to her house to cause problems if she didn’t share her computer login. “I know it sounds strange, but I can’t really remember what happened,” Olivia said. “I was so physically and emotionally exhausted, I had so much terrible guilt about working nights and not being there for my infant daughter, and he was relentless.” She later learnt he used her password to access restricted information, including checking up on ex-partners. 

“With coercive and controlling behaviour, someone is purposely going out of their way to remove your ability to make any decisions, to control you and everything you do, in order to keep you there,” said Kris Windsor, a detective superintendent with Avon and Somerset Police. The force has no relationship with Olivia. “Many victims don’t even know what they want to watch on TV because that's not a choice they have, let alone anything else. 

“In many cases victims are operating in that survival mode, so how can they possibly make rational or clear decisions? They can't.”

Olivia was suspended and charged alongside David in October 2021 with misconduct in public office. Her biggest concern was for her daughter Pearl. Both her and Sarah’s eyes welled up as she described the extreme fear that her child would be taken away. “It’s just when we talk about Pearl, the idea of being separated from her,” she said.

Fear of losing their child is the “first impact” of an arrest, said Lina, who works with the Diversion Project, an initiative run by the charity Advance to help women who commit low-level offences towards community-based solutions. “It causes a lot of anxiety and depression.” 

This was the case for Olivia, who became suicidal. But because she was not identified as a victim of domestic abuse, she was not offered any support. Instead, she was forced to attend court sessions alongside her alleged abuser. “It was like they wanted her to kill herself,” Sarah said darkly. 

Olivia’s solicitor said it was one of the worst cases of coercive control he had ever seen. But during the court case, which took place nearly two years later, the prosecution aggressively accused Olivia of lying. The judge described her as “besotted” with David. “They made out they were in it together, like Bonnie and Clyde,” said Sarah. The judge rejected claims that David’s alleged abuse was a factor in Olivia’s actions, and both received equal suspended sentences.

“These women show this dual status of victim and offender, but they are only seen as an offender as the system currently stands,” said Vanessa Bettinson, an academic in criminology at Northumbria University. 

Bettinson warned that “almost any offence could be a result of domestic abuse, for example a woman shoplifting because her perpetrator controls the household’s finances.” She said “the criminal justice process is not geared up towards looking for domestic abuse. So abuse does not feature in the court cases.”

## **Accused of abuse**

Alexsandra\* was running out of options. 

Trapped in a custody battle with her coercively controlling ex-partner Harrison\*, Children’s Services spoke to Alexsandra about her daughter Emily\*, leaving her “seriously worried.” 

“They said they saw me as a weak mother,” she told openDemocracy when we met in her flat over the summer. Anxious that Emily would be taken into care, she filed a police report against her ex in January 2023\. 

Initially, Alexsandra had attributed Harrison’s controlling behaviour to stress. That started to change when he built a complex surveillance system with cameras to monitor when she left the house. He would quiz her on her movements until going out became too stressful. “I started to see my friends less; I was not able to visit my family as often as I would have liked,” she explained. Then his behaviour started to impact her daughter. 

“Emily was unwell and he wouldn’t let me take her to hospital,” Alexsandra said. “He tried to give her medication she was allergic to.” He put temporary tattoos on their infant daughter, causing her distress. “I managed to prevent these things,” she said. “But the consequences of challenging his behaviour were extreme and I was scared.”

Determined to keep Emily safe, Alexsandra left Harrison, eventually filing a complaint with the police alleging coercive control. Harrison was interviewed under caution in summer 2023\. But as the police investigating Alexsandra’s allegations built their case, Harrison hit back – making a counter-allegation of coercive control. “His evidence included that I had reported him to the police,” she said, baffled. 

Documents reviewed by openDemocracy show that Harrison’s police team initially planned to interview Alexsandra under caution, as he had been. However, the police then changed their approach, with the female officer investigating his allegations putting out an alert across the force, stating “can she please be arrested whenever you get the chance.” This is despite having assessed that Harrison was not in physical danger. When the police asked Harrison what outcome he preferred, he said he wanted Alexsandra arrested. 

“I just do not understand why I was treated this way, why I was treated differently to him,” Alexsandra said. “Is it because I am a woman, is it because he is a police officer? I never got an answer to this question.”

[Hundreds of abuse victims arrested when calling for help, new data findsopenDemocracy’s reporting praised at parliamentary event on abuse victims arrested for assaulting emergency workers![](https://storage.ghost.io/c/3f/80/3f804bea-4b2d-4ddf-9ff0-6ec7d0afa5fa/content/images/icon/multi_solo-fa2d8083-2e0d-4111-a7c6-fc1025b59bcc.png)openDemocracySian Norris![](https://storage.ghost.io/c/3f/80/3f804bea-4b2d-4ddf-9ff0-6ec7d0afa5fa/content/images/thumbnail/police-officer-outside-house-GEOFF-CADDICK-AFP-via-Getty-Images-1b7e8283-26dd-4fd2-b20e-6799a85b56f5.jpg)](https://www.opendemocracy.net/domestic-abuse-victims-jail-theresa-may-conservatives/)

The police documents also show that Harrison claimed Alexsandra had harassed him by asking him not to put temporary tattoos on Emily. He urged the police to arrest her, so he could have “respite” from what he termed her “continuous negative actions”.

At no point did the officers in Harrison’s case liaise with their colleagues investigating Alexsandra’s allegations. As a result, her team had no idea that she was under investigation. Nor was Alexsandra aware, telling openDemocracy that “the first I heard of the report was during a family court hearing in December 2023, where he told the judge that I was being investigated for coercive control.” Shocked, she denied it, only to learn later it was true. 

In the same month, the police were ready to present their case to the Crown Prosecution Service, with the aim of charging Harrison with coercive control. At the same time, Harrison was contacting his investigating officer, asking when Alexsandra would be arrested. He only had to wait a few days: in the new year, the police arrested Alexsandra in her flat. 

“They came to my door, I had just put Emily to bed and my parents were visiting,” she recalled. “I was wearing scruffy clothes because I was doing some DIY, and I asked if I could get changed. I know that might sound strange, but I didn’t want to look a mess.” The police refused, putting her in handcuffs and saying that she “should be grateful they put the handcuffs on at the front rather than behind me.” 

The force’s arrest notes, also seen by openDemocracy, corroborate Alexsandra’s account. She later learnt that Harrison had told the police when she would be home, knowing Emily would be there. “I felt so guilty that she would wake up and see this.”

Alexsandra was put in a holding cell, which triggered memories of the surveillance Harrison enforced during their relationship. The arresting officer kept referring to Harrison as “her victim”, something Alexsandra found deeply distressing. “It cuts like a knife through your heart, hearing her say she had to ‘protect her victim’,” she said. 

No charges were ever brought against Alexsandra, who maintains her January 2024 arrest was an extension of Harrison’s abuse, aided and abetted by the police. “The purpose of his life is to exclude me from my daughter’s life,” she said. 

The case against Harrison was dropped in May 2025, when the Crown Prosecution Service declined to press charges, saying there was no realistic prospect of conviction, which is a common outcome for allegations of coercive control.

The police force has since acknowledged that Alexsandra was “let down” and that “more could have been done” to prevent her arrest. But for Alexsandra, there are still so many unanswered questions about the way she was treated by the police. 

“I was treated differently to him,” she said. “They did not see me as human. They considered that he was a police officer but not that I was a victim.”

“Perpetrators do use the system as a tool for controlling coercive behaviour,” said Avon and Somerset’s detective superintendent Kris Windsor, who is training her officers to recognise when “perpetrators groom us.” 

“I need officers to see it and to recognise it, and the system needs to support police officers in doing that,” Windsor said. The force has no link to Alexsandra’s case.

****Methodology:** openDemocracy asked police forces in England and Wales how many women were arrested for three offences commonly associated with coercive control: carrying drugs and weapons, and handling stolen goods, between June 2024 and June 2026\. We identified these offences through conversations with experts and desk research. We then asked how many of the women arrestees “were flagged with a domestic violence marker associated with their current or former partner, where their current or former partner was the perpetrator of domestic violence.” Eighteen forces responded, revealing that of the 4,112 instances of a woman arrested over these offences, 894 involved domestic abuse flags. The figures do not confirm that the offence was committed directly as a result of coercive control. A further three forces – London’s Metropolitan, Avon and Somerset, and Durham – applied a domestic abuse tag to 560 women arrested for the three offences, but did not record if the arrestee was a victim or perpetrator. The remaining 22 forces either refused the request on cost grounds or did not respond. A second Freedom of Information request asked the same question for women arrested for coercive control. The 11 forces that responded had recorded 492 arrests, of which 248 were flagged with a domestic violence marker where the perpetrator was a current or former partner. 

## **Time for change**

A coalition of women’s organisations, including Women in Prison, Hibiscus, Advance and the [Centre for Women’s Justice](https://www.centreforwomensjustice.org.uk/updates/q5hix0f028gbl9buyemmrg5cj7ku1e?ref=opendemocracy.net), which published a landmark report on domestic abuse and women's offending, is urging the government to reform sentencing so that women’s experiences of domestic abuse are considered in relation to their offending. 

Doing so will help ensure that victims of domestic abuse who have committed crimes are recognised as vulnerable and can get the help they need. 

Sentencing reform is just one potential route to improving the criminal justice system’s treatment of victims coerced into offending, or facing counter-allegations.

Other approaches include introducing domestic abuse evidence protocols, modelled on an existing initiative in Western Australia, where the impact of domestic abuse is considered at every stage of the criminal justice process. Right now, “who is even looking for coercive control?” asked Vanessa Bettinson. “These provisions would make it ‘everyone’.” 

The coalition is also calling for better training for frontline services, including police officers, to ensure a more trauma-informed approach when responding to domestic abuse call-outs, to reduce the harms of counter-allegations.

Such work is already underway in Avon and Somerset Police, where domestic abuse makes up one-fifth of the force’s demand. [Project Bright Light](https://www.college.police.uk/research/projects/project-bright-light-transforming-police-response-domestic-abuse?ref=opendemocracy.net) brought together academics with policing to transform the force’s response to domestic abuse, implementing what detective superintendent Kris Windsor terms “a victim-centred, suspect-focused, context-led approach”.

Bright Light, said Windsor, was a “deep dive to understand what are the problems, what are the things that we're seeing, and how can we make it better. We're only going to do that if we think differently.”

Windsor and her team provide training via a continuous improvement plan that will feed into policy and help ensure officers understand the full picture when arriving at a call-out that might involve domestic abuse. 

“We need to ensure that when an officer goes out, they can see the full context: who is the victim, who is the perpetrator. We are looking at changes that will enable officers to have access to more information, so they can make context-based decisions.” This approach, she said, could help assess counter-allegations at domestic abuse call-outs, so both allegations are “not weighted the same”.

Such a change will tackle an issue raised by Advance’s Lina, who said that when it comes to counter-allegations, “if a perpetrator calls the police, they don’t look at the history. They don't look at the impact on the woman. There's actually no one to help her because she's now seen as a perpetrator and not a victim of domestic abuse.”

Windsor offers the force what she describes as “bite-size reflections”, designed to train officers on the complexities of domestic abuse and improve understanding of unhelpful myths about victims and coercive control. 

The focus, Windsor said, “is on what victims need from us. The importance of getting there quickly, getting the basics right, listening to people.”

Ultimately, Windsor said, “we know that primary perpetrators will use our system. And the better we get at identifying it, the less the perpetrators will try, because they know it won’t work. I want perpetrators to know there is no point trying to use our system as a lever of controlling and coercive behaviour. I will come after you and stop you, as this is not a space where you can brazenly come in and start to use us. This is a space where victims and survivors are going to be safe.”

Today, both Olivia and Alexsandra are receiving support from the Centre for Women’s Justice as they try to secure answers for their treatment by the criminal justice system. 

For Olivia, this means a fight to get her conviction overturned. She and mum Sarah have many questions about how David was permitted to remain in post as a PC at all, when numerous people raised concerns about his behaviour. “He was trained to be a taser officer when he was on a force anti-corruption noted person list at the highest threat level,” said Sarah. “How was that allowed to happen?”

They also want answers on an alleged failure by the Police Federation – a staff association representing police officers, who are banned from joining a union – to pass on to investigating officers a dossier the pair compiled after Olivia’s suspension detailing David’s alleged abuse. “Why wasn’t this passed on?” Sarah demands. “It didn’t suit them for her to have answers.”

The abuse has had lasting effects on Olivia’s daughter, although the good news is that she is a happy, confident child and flourishing at school. “She thinks the police are dangerous,” said Olivia. “She won’t even say ‘police’; she says ‘the p-word.’ Even I – if I see a police officer, or a police van, it’s difficult.” 

Alexsandra also continues to pursue justice. She has filed a complaint with the Independent Office for Police Conduct and wants to know why she was arrested while Harrison was not. 

But the impact of her arrest means Alexsandra no longer believes she could report abusive behaviour to the police. “I have learned my lesson,” she said.

### Brazil election: Trump’s ‘Donroe Doctrine’ faces its most decisive test yet
