Last updated: 2026-10-27T17:47:23.000Z
Donald Trump’s goal of regional dominance will be put to the ultimate test this weekend – not in the United States, but at the ballot box in Brazil.

On Sunday 25 October, incumbent centre-left president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva will face off against right-wing opposition senator Flávio Bolsonaro, a key Trump ally and the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, now imprisoned for his role in an attempted coup after losing the 2022 election. Trump called Bolsonaro’s first-round lead [“a great victory”](https://valorinternational.globo.com/politics/news/2026/10/06/trump-calls-first-round-great-victory-for-flavio-sees-close-race.ghtml?ref=opendemocracy.net). [The final polls](https://www.poder360.com.br/poder-eleicoes-2026/saiba-como-estao-lula-e-flavio-a-6-dias-da-eleicao/?ref=opendemocracy.net) have him ahead by one to four points.

Brazil’s presidential election has become a proxy war for the ‘[Donroe Doctrine](https://cepr.net/the-donroe-doctrine-fan-club-kicks-off-in-miami/?ref=opendemocracy.net)’, as the media has dubbed the current White House’s reimagining and expansion of the 19th-century Monroe Doctrine that sought to exert aggressive US dominance over the Western Hemisphere. 

The younger Bolsonaro’s victory is key to Washington’s aims of securing a reliable supply of oil, minerals, electricity and territory for data centres – and in particular to preserving US supremacy over China in a conflict underpinned by two pillars.

The first is ‘energy dominance’, declared on the day of Trump’s inauguration. A[ council based in the White House](https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/02/establishing-the-national-energy-dominance-council/?ref=opendemocracy.net) has been tasked with extending the lifespan of fossil fuels, supplying factories with the cheap energy that the tariff policy aims to bring home, tying allied countries to US gas, and controlling a strategic point for oil imported by China. 

The second is the computing infrastructure, ranging from chips to data centres and cutting-edge artificial intelligence models. In Beijing in May, Washington negotiated over soy, Boeing aircraft and rare earths, and [refused to back down on export controls for chips](https://orfonline.org/research/selective-cooperation-enduring-rivalry-reading-the-trump-xi-summit?ref=opendemocracy.net).

Both pillars converge on the voracious energy consumption of AI. The method is the same in both cases: when Washington cannot secure a central position within a network, it seizes control of the chokepoint.

The American continent is where this method proves most cost-effective, as shown in Venezuela. In August, six months after arresting Venezuela’s president, Washington announced it has [majority control of 65,000 million barrels](https://www.opb.org/article/2026/08/29/trump-says-u-s-has-entered-deal-with-venezuela-to-take-control-of-65-billion-barrels-of-oil-reserves/?ref=opendemocracy.net) of the country’s oil through a joint venture that gives it [a 35% stake](https://www.opendemocracy.net/es/venezuela-eeuu-petroleo-delcy-rodriguez-donald-trump-betancourt-maduro/) – and the right to purchase a further 20% of production at cost price – for 100 years. The White House credited the agreement with having re-established the Monroe Doctrine. 

[Venezuela: From Monroe’s Doctrine to Trump’s Jungle LawThe US has a long history of military intervention in Latin America, but never before has it been so brazen![](https://storage.ghost.io/c/3f/80/3f804bea-4b2d-4ddf-9ff0-6ec7d0afa5fa/content/images/icon/multi_solo-78862492-5292-4376-8c45-050881ff945a.png)openDemocracyDiana Cariboni![](https://storage.ghost.io/c/3f/80/3f804bea-4b2d-4ddf-9ff0-6ec7d0afa5fa/content/images/thumbnail/GettyImages-2253891367_1-1776273162376-8a88533c-f5b9-4530-b187-4ce8d2168289.jpg)](https://www.opendemocracy.net/en/venezuela-coup-trump-united-states-monroe-doctrine-maduro/)

The following month, US secretary of state Marco Rubio undertook a tour of the Andean countries, [returning with a framework agreement on minerals and a nuclear memorandum with Colombia](https://www.as-coa.org/articles/trump-latin-america-rubio-courts-allies-colombia-ecuador-and-peru?ref=opendemocracy.net), while Peru joined the ‘Shield of the Americas’, an informal coalition of governments aligned with the White House in the war against cartels.

But Brazil is the missing piece of the jigsaw. The country is Latin America’s largest oil producer, [with 3.8 million barrels a day by 2025](https://diariodocomercio.com.br/economia/producao-petroleo-gas-pais-cresce-133-2025-bate-recorde/?ref=opendemocracy.net), mostly from fields in the Atlantic Ocean. It has [the world’s second-largest reserves of rare earths](https://www.netzerocircle.org/news/brazil-retains-second-place-in-global-rare-earth-reserves-despite-revised-estimates?ref=opendemocracy.net). Its electricity grid is [89% clean](https://ember-energy.org/countries-and-regions/brazil?ref=opendemocracy.net), which is why it already hosts [half of Latin America’s data centre capacity](https://www.spglobal.com/energy/en/news-research/latest-news/energy-transition/082726-brazil-leads-latin-america-in-data-center-growth-on-renewable-energy?ref=opendemocracy.net).

The Trump administration wants access to these resources, and has shown just how far it is prepared to go to get them.

### **Learning to coerce**

In July last year, Trump imposed a [new 50% tariff on imports from Brazil](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2025/08/05/2025-14896/addressing-threats-to-the-united-states-by-the-government-of-brazil?ref=opendemocracy.net), blaming Jair Bolsonaro’s trial, which he described as “insidious attacks on free elections”. The US Treasury also [sanctioned the Brazilian Supreme Court judge](https://home.treasury.gov/news/press-releases/sb0211?ref=opendemocracy.net) leading the case against the former president. 

The court found Jair guilty anyway. The prices of Brazilian coffee and beef rose in US supermarkets, and the US withdrew the tariff in November without Brazil having made any concessions. In February, the US Supreme Court overturned the legal basis for the tariff.

Washington’s second attempt drew lessons from its first. In July this year, the US imposed [a new 25% tariff](https://ustr.gov/about/policy-offices/press-office/press-releases/2026/july/ustr-section-301-action-brazils-unreasonable-acts-policies-and-practices?ref=opendemocracy.net) on Brazil, this time with 1,000 exemptions on things the US needs to buy: coffee, beef, orange juice, aeroplanes, and more. A lower tariff may sound better but can amount to greater coercion; as the smaller of the two economies, Brazil cannot afford to lose access to the US market and is more likely to absorb the financial shocks than cease trading.

The new tariff followed what the US described as a [“year long investigation”](https://ustr.gov/trade-topics/enforcement/section-301-investigations/section-301-brazils-acts-policies-and-practices-related-digital-trade-and-electronic-payment?ref=opendemocracy.net) into whether Brazil’s “acts, policies, or practices are unreasonable or discriminatory and burden or restrict US commerce”. 

Washington said the investigation looked at Brazilian court rulings against US social media companies; patents; the US’s access to Brazil’s ethanol market; illegal deforestation; and Pix, the free instant payment system managed by Brazil’s Central Bank. Pix has [processed more Brazilian transactions than credit and debit cards combined since 2023](https://finance.yahoo.com/news/instant-payment-system-pix-poised-100506841.html?ref=opendemocracy.net), exposing the threat that a public system can pose to the global card networks dominated by US firms Visa and Mastercard.

As economics professor [Guilherme Klein noted in a column for openDemocracy](https://www.opendemocracy.net/brazil-election-lula-flavio-bolsonaro-trump-tariffs-shape-race-future-democracy/), one of the US’s demands in the tariff relief negotiations was a guarantee that ‘political dissidents’ – a reference to Jair Bolsonaro – could participate in the election. While Brasília said it will not concede to this and the majority of the US’s demands, it indicated that it has not ruled out agreements on Brazil’s rare earths and hyperscale data centres. The latter is to this empire what the railway concession was to the previous empire: the physical clause of subordination, inscribed on foreign territory and sustained at the expense of others.

[The US is inciting a global fight against ‘far-left’ protestUnder the pretext of fighting ‘terrorism’, the Trump administration warned allies to back its political persecution![](https://storage.ghost.io/c/3f/80/3f804bea-4b2d-4ddf-9ff0-6ec7d0afa5fa/content/images/icon/multi_solo-2d72807e-6ba6-47df-8821-4699f880e548.png)openDemocracyCentro de Estudios Legales y Sociales (CELS)![](https://storage.ghost.io/c/3f/80/3f804bea-4b2d-4ddf-9ff0-6ec7d0afa5fa/content/images/thumbnail/GettyImages-2286382591-dc997406-ef10-43b9-b3f2-47f9a8457f64.jpg)](https://www.opendemocracy.net/united-states-far-left-terrorism-protest-activism-direct-action-trump-rubio-argentina/)

The US has also pursued another avenue of coercion. In May 2026, Washington [added Brazil’s two largest criminal groups to its list of terrorist organisations](https://agenciabrasil.ebc.com.br/en/internacional/noticia/2026-05/us-designates-two-brazilian-factions-terrorist-organizations?ref=opendemocracy.net), which exposes any Brazilian official or bank – including Pix – deemed to be providing them with “material support” to secondary sanctions. Flávio Bolsonaro has said he requested this move, which came three days after he met with Trump. The US’s [National Counter-Terrorism Strategy](https://www.armytimes.com/news/pentagon-congress/2026/05/07/white-house-casts-cartels-jihadists-and-left-wing-extremists-as-significant-and-pervasive-threats-to-us/?ref=opendemocracy.net), published the same month, also included “[violent left-wing extremists](https://www.opendemocracy.net/es/eeuu-propone-una-cruzada-de-persecucion-politica-a-escala-global/)” alongside cartels and jihadists. 

Brazil, Mexico and Colombia [were excluded](https://www.stimson.org/2026/trumps-shield-of-the-americas-leaves-many-outside-the-armor/?ref=opendemocracy.net) from the Shield of the Americas when Trump launched it in March. Colombia, which has since elected a new right-wing president, joined last month. Brazil entered the hemispheric war on terrorism not as an ally, but as a theatre of operations.

### **How Brazil withstood sanctions**

Coercion is a relationship, not an instrument. 

In the 1980s and 1990s, Brazil had a dollar-denominated debt, held just weeks’ worth of foreign exchange reserves, and followed the economic policies of the International Monetary Fund. 

Today, Brazil is Latin America’s largest economy. It has long [paid off its debt to the IMF](https://www.imf.org/external/np/sec/pr/2005/pr05275.htm?ref=opendemocracy.net), and its reserves exceed [$350bn](https://www.bcb.gov.br/content/publicacoes/relgestaoreservas/GESTAORESERVAS202603-relatorio%5Fanual%5Freservas%5Finternacionais%5F2026.pdf?ref=opendemocracy.net), having benefited from two decades of growing Chinese demand for its raw materials. In 2000, the US still accounted for[ 24% of Brazil’s exports, compared to less than 2% for China](https://datamarnews.com/noticias/exports-to-china-from-us1-billion-in-2000-to-more-than-us87-billion-today/?ref=opendemocracy.net). By 2025, China accounted for[ 29% and the US for 11%](https://istoedinheiro.com.br/ranking-paises-exportacoes-brasil-importa-2025?ref=opendemocracy.net). 

What remains susceptible to coercion is the network layer: the international dollar payment system, the platforms, the chips. The path leading from a 50% tariff to a more targeted 25% one and to the designation of terrorist organisations leads towards these chokepoints.

Argentina illustrates the alternative. The country has negative net reserves and was forced to agree to a $20bn currency swap with the US Treasury in late 2025 – a bailout that Trump said [depended on president Javier Milei’s party winning the midterms](https://www.cnn.com/2025/10/14/politics/javier-milei-president-trump-argentina?ref=opendemocracy.net). Milei’s party won the elections; Argentina received the money and, months later, signed a trade deal and an agreement with Trump allowing the US access to Argentina’s critical minerals. 

The structure determines the choice. A Milei in Brasília could not hand over what Brazil does not owe. He could concede what cannot be taken from him.

### **Dependence as a project**

Washington did not invent coups d’état in Brazil; it just made them cheaper. 

In 1964, the US ambassador coordinated with the plotters of a military coup that overthrew Brazil’s democratically elected progressive government and led to a 21-year dictatorship. [Declassified documents show](https://nsarchive2.gwu.edu/NSAEBB/NSAEBB465/?ref=opendemocracy.net) a US naval task force waited on the high seas during the coup, while Lyndon Johnson’s White House sent congratulations to the new government the day after the military seized control [without waiting to see what the Brazilian Congress would do](https://history.state.gov/historicaldocuments/frus1964-68v31/d207?ref=opendemocracy.net). 

The US may have lent its support, but the military officers, newspapers, industrialists and middle classes who sought to overthrow the government in the name of ‘tradition, family and property’ were Brazilian. Similarly, in 2016, president Dilma Rousseff was impeached based on an anti-corruption operation whose Brazilian prosecutors secretly [co-operated with the US Department of Justice](https://www.intercept.com.br/2020/03/12/lava-jato-driblou-governo-ajudar-americanos-doj/?ref=opendemocracy.net). Each coup d’état was followed by a handover: oil, mining, state-owned banks, labour rights.

I have termed this pattern ‘dependence as a project’ – that is, subordination chosen by a ruling class because it costs less than sharing power and wealth at home. The elites, who imagine themselves to be white in a country that is not, call for intervention against governments whose voters are darker-skinned and poorer than they are. US Latinophobia finds its distorted mirror image in the ‘Americanism’ of the Latin American elite.

Former MP Eduardo Bolsonaro, Flávio’s younger brother, moved to the US in early 2025 to lobby for sanctions against judges in his own country, and [was in June this year convicted in absentia of courting US ⁠interference in his father’s coup plot trial](https://www.upi.com/Top%5FNews/World-News/2026/06/17/8871781723855/?ref=opendemocracy.net). Weeks after his conviction, Flávio [asked the US Trade Representative to suspend the tariff for 180 days](https://www.thestar.com.my/news/world/2026/07/06/in-race-against-lula-flavio-bolsonaro-lobbies-washington-to-delay-brazil-tariff?ref=opendemocracy.net), until after the elections. A tariff now, he wrote, “would hand the current Brazilian government precisely the political victory it has been engineering”. His programme for the Amazon – involving illegal gold mining on Indigenous lands – is a Brazilian contribution to the extractivist agenda that Trump would gladly accept and which, in this case, he did not even have to ask for. 

A tariff hits Brazilian exporters and the jobs behind them. Flávio’s submission [did not ask for it to be lifted, only delayed](https://www.poder360.com.br/poder-eleicoes/flavio-pede-aos-eua-pausa-de-180-dias-antes-de-novas-tarifas/?ref=opendemocracy.net), with automatic reinstatement if talks failed, and it offered Washington a new negotiator immediately after an opposition victory. For the Bolsonaros, the tariff was never about Brazilian jobs. It was about who would govern.

### **Elections as a stage for the doctrine**

The Monroe Doctrine does not suppress elections. It orchestrates them. 

In June, Colombia elected a Trump-backed president [by a single point](https://www.aljazeera.com/amp/news/2026/6/22/colombian-right-wing-candidate-de-la-espriella-wins-tight-presidential-race?ref=opendemocracy.net), after Washington sanctioned the incumbent. In Venezuela, oil started flowing to US companies – with a Washington-approved Chavista running the government and the state oil company – months after US forces [detained president Nicolás Maduro](https://www.cnn.com/2026/01/03/americas/venezuela-explosions-intl-hnk?ref=opendemocracy.net). Democracy was the wrapping paper; the concessions were the gift.

In Brazil, we have not returned to 1964, because 1964 failed when it was tried again. The attempted coup of 2022/23 collapsed, and the Supreme Court tried its perpetrators despite US sanctions. The far right was unable to seize power by force, so it is trying to take it through the ballot box, and Flávio has already promised his father amnesty if he wins.

Washington, which cannot influence Brazil’s financial stability, is instead exerting pressure on its voters. Since Trump resumed power, Washington has put pressure on elections held in Chile, Honduras, Bolivia, Colombia and Peru, but none has faced tariffs linked to a court case, sanctions against a judge, inclusion on terrorist lists affecting the financial system, and a candidate who has called for all of this.

The pressure is cruder than during the Cold War because the US is weaker: no loans, no promises of modernisation, just tariffs and a candidate. What is coming to an end is an empire – the institutional form that US power bestowed upon itself when it could afford to seek consent. What persists is the imperial relationship, without the emperor’s new clothes.

### **What each outcome will bring**

For Latin America, a victory for Flávio Bolsonaro would signal that the last counterweight has fallen into line and the right-wing wave is firmly underway. For Washington, it would signal that a client government can deliver what coercion failed to. 

Brazil’s oil reserves and electricity grid would become part of a hemispheric energy bloc, while its rare earths would be refined for US supply chains, and Pix and other platforms would be opened up to US card networks and tech companies. Data centres would be powered at Brazil’s expense. The designation of criminal groups as terrorist organisations would remain a permanent lever over Brazilian finances.

And Bolsonaro would tell anyone attempting a coup on the continent that, if they lose, they can expect an amnesty. The Senate elected on 4 October will, from February onwards, have[ 49 right-wing senators](https://www.poder360.com.br/poder-eleicoes-2026/senado-sera-dominado-pela-direita-a-partir-de-2027/?ref=opendemocracy.net) – exactly the number needed to amend the Constitution and enshrine an amnesty that the Federal Supreme Court could overturn if it were passed as ordinary legislation.

The central two pillars of Trump’s strategy have been called into question by a war waged to secure the Strait of Hormuz, which has turned that maritime passage into an Iranian toll road, and Chinese open-weight AI models circumventing controls on chips.

A victory for Lula would confirm that the doctrine has failed to make coercion work in the face of Brazil’s size and diversified trade, nor has it succeeded in getting its client governments to abandon Chinese demand; nor has it managed to win the elections that mattered most to it. Brazil would remain where it has been: trading with everyone, without aligning itself with anyone – a democracy that condemned its coup plotters despite foreign sanctions and voted against those who called for them.

There is a lesson here for the left. Bolsonaro failed to secure an outright majority at the election’s first round, but still led over Lula by almost two percentage points; Brazilians did not vote with sovereignty in mind – they voted with their debts in mind. Half of all adults are behind on their bills due to the world’s highest real interest rate. The fiscal rule upheld by Lula froze the main state benefit for poor families (Bolsa Família) at 600 reais a month from March 2023 until September, when the government [decreed a 15% rise](https://jornalgrandebahia.com.br/2026/09/presidente-lula-assina-decreto-que-reajusta-bolsa-familia-em-1504/?ref=opendemocracy.net), paid from 19 October. That very rule is the reason why Brazil’s ties with China have not led to any development strategy.

In concrete terms, sovereignty is also the ability to navigate between poles of power. It wins elections when it delivers results. Last week, the Senate passed an amendment to end the six-day working week by [75 votes to one](https://www.otempo.com.br/politica/congresso/2026/10/14/flavio-e-base-de-lula-votam-a-favor-do-fim-da-escala-6x1-veja-como-se-posicionou-cada-senador?ref=opendemocracy.net) – something seven out of 10 people in Brazil want, and which Bolsonaro’s party had blocked for months until, with the polls tied, Flávio [announced he would vote for it](https://www.cartacapital.com.br/politica/apos-visitar-o-pai-flavio-bolsonaro-anuncia-voto-a-favor-do-fim-da-escala-6x1/?ref=opendemocracy.net). 

A fourth term for Lula that breaks with his own austerity measures would make independence from Washington something even a shop assistant could feel. That is how dependence ceases to be a project.

*Pedro Paulo Zahluth Bastos is a professor of political economy at the University of Campinas, Brazil.*
### Periodismo en México: Anatomía de un silencio
URL: https://www.opendemocracy.net/es/mexico-periodismo-asesinatos-persecucion-crimen-organizado-gobierno-censura-silencio/
Last updated: 2026-10-20T16:20:52.000Z
*Esta es una versión traducida y editada de un artículo* [*publicado originalmente*](https://lab.imedd.org/en/journalism-in-mexico-anatomy-of-a-silence/?ref=opendemocracy.net) *en*[ *iMEdD*](https://www.imedd.org/?ref=opendemocracy.net) *(Incubator for Media Education and Development), bajo licencia Creative Commons 4.0 Internacional. Hemos obtenido permiso de los autores de las fotografías y de las personas fotografiadas para reproducir las imágenes.*

Los periodistas Carlos Castro, Roxana Guzmán, Luis Ángel López, Alex Serna, Josué Martínez, Alejandro Leyva Aguilar y Ricardo Zúñiga fueron asesinados este año en México; seis de ellos en apenas tres meses, entre junio y septiembre,[ según el Comité para la Protección de los Periodistas](https://cpj.org/2026/08/amid-spike-in-journalist-killings-in-mexico-cpj-urges-federalizing-cases-to-end-impunity/?ref=opendemocracy.net) ([CPJ](https://cpj.org/?ref=opendemocracy.net)).

Estas son solo las últimas víctimas de una crisis que tiene al menos dos décadas en México. Desde 2006, han sido asesinados [153 periodistas](https://cpj.org/data/killed/2025/?status=Killed&type%5B%5D=Journalist&type%5B%5D=Media%20Worker&motiveConfirmed%5B%5D=Confirmed&motiveUnconfirmed%5B%5D=Unconfirmed&cc%5Ffips%5B%5D=MX&start%5Fyear=2006&end%5Fyear=2026&group%5Fby=location&ref=opendemocracy.net), según el CPJ. En 2025, se cometieron nueve asesinatos – una cifra solo superada por los 12 asesinatos de periodistas en Gaza –, según [datos de Reporteros sin Fronteras (RSF)](https://rsf.org/en/2025-deadly-year-journalists-where-hate-and-impunity-lead?ref=opendemocracy.net).

Se trata de números más propios de lugares que viven guerras, como las de Yemen, Ucrania o Gaza, según explicó a iMEdD el representante del CPJ en México, Jan-Albert Hootsen. "México se enfrenta a una crisis permanente de libertad de expresión", dijo Hootsen, para quien los últimos asesinatos son una continuación de la tendencia de violencia contra los periodistas mexicanos que se prolonga desde hace años.

Sin embargo, Hootsen señaló un "matiz importante": en la historia política reciente de México, la violencia tiende a disminuir en el primer año de una nueva presidencia, para dispararse en el segundo, especialmente contra periodistas y defensores de los derechos humanos.

Como en 2026 se cumple el segundo año de mandato de la presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum, Hootsen cree que los recientes asesinatos podrían formar parte de ese "repunte del segundo año". Su hipótesis apunta a la relación entre los grupos del crimen organizado y quienes ocupan cargos públicos: cada nuevo gobierno trae consigo nuevos cargos, lo que brinda a los grupos criminales la posibilidad de explorar potenciales relaciones de colaboración con ellos antes de recurrir de nuevo a la violencia. Para el segundo año, estas dinámicas de poder se han reestructurado en gran medida, "todas las piezas están colocadas", y la violencia comienza a aumentar de nuevo, dijo Hootsen.

*Periodistas y trabajadores de medios asesinados en México entre 2006 y septiembre de 2026\. Fuente: CPJ | Elaboración de datos y gráfico: Pavlos Methodios/iMEdD | Creado con Datawrapper*

## ¿Quién ataca a la prensa mexicana? 

Si bien el papel de los grupos del crimen organizado en México ya es bien conocido, Hootsen señaló que "los funcionarios públicos suelen formar parte de esta dinámica". Los actores estatales fueron responsables de algo más de la mitad de los ataques documentados contra la prensa en 2025,[ según el informe anual de la organización Artículo 19](https://articulo19.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Estructuras-del-Silencio-Informe-Anual-2025-A19-MXCA%5Fcompressed.pdf??ref=opendemocracy.net).

"Confío más en estos tipos, los delincuentes, que en la policía", dijo Ulises Escamilla, un productor y enlace local de Ciudad de México que ha trabajado para medios internacionales como la BBC y Sky News. "Los delincuentes dan su palabra y la cumplen si tú cumples la tuya", añadió.

Escamilla recordó que, hace unos dos años, lo siguió una persona que él supuso era un agente de policía. En aquel momento, estaba trabajando con VICE en un documental sobre la [muerte de Jesús Ociel Baena](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2023/nov/13/mexico-magistrate-lgbtq-jesus-ociel-baena-found-dead?ref=opendemocracy.net), el primer magistrado abiertamente no binario de México, que había muerto en su domicilio, en el estado central de Aguascalientes.

La persona – que llevaba un tiempo siguiendo a Escamilla – desapareció cuando este intentó fotografiarla. "Estoy seguro de que, en ese caso, el gobierno podía estar relacionado con el asesinato", afirmó Escamilla, quien cree que esa fue la razón por la que lo seguían.

A menudo, funcionarios públicos y cárteles actúan en connivencia. "En algunas partes del país, es difícil distinguir dónde terminan las organizaciones criminales y entran en escena las autoridades locales, porque a veces se trata de las mismas personas", dijo Armando Talamantes, director ejecutivo de [Quinto Elemento Lab](https://quintoelab.org/?ref=opendemocracy.net), una organización mexicana sin ánimo de lucro dedicada al periodismo de investigación.

El reciente crimen de la periodista Roxana Guzmán en el estado oriental de Veracruz es un ejemplo.[ Cuatro de los ocho sospechosos detenidos por su asesinato son agentes de la policía municipal](http://lemonde.fr/en/international/article/2026/07/04/in-mexico-journalist-roxana-guzman-who-was-abducted-in-june-has-been-found-dead%5F6755135%5F4.html?ref=opendemocracy.net#:~:text=Eight%20people%20were%20arrested%20and,the%20journalist%2C%20the%20statement%20added.) y están acusados de proporcionar apoyo logístico a la organización criminal que secuestró a la periodista el 2 de junio de 2026 antes de matarla.[ A principios de agosto, la Asamblea Legislativa de Veracruz levantó la inmunidad de Raúl González Martínez](https://elpais.com/mexico/2026-08-06/el-congreso-de-veracruz-quita-la-inmunidad-procesal-al-alcalde-implicado-en-el-asesinato-de-la-periodista-roxana-guzman.html?ref=opendemocracy.net), alcalde de Ixhuatlán del Sureste (una localidad cercana a Nanchital, donde trabajaba Guzmán), allanando el camino para su enjuiciamiento por su presunto papel como cerebro del secuestro y asesinato de Guzmán.

![](https://storage.ghost.io/c/3f/80/3f804bea-4b2d-4ddf-9ff0-6ec7d0afa5fa/content/images/2026/10/data-src-image-bdf6fdf9-d5aa-4301-809c-c979db238d7f.jpeg)

Ulises Escamilla, productor y enlace periodístico mexicano |Foto cortesía de Ulises Escamilla

## **Una impunidad de 98%**

Tanto si los autores son funcionarios públicos como si son cárteles de la droga, hay un factor que une todos estos ataques, según Hootsen: la impunidad. "Lo que todos tienen en común es que se producen en lugares donde la probabilidad de que los agresores sean realmente castigados por sus delitos es prácticamente nula", dijo. Las cifras son abrumadoras: alrededor de [98% de los delitos mortales contra la prensa mexicana quedan impunes](https://articulo19.org/periodismoenriesgo/??ref=opendemocracy.net). "La impunidad fomenta los ataques contra la prensa", afirmó.

¿Las autoridades mexicanas son incapaces o no están dispuestas a procesar a los agresores? "Si existe la voluntad política, el Estado mexicano es muy capaz de perseguir a los agresores", dijo Hootsen. Lo que provoca esta impunidad, según él, es la indiferencia del Estado.

En algunos casos – cuando hay funcionarios públicos implicados – existe incluso un incentivo para llevar a cabo una operación de encubrimiento. El gobierno tiende a actuar más cuando el ataque se convierte en un "problema de relaciones públicas". Eso es lo que ocurrió en el caso de Guzmán, cuando el [vídeo de su secuestro](https://www.youtube.com/shorts/lNzZBebR5Mc?ref=opendemocracy.net) se difundió ampliamente por las redes sociales, lo que provocó lo que Hootsen denomina "una tormenta en la opinión pública mexicana".

## **Menos acceso a la información y presión legal**

Lilia Saúl Rodríguez, periodista de investigación con sede en Ciudad de México y que trabaja para el Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting ([ΟCCRP](https://www.occrp.org/en?ref=opendemocracy.net)), mencionó otro gran reto para el periodismo en el país: "El acceso a la información en México se está convirtiendo en letra muerta", dijo.

Aunque el derecho a la información pública se amplió a principios de la década de 2000 con la aprobación de leyes de transparencia, la situación se ha deteriorado desde entonces. A finales de 2024, la administración de Sheinbaum [decidió desmantelar el INAI](https://www.wilsoncenter.org/article/elimination-inai-blow-transparency-and-accountability-mexico?ref=opendemocracy.net) (Instituto Nacional de Transparencia, Acceso a la Información y Protección de Datos Personales), que, como explicó Talamantes, había sido un organismo independiente que actuaba como "árbitro" cuando los organismos estatales denegaban solicitudes de información pública.

Quinto Elemento ha empleado reiteradamente la ley de transparencia para solicitar información. Talamantes recordó haber solicitado documentos públicos sobre el [escándalo de corrupción de la constructora brasileña Odebrecht](https://quintoelab.org/project/el-expediente-secreto-de-odebrecht??ref=opendemocracy.net) (la trama de sobornos de la empresa en 10 países latinoamericanos). La fiscalía finalmente aceptó entregar los documentos en 2021, [pero a cambio de un pago de 1,7 millones de pesos mexicanos](https://quintoelab.org/project/fgr-pide-millones-pesos-transparencia-odebrecht?ref=opendemocracy.net), unos 93.000 dólares de la época. Los periodistas recurrieron ante el INAI, que concluyó que los documentos [debían entregarse de forma gratuita](https://quintoelab.org/project/fgr-desclasifica-expediente-odebrecht-lozoya?ref=opendemocracy.net).

Hoy en día, esto ya no es posible, según Talamantes. El control del acceso a la información pública que ejercía el INAI se transfirió a un órgano dependiente del Ministerio Anticorrupción, lo que genera muchas dudas sobre su independencia.

Mientras tanto, el registro del INAI, que incluye los archivos de todas las solicitudes de información y sus correspondientes respuestas, ha "desaparecido en algún limbo en la nube, al que el público ya no tiene acceso", dijo Saúl Rodríguez.

El acoso judicial también está pasando factura a los medios de comunicación mexicanos, según Talamantes.[ Artículo 19](https://articulo19.org/las-leyes-como-mecanismo-de-censura-aumento-del-acoso-judicial-contra-periodistas-en-mexico/?ref=opendemocracy.net) documentó que, entre el 1 de enero y el 31 de julio de 2025, cada cuatro días se abría un nuevo procedimiento judicial o administrativo contra periodistas y medios.

Quinto Elemento se ha enfrentado a demandas en el pasado, aunque a ninguna en los últimos años. Su estrategia para prevenir desafíos legales consiste en obtener asesoramiento jurídico de organizaciones sin ánimo de lucro, como Artículo 19 y[ Propuesta Cívica](https://propuestacivica.org.mx/?ref=opendemocracy.net), al tiempo que participa en[ Reporters Shield](https://www.reporters-shield.org/?ref=opendemocracy.net), un programa de afiliación que proporciona asistencia jurídica y apoyo financiero a las redacciones que se enfrentan a demandas destinadas a silenciar sus reportajes.

![](https://storage.ghost.io/c/3f/80/3f804bea-4b2d-4ddf-9ff0-6ec7d0afa5fa/content/images/2026/10/data-src-image-94f80a15-1220-4635-b31e-e00b2efd8815.jpeg)

Armando Talamantes, director ejecutivo de Quinto Elemento Lab | Foto cortesía de Armando Talamantes

## **Zonas de silencio**

En algunas partes de México, las presiones que soportan los periodistas han adoptado una forma aún más extrema. Sometidos a violencia e intimidación, principalmente del crimen organizado, las y los periodistas deben restringir o abandonar por completo la cobertura de temas delicados, como el narcotráfico, un fenómeno conocido como "zonas de silencio" o "desiertos informativos".

La ciudad de Iguala, en el estado de Guerrero, suroeste del país, es una de estas zonas de silencio. “Por un lado, debido a la fuerte presencia del crimen organizado, pero, por otro, también a causa de la connivencia entre las autoridades gubernamentales y el crimen organizado", dijo Jonathan Cuevas, periodista de la ciudad que ha trabajado para medios mexicanos e internacionales.

Para la gran mayoría de los periodistas, esto significa abstenerse de cubrir temas que perjudiquen los intereses del crimen organizado y, en ocasiones, de ciertos funcionarios públicos, según Cuevas. "La autocensura es obligatoria para todos nosotros", dijo. La zona de silencio tiene una larga historia, muy anterior a que Cuevas comenzara a trabajar como periodista en 2007, observó.

El periodismo se ve gravemente limitado en casi la mitad del territorio de Sinaloa, estado del noroeste de México, y en algunos de sus municipios no hay ningún periodista local, [según un estudio de 2025](https://iniciativasinaloa.org.mx/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/Voces-en-resistencia-1.pdf?ref=opendemocracy.net) realizado por[ Iniciativa Sinaloa](https://iniciativasinaloa.org.mx/?ref=opendemocracy.net), una organización sin ánimo de lucro con sede en la capital estatal, Culiacán.

La versión oficial del estado alega falta de interés comercial en estos municipios, según Sibely Cañedo, periodista residente en la ciudad de Mazatlán y coordinadora de proyectos de Iniciativa Sinaloa. Sin embargo, los periodistas y activistas entrevistados por Iniciativa Sinaloa también señalaron la presencia del crimen organizado como un factor determinante.

[Una violenta guerra por el control del territorio](https://www.crisisgroup.org/rpt/latin-america-caribbean/mexico-united-states/112-sinaloas-war-splinters-fighting-crime-mexico-under-us-threat?ref=opendemocracy.net) que estalló en septiembre de 2024 entre facciones rivales de uno de los mayores grupos de narcotraficantes del mundo, el Cártel de Sinaloa, constituye el contexto más reciente de esta zona de silencio. Sin embargo, el fenómeno es mucho más antiguo. Cañedo cree que empezó al menos en 2008, cuando otra escisión dentro del Cártel de Sinaloa desencadenó un recrudecimiento de la violencia en todo el estado.

En ocasiones, el acceso a determinados territorios de Sinaloa está completamente restringido. Según Cañedo, periodistas no pueden ingresar a ciertas comunidades porque se lo impiden puestos de control ilegales custodiados por grupos armados. Ella misma no pudo llegar a una comunidad del municipio de Choix, al norte de Sinaloa, en julio de 2026, ya que nadie estaba dispuesto a llevarla allí debido a su trabajo como periodista.

Incluso en Culiacán, donde se mantiene un cierto grado de pluralidad, los periodistas recurren habitualmente a la autocensura cuando se trata de informar sobre actividades del crimen organizado. "No pueden mencionar los nombres de los grupos criminales. Solo se refieren al crimen organizado, pero no dicen ‘Los Chapitos’ ni ‘La Mayiza’", dijo Cañedo, en referencia a las dos facciones rivales dentro del Cártel de Sinaloa.

Las consecuencias para quienes siguen cubriendo temas delicados van desde amenazas y palizas hasta el desplazamiento y el asesinato, según Cuevas. Él mismo tuvo que marcharse de Iguala y vivir en Ciudad de México entre 2020 y 2023 tras recibir mensajes y una llamada, en octubre de 2020, con amenazas de asesinarlo y dejarlo "desmembrado en la calle o en algún canal", aseguró. En 2023, Cuevas se vio obligado a regresar a Iguala porque el desplazamiento le hizo perder el 70% de sus ingresos.

En 2021, mientras Cuevas estaba en Ciudad de México, “funcionarios municipales de Iguala [habían encargado a un grupo del crimen organizado](https://www.facebook.com/watch/?v=4491309794260578&rdid=Qjcq9zBesuViCuVT) que me asesinara, y ofrecían una suma de 25.000 pesos mexicanos \[1.200 dólares en aquel momento\], según una serie de capturas de pantalla que me enviaron por WhatsApp", dijo Cuevas. Él relacionó este intento con sus reportajes sobre irregularidades financieras en el ayuntamiento de Iguala. En Guerrero, su familia estaba siendo acosada y vigilada, "hasta el punto de que unos hombres armados interceptaron a mi hermana y a su pareja, los amenazaron y les entregaron un mensaje para mí mientras les apuntaban con armas a la cabeza", recordó.

Las zonas de silencio han alterado la relación entre periodistas y público. "La gente no confía en los medios de comunicación", dijo Aarón Ibarra, periodista independiente y residente en Culiacán. El público sospecha que los medios podrían estar mintiendo o incluso omitiendo por completo la cobertura de ciertos temas, indicó.

Para Hootsen, del CPJ, las consecuencias afectan a la propia democracia. "Cada vez que se acercan unas elecciones, sería muy positivo que los votantes supieran si los candidatos son corruptos o están en la nómina del crimen organizado. Si desaparece el periodismo crítico, se priva a los votantes de esa capacidad de saber, porque los periodistas ya no informan".

## **¿Rendición de cuentas o censura?**

En un entorno extremadamente peligroso para la libertad de prensa en México, [una nueva normativa](https://articulo19.org/no-corresponde-al-estado-mexicano-el-monitoreo-y-calificacion-de-la-conversacion-publica/?ref=opendemocracy.net) destinada a proteger los derechos del público ha abierto otro frente. Los [Lineamientos Generales para la Protección de los Derechos de las Audiencias](https://portal.crt.gob.mx/ConsultaPublica/Detalle/15?ref=opendemocracy.net), aprobados a finales de agosto por la Comisión Reguladora de las Telecomunicaciones, exigen a las emisoras de radio y TV, entre otras cosas, contar con mecanismos de reclamación y defensores de los derechos de la audiencia.

La versión final de la normativa, que recibió muchas críticas, es menos restrictiva que [la propuesta inicialmente](https://latamjournalismreview.org/articles/audience-rights-or-media-control-government-proposal-sparks-debate-in-mexico/?ref=opendemocracy.net) por la administración de Sheinbaum, pero la cuestión clave que plantea su inminente aplicación parece seguir siendo la misma: cómo garantizar que los esfuerzos por reforzar la rendición de cuentas de los medios de comunicación no se conviertan en otro instrumento para presionar a los periodistas.

En agosto, la asesora jurídica del gobierno mexicano, Luisa María Alcalde, [presentó una lista de periodistas, medios de comunicación y figuras de la oposición](https://www.eluniversal.com.mx/nacion/luisa-alcalde-presenta-lista-de-periodistas-y-politicos-que-difunden-mensajes-anti-4t-oposicion-ve-mensaje-de-intimidacion/?ref=opendemocracy.net) que, según ella, atacan al gobierno de Sheinbaum. "En ella figuran los nombres completos \[de los periodistas\] y sus cuentas en redes sociales, lo que los convierte en objetivos directos y facilita que la gente los ataque", advirtió la periodista del OCCRP, Saúl Rodríguez.

Sin embargo, en medio de este panorama cambiante de presiones, "el periodismo mexicano ha demostrado ser increíblemente resiliente", dijo Hootsen. "Los periodistas suelen ser resilientes, suelen sentir una gran pasión por su trabajo y son muy tenaces. Cuanto más se los presiona, más resisten. Y es realmente difícil para un gobierno o para las redes criminales acabar por completo con el periodismo, porque siempre resurge".
### Latin America is the first target in Trump's global plan. It won't be the last
URL: https://www.opendemocracy.net/project-2025-trump-heritage-foundation-latin-america-argentina-chile-far-right/
Last updated: 2026-11-06T09:17:00.000Z
When Kevin Roberts, the president of the US-based Heritage Foundation, took the podium at the [fourth regional meeting of the right-wing Madrid Forum](https://encuentroregional.foromadrid.org/faq/?ref=opendemocracy.net) in Santiago, Chile, last month, he and his foundation had much to celebrate.

In much of Latin America, until last decade a bastion of progressive and centre-left, far-right governments have surged to power on platforms that seemed inspired by Project 2025, an authoritarian blueprint, accompanied by a [900-page manual](https://static.heritage.org/project2025/2025%5FMandateForLeadership%5FFULL.pdf?ref=opendemocracy.net), that first came to prominence in the US president Donald Trump’s second presidential run in the United States.

Project 2025 did not start the global ultra-conservative surge that continues to claim fresh victories in Latin America and Europe. Across the world, a network of organisations – largely based in the US, Europe and Latin America, and rooted in Christian nationalism – has sought to fund, train and develop conservative activists in an effort to roll back rights and civil liberties. The Heritage Foundation is one of many organisations working to advance a conservative agenda. 

But in his speech, Roberts said his foundation was “proud to have helped unify this movement”.

Roberts was far from the biggest draw at the conference. Speakers at the Madrid Forum included Chile and Argentina’s far-right presidents José Antonio Kast and Javier Milei. But his presence in Santiago and his regional itinerary reveals the expanding influence of Project 2025 south of the US border.

The Chilean capital was not the only destination in Roberts’ whistle-stop tour of Latin America last month. He also visited Colombia, where he met with senior members of government in the newly elected president Abelardo de la Espriella and offered to provide “training” to Colombian civil servants. 

President de la Espriella – who has been photographed posing the bodies of alleged militants slain by his security forces and whose government Roberts praised as “impressively bold” – took office at a religious ceremony at which he vowed to “put God at the centre of every decision”.

In Peru, Roberts’ visit was around the same time as the country’s new president Keiko Fujimori – the daughter of one of Latin America’s most brutal dictators, Alberto Fujimori – met with US secretary of state Marco Rubio in Lima and announced her support for the ‘[Shield of the Americas](https://www.connectas.org/analisis/el-comando-sur-la-nueva-frontera-del-poder-de-washington-en-america-latina/?ref=opendemocracy.net)’, an informal alliance between the US and like-minded governments to enable intelligence-sharing and expand Washington’s military action in the region, ostensibly to combat ‘narco-terrorism’.

Here, Roberts [emphasised the strategic importance of Latin America in realising the *‘America First’*](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DdHwwXshXt1/?utm%5Fsource=ig%5Fweb%5Fcopy%5Flink&stkn=NTc4MTIwNjQ2YQ==) policy.

### **God’s Plan**

Project 2025, and its 900-page [*Mandate for Leadership*](https://static.heritage.org/project2025/2025%5FMandateForLeadership%5FFULL.pdf?ref=opendemocracy.net), was drafted by the Heritage Foundation with the support of more than 100 Christian nationalist organisations in the US with the aim of laying out an agenda for Donald Trump’s second presidential term.

Its agenda includes[ a hard line on immigration](https://democracyforward.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/FINAL-PRESS%5F-Project-2025-Fact-Sheet-on-Immigration.pdf?ref=opendemocracy.net), with widespread arrests and deportations and [the gradual erosion of the right to asylum](https://democracyforward.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/FINAL-PRESS%5F-Project-2025-Fact-Sheet-on-Immigration.pdf?ref=opendemocracy.net); [tax cuts for the wealthiest](https://www.americanprogress.org/article/project-2025s-tax-plan-would-raise-taxes-on-the-middle-class-and-cut-taxes-for-the-wealthy/?ref=opendemocracy.net); the[ dismantling of environmental](https://earthjustice.org/article/what-project-2025-would-do-to-the-environment-and-how-we-will-respond?ref=opendemocracy.net) and[ health protections](https://www.apha.org/topics-and-issues/public-health-under-threat/project-2025?ref=opendemocracy.net);[ restrictions on trade union rights](https://betterinaunion.org/project-2025?ref=opendemocracy.net);[ the withdrawal of benefits for single-parent families](https://itep.org/effort-to-make-single-parenthood-more-expensive-project-2025/?ref=opendemocracy.net); the [dismantling of public education](https://globalextremism.org/post/project-2025-climbs-the-education-mountain/?ref=opendemocracy.net); an absolute ban on abortion (even invoking an[ anti-obscenity law from 1873](https://www.americanprogress.org/article/project-2025s-distortion-of-a-reconstruction-era-law-could-enact-a-national-abortion-ban/?ref=opendemocracy.net)) and[ restrictions on access to contraception](https://nwlc.org/all-the-ways-project-2025-wants-to-undermine-birth-control-access/?ref=opendemocracy.net).

While Trump publicly distanced himself from the project, his administration [passed around half of its policies](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c5yvvjw8pdvo?ref=opendemocracy.net) in his first year in office. Rights organisations responded with alarm, with the Global Project Against Hate and Extremism [warning](https://globalextremism.org/reports/project-2025-goes-global/?ref=opendemocracy.net): “Within this worldview, pluralism, gender equality, and LGBTQ+ rights are treated not as democratic principles but as threats to a divinely ordered society.”

Yet, as Roberts’ Latin America tour demonstrated, Project 2025 is not only being used to roll back rights in the US. Its[ policies are being implemented by right-wing presidents](https://www-opendemocracy-net.translate.goog/en/trump-project-2025-argen
